#9059. Spike Jonze Brings Impressionism to His Portraits of Alysa Liu for ‘LIFE’ Magazine

Spike Jonze Brings Impressionism to His Portraits of Alysa Liu for ‘LIFE’ Magazine

LIFE Magazine has begun publishing regularly again after a 26-year hiatus, and Olympic figure skater Alysa Liu is on the cover this week, photographed by Spike Jonze.

Jonze is a filmmaker and photographer who made his name in the world of skateboarding before moving into music videos and directing films like Being John Malkovich.

Liu won the gold medal for Team USA at this year’s Winter Olympics in Milan-Cortina. Given Jonze’s skating background, he was a great pick to shoot Liu on the ice and LIFE has released a video detailing exactly how he did it.

Jonze says he set out to capture what it feels like for Liu when she’s out there on the ice. “The first thing I thought would be really cool was to do these really dreamy, streaky photos,” Jonze explains.

Jonze achieved this by using a tungsten lamp (constant light source) and a strobe light synced to his camera.

Using a two-second exposure, Jonze pressed the shutter at the exact moment he wanted to capture. The long exposure meant he could then “streak” the camera, either by panning or zooming, making additional ghostly images of Liu, allowing for creative expression.

“I kind of moved the camera around to almost paint with the color of her dress or her face and it becomes very impressionistic,” Jonze says.

Jonze then made a second setup, which was borrowed straight out of his skateboarding days.

“It was multiple strobes of a trick caught on one frame of film,” he says. “So again, I would do a two-second shutter, but I would take the flash off-sync from the camera and just manually press the button and go ‘pop, pop, pop, pop, pop’ and pop the strobe as many times in the two seconds as it can recharge in.”

The resulting image captures an entire trick or sequence from beginning to end on a single frame.

“The first time I did it was with Natas Kaupas or Jeremy Klein, who were pro skaters in the late 80s and so I thought I would try to do a version of that, but more impressionistic,” Jonze explains.

“I wanted it to be all on top of each other so you couldn’t quite see the beginning and the end. It was a blur of the different shapes that she takes when she’s going through the course of the tricks. And that’s what these photos are; they’re sort of the dream images of Alysa’s world of skating.”

LIFE has published the interview with Liu and Jonze’s photos on its website.

#9056. Frieze Artist Award reimagines endangered Lebanese site

Dala Nasser’s installation Adonis River (2023). The Lebanese artist is the recipient of the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, for which she is creating a new installation for the fair’s atrium Courtesy Frieze Abu Dhabi

One of Lebanon’s most intriguing archaeological sites is the inspiration behind the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, given to the fast-rising Lebanese artist Dala Nasser to create her installation Qubbat Duris. The work takes its name from a 13th-century Muslim shrine near Baalbek, northeast of Beirut, which is composed from the ruins of two separate ancient Roman sites: granite columns from Baalbek’s Temple of Jupiter hold up limestone sarcophagi from a necropolis.

Placed in the atrium of the fair, the work will comprise a timber frame evoking Qubbat Duris’s structure, with fabrics covered in charcoal rubbings of the remaining ruins and painted with ash, raw clay and terracotta draped over it.

Nasser is best known for her archaeological frottage paintings—made using the surfaces of endangered historical sites—which consider the artist’s role in reproducing, and bearing witness to, history and landscape.

Though Nasser is not the first artist to engage with Qubbat Duris, she points out, many of her antecedents are problematic. “The site has already been extensively imagined and reimagined in art historical painting,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “From Orientalist depictions to the backdrop to one of Gertrude Bell’s most circulated photographs, taken in costume on horseback.”

Similar works of Nasser’s—such as Adonis River (2023) and Wedding at Qana (2024)—have also taken as their subjects “landscapes that loom large in historical painting but look nothing like the landscape itself in Western Asia, either overwhelmed by Orientalist tropes or painted as scenes of European countryside, betraying the artists’ lack of knowledge and limits of imagination”, she says. “I am trying to make paintings that are truthful to the landscape.”

The question of “truth” pertains to Qubbat Duris’s position as a site that reflects the layered cultural histories and religions of Lebanon. “It exists as a palimpsest from the second century AD until today, carrying all of the traces in between,” Nasser says.

Meanwhile, the role of evidence and recording in Nasser’s practice also considers the risks of erasure faced by much of Lebanon’s cultural artefacts, particularly from Israel’s longstanding and continued occupation of the country. On 15 October 2024, Qubbat Duris sustained slight damage from Israeli airstrikes; previously during the 2006 Israel-Lebanon war, an Israeli airstrike dislodged one of the shrine’s stones. “I’m interested in how a place like Qubbat Duris carries physical evidence of everything it’s endured, including scars of damage,” Nasser says.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November

#9055. This New Website Aims to Document Every Film Camera Ever Made

This New Website Aims to Document Every Film Camera Ever Made

Film camera repairer and enthusiast Pierro Pozella has launched a website with an ambitious aim: to document every film camera ever made.

Pozella of PPP Cameras has spent 15 years repairing, restoring, and selling analog cameras. So there is perhaps no one better placed than him for this project that he calls the Camera Index.

“I’ve always wanted to find a way to organize that knowledge into something accessible to everyone,” Pozella tells PetaPixel.

“There’s a tremendous amount of information out there, but it’s scattered across old books, websites, forums and manuals. Some cameras are incredibly well documented, while others have very little information available.”

Camera Index features illustrations, technical information, instruction manuals, and external links to sample shots.

Pozella says that it is easy for technical knowledge of something niche like film cameras to disappear — Camera Index is his attempt at centralizing that knowledge into one resource.

“I also wanted something that was straightforward to navigate. Being autistic, I personally find information much easier to process when it’s clearly organised and presented without unnecessary clutter. That has influenced how I’ve approached the design and structure of the website,” he says.

“Ultimately, I wanted to create the sort of resource I wish had existed when I first started working with cameras.”

Pozella has already included 1,300 cameras on the Camera Index, and that’s just for the launch. The website is a long-term project that he intends to work on for a number of years.

“Nobody seems to have a definitive answer to exactly how many analog camera models have been produced,” he says.

“We’re talking about well over a century of camera manufacturing, with thousands of manufacturers producing everything from mass-market consumer cameras to extremely obscure models that were only manufactured in small quantities.

“The number quickly grows when you start considering different variations, regional models and cameras sold under alternative brand names.”

Pozella has opted for illustrations rather than photos since he doesn’t have access to every single camera model ever made.

“The Camera Index is about making camera information accessible and signposting people to useful information under one roof,” he explains.

“As well as the practical limitations of having to source and photograph over 10,000 plus cameras — I opted for illustrations as they provide a standardized way of identifying each camera. They function as simple visual references or thumbnails for each camera and are not intended to replace photography or be the main focus of the project.”

Pozella says the Camera Index is for anyone with an interest in analog photography: from people completely new to it and looking to buy their first camera, to seasoned collectors looking for information about a particular model.

“More than anything, I hope that the Camera Index will become a lasting reference for analog photography,” he adds.

“A lot of the knowledge surrounding older cameras exists in ageing publications, discontinued websites or in the heads of people who have spent their lives working with them. As time passes, there’s a genuine risk that some of that information will disappear.

“I’d like to help prevent that by bringing together as much information as possible and making it freely accessible.”

“In the longer term, I also want to expand the archive beyond cameras themselves, documenting accessories and more obscure photographic equipment,” he adds.

“I’m already building a useful links section to connect visitors with camera repairers, specialist shops, manuals and other valuable resources. I think it’s important that the archive doesn’t just document cameras, but also helps people find the information and services needed to keep using them.

“If Camera Index eventually becomes somewhere people instinctively go when they want to learn about an analog camera, then I’ll feel I’ve achieved what I set out to do.”

#9052. The Lomo72 Is a Stylish Half-Frame Film Camera for Just Under $80

The Lomo72 Is a Stylish Half-Frame Film Camera for Just Under $80

Lomography has announced the Lomo72, a new 35mm half-frame analog camera that captures 72 frames per 36-shot roll.

This is actually Lomography’s second half-frame camera of the year, following the Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Half Frame the company unveiled in July. Like that camera, the new Lomo72 records a vertical 17x24mm image on half of a standard 35mm frame, fitting two photos onto a single frame. Where a typical 35mm camera captures a horizontal 36x24mm shot, the Lomo72 captures two 17x24mm ones.

As Lomography says, photographers can get creative with this. They can capture 72 “normal” shots or create diptych compositions on a single frame, pairing two thematically related shots side by side. Lomography also notes that the vertical orientation of the Lomo72’s photos is “perfect for sharing on social media.”

The Lomo72 separates itself further from the Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera through its build quality and design. While both cameras sport a relatively similar squarish look, the Lomo72 opts for a more robust design and a glass lens. Although Lomography hasn’t revealed the complete optical formula, it confirmed that the 27mm lens features a fixed f/8 aperture. Thanks to its half-frame design, the 27mm lens offers a 40.5mm-equivalent field of view. The lens can focus as close as 0.4 meters (1.3 feet).

The Lomo72 has a decidedly old-school design, like many of Lomography’s cameras. It’s quite stylish, though it is presumably made mostly of plastic given its $79 price tag. It has an optical viewfinder and, in good news for all the trendy shooters out there, a traditional flash. The built-in flash also works with colorful gel filters.

The camera features a 1/100s shutter speed, though it also includes a bulb mode for long exposures. It also has a tripod thread, works with a cable release, and supports multiple exposures.

Analog photography can be quite pricey, so a big advantage of a half-frame camera like the new Lomo72 is that photographers get twice as many shots per roll of film. While users give up a bit of resolution and image area with the format, it is certainly a more economical way to shoot film.

“The Lomo72 Half-frame 35 mm Film Camera is inspired by the golden era of half-frame photography, made for every unhurried, imperfectly perfect moment. It is the kind of camera that makes you smile before you’ve even taken a photo,” Lomography says. “This camera is made for letting the mind wander. It’s about finding creativity everywhere and capturing real moments, ones that you get to relive in nostalgic comfort when you develop the roll.”

The Lomo72 comes in black and silver colorways, though both feature the same central silver area around the viewfinder and lens. Both versions are just $79.

For customers in Asia-Pacific, the Lomo72 begins shipping this month. For everyone else, including photographers in Europe and North America, shipments start in December. Lomography says that worldwide delivery will occur before December 24, making the Lomo72 a potential Christmas present for analog photographers.

#9050. Cameraman Beaten and Equipment Stolen in Attack on Journalists at French Protests

Cameraman Beaten and Equipment Stolen in Attack on Journalists at French Protests

A cameraman was badly beaten and his camera equipment stolen while covering protests in France this weekend.

Warning: The following video contains content that some may find upsetting.

On Saturday, a team of journalists from French television and radio network BFM TV was attacked by protesters in Lyon. Demonstrations have taken place across France over the past two months over school funding, social inequality, and rising living costs.

💥 | Des journalistes de @BFMTV ont été pris à partie par des manifestants à #Lyon Vue sur des angles différents https://t.co/72meLvWc19

— Gabriel BOYER (@BoyerGabriel042) November 14, 2026

According to a report by Le Monde, the television crew consisted of two journalists, including a cameraman, and two security guards. Local government officials in France say protesters “threw themselves upon them” in an attack that was “very violent.” Riot police then launched “an offensive” to protect the journalists.

In an open letter published on X (the platform formerly known as Twitter), one of the BFM TV journalists who was attacked says she “truly feared for (their) lives.” According to a report by French news outlet 20 Minutes, the BFM TV journalist says her cameraman was thrown to the ground and beaten, with some protesters shouting threats before stealing his camera. She also says he spent five hours in the emergency room. The extent of his injuries was not specified.

“My cameraman was violently thrown to the ground and then beaten. Some even shouted ‘Burn him!’ before snatching his camera. He spent five hours in the emergency room,” she recounted.

“You can dispute what journalists say. You can criticize their work. You can even hate them. But you don’t hit them,” she added.

Another freelance journalist who witnessed the incident says the cameraman was hit several times and that his camera was smashed and stolen. The journalist also says he had to remove his press badge to avoid being targeted and was struck twice in the foot during the incident.

“It was very, very violent. One of them was hit several times. His camera was thrown to the ground, broken, and then they picked it up and stole it. He was in shock,” the freelance journalist, who publishes under the name Medave Prod on social media, tells Le Monde.

“I had to take off my press badge myself, otherwise I would have been lynched too,” the journalist says, adding that he had been hit “twice in the foot.”

An investigation into “intentional violence committed by a group and with faces concealed” was opened, the Lyon prosecutor’s office announced on Sunday. The investigation also covers “damage to private property,” referring to the journalists’ equipment.

#9048. Manuscript filled with 16th-century apocalyptic visions could fetch £1 million at auction

A page from the The Book of Miracles (around 1552) CHRISTIE'S IMAGES LTD. 2026

Giant comets blaze across dark skies, volcanoes rain down fire on hapless cities, floods rage and the moon turns blood red in a spectacular 16th-century manuscript coming up for auction at Christie’s in London, estimated between £700,000 and £1m.

The Book of Miracles, with 167 vivid watercolours illustrating natural phenomena—real and imagined—and scenes from the Old and New Testaments, was completed in Augsburg, Germany, around 1552. It is attributed to Hans Burgkmair the Younger and Heinrich Vogtherr the Younger, painters, print makers and designers who had separate workshops but sometimes collaborated on important commissions.

A page from the The Book of Miracles (around 1552) CHRISTIE'S IMAGES LTD. 2026

Eugenio Donadoni, the director and international specialist in Medieval and Renaissance manuscripts at Christie’s, called the book an exquisite work, with its illustrations as vibrant after nearly 500 years as the day they were made. “Beyond their extraordinary beauty, these images offer us a glimpse into how people in the 16th century made sense of a world that could often seem mysterious and unpredictable. Today, we might understand a comet, an eclipse or an earthquake through science, but in the Renaissance these phenomena could be interpreted as signs of something greater, even as warnings of what was to come,” he says. “The manuscript brings together the remarkable visual imagination of the period, the events that captured people's attention and provoked their wonder and fear. Nearly 500 years later, these images remain as compelling as ever.”

A page from the The Book of Miracles (around 1552) CHRISTIE'S IMAGES LTD. 2026

The book is included in a series of sales of works from the Mickey Cartin collection. Cartin, who is based in Connecticut and built the electrical supply firm founded by his grandfather into a national company, began collecting in the 1980s across many categories, including books and manuscripts, old master paintings, furniture and contemporary art. Artnews included in him in its Top 200 Collectors list every year from 2007-13. He bought The Book of Miracles in 2010, three years after it was rediscovered in a private collection in Bavaria, and it acquired wider fame when the art publisher Taschen published a facsimile edition in 2013.

The manuscript, part of the sale An Alchemy of Ideas: Works from the Mickey Cartin Collection, will be on public view at Christie’s King Street sales room in London on 4-10 December, before the sale on 10 December.

#9046. Redesigned Voigtländer Nokton 35mm f/1.2 Coming Soon to Sony and Nikon Cameras

Redesigned Voigtländer Nokton 35mm f/1.2 Coming Soon to Sony and Nikon Cameras

Cosina has announced the Voigtländer Nokton 35mm f/1.2 Aspherical lens for full-frame Sony and Nikon mirrorless cameras.

Slated to launch next month, the Voigtländer Nokton 35mm f/1.2 Aspherical is a new and improved version of Cosina’s Voigtländer VM-mount 35mm f/1.2 lens, which the company notes is prized for its “excellent performance and compact design.” The new version has been optimized for mirrorless cameras while maintaining the image quality and silky-smooth bokeh of its VM-mount inspiration.

As is often the case with Voigtländer lenses, the E-mount and Z-mount versions sport slightly different designs but have the same internal components and optical formula. The E-mount lens has a relatively smooth barrel shape with diamond-knurled focus and aperture control rings. The Z-mount lens, on the other hand, has a scalloped focus ring with vertical ridges and simple ridges on its aperture ring. It also trades red accents for yellow ones, embracing Nikon’s classic color scheme.

In both cases, the lens is compact. The E-mount lens is just over 60 millimeters (2.37 inches) long and weighs 380 grams (13.4 ounces). The Z-mount lens is 62.4 millimeters (2.46 inches) long and weighs 390 grams (13.8 ounces). Both versions accept 58mm filters.

Both manual-focus lenses can focus as close as 0.3 meters (0.98 feet), which results in a maximum magnification ratio of just 1:5.8. Macro lenses these are not. Cosina says that the manual focusing experience is top-notch thanks to a precise, full-metal helicoid unit and high-quality grease. The company promises “appropriate torque.”

Optically, the lens features nine elements arranged across seven groups in front of a 12-bladed aperture diaphragm. There are two aspherical elements, and Cosina promises high-resolution performance across the entire frame, even wide open at f/1.2. The company adds that “color shifts are well controlled,” meaning that the lens minimizes chromatic aberrations.

As for bokeh, a key selling point for an f/1.2 lens like this, Cosina says that out-of-focus areas are “drawn naturally and point light sources, etc., are drawn as soft round bokeh rather than as polygonal shapes.” The aperture ring can also be de-clicked, which should bode well for video applications.

The Cosina Voigtländer Nokton 35mm f/1.2 Aspherical lens will begin shipping next month. While global pricing has not yet been revealed, Asobinet notes that the Japanese price is 140,000 yen, which is around $880. Final global pricing may vary, of course. It is worth noting that the Nokton 35mm f/1.2 Aspherical IV for Leica M-mount is $999 right now thanks to a $150 holiday discount. There’s no word yet on a Canon RF-mount version, although Cosina does make a handful of Voigtländer lenses for Canon mirrorless cameras.

Image creditsCosina Voigtländer. Sample photos by Maconyan and Thom Yoshida.

#9044. How to Film and Edit a High Energy Event Sizzle Reel

How to Film and Edit a High Energy Event Sizzle Reel

Earlier this fall, I wound up at a music festival in Southern California called Same Same But Different. I was there helping film a documentary with a friend and decided to actually document my whole process.

I used to regularly film festival sizzle reels and promos over a decade ago, and while I don’t do it much anymore, I still have the muscle memory to capture some good content. Here’s a crash course on how I used to put together these festival sizzles and recap videos.

First, you have to actually get to the festival. I’ve been to enough of these in the past that I know how to pack light, and thanks to Tucker, The Festival Guy, I had some extra backstage credentials. That said, don’t put too much weight on that. Credentials don’t change how you film a festival; they get you a few extra cool angles, but most of what you’ll see here was captured from the GA section, since that’s where the real audience experience lies.

Because you’re capturing something so unpredictable, there are moments happening everywhere, so the first key thing is to always keep a lookout. Scan around you and find people dancing, action moments, anything that captivates and grabs your interest. The second thing I do for these high-energy reels is look for ways to match movement across the camera. If I pan left, I’ll pan left again into the next scene. If I tilt up on one shot, maybe I tilt down out of the next. I’m always editing in my head, picturing how these pieces will fit together.

The last thing, and maybe the coolest part of festivals like this, is how much color and geometry surround you. I look for ways to build themes out of that. If there’s an umbrella spinning, I’ll find that shape and match it to another sphere or circle somewhere else. Match cuts are a huge part of this, and they add a lot of dynamic energy.

It’s important to note something here about appearance and consent. These festivals often tend to have a very friendly, open, and vibrant crowd, and most people are actually excited to appear in front of the camera and show off their outfits and their moves. Almost all festivals now have a waiver along with your ticket binding the festivalgoer to consent to be filmed, so they can use it for their own sizzle reels. Having said that, you should always approach people with respect, and if you’re unable to ask for consent due to high volume or energy, always visually check in with your subject—if they appear to be uncomfortable, put a hand up, or turn away, then pivot your camera away, give a sign of apology, and don’t use that clip in your edit—always be kind, polite, and respectful.

Before I even touch the edit, I always like having music in the back of my mind, a playlist or a selection of some kind, because a piece like this is driven by the track. I pulled up Audiio, our partners, to find it. For this one, I wanted something upbeat. It was an electronic music festival, so I narrowed the genre to electronic, then the mood to energetic. Instrumental only is a good call here so vocals don’t step on the footage or change the tone.

The way I listen is to click through very fast because I know within the first second or two whether the tone, style, rhythm, and pacing will work. I also tend to click into the sections with transitions to find out how the song’s energy moves and develops. There’s a ton to run through, so moving quickly is how I get through it, and I already know the flavor I’m after.

With the song picked, I drop it into the timeline. For the purpose of this sizzle, I trimmed it down to about a minute, landing on that first transition or breakdown before the second part of the song kicks in, which makes for a clean cut. A trick that helps me work faster: I find the different sections of the song and make cuts on the track itself. That helps me remember where each section starts and ends, and snapping to those cuts helps with timing. You can use markers or whatever tools your NLE offers; I like cuts because I can snap to them quickly.

Next are the selects. I run through each shot, set the in and out points, and look for what I was filming for: the transitions and the movements. I’d hold on a shot, whip pan out of it, find another, and whip pan into it, so I want to retain those moments and not trim into them. Then I categorize everything, which keeps me working fast. In this case, I’m using clip color as it’s quickly recognizable. One category is crowd shots: attendees dancing and looking at the camera. Another is transitional elements. Beyond the whip pans and tilts, I was hunting for spherical elements while filming, and I caught a lot of them on the day: parasols, flow toys spinning in circles, staffs people were twirling. Those made great transitions, and it turned filming into a fun challenge, always looking for the next spherical thing to match cut.

I also separated general B-roll, a walk-through category showing the different sections of the festival and its interactive experiences, a category just for flow toys and tools (poi, fire staff, hoops), stage elements, and stage close-ups. With everything categorized and color-coded, I can drop things in quickly and track where each element is going.

I start from my song cuts, and I like to place the transitional elements first—the movements and match cuts with the spherical elements—right on those cuts. Then I use the space in between to fill in as I go. For the opening, I listen to how the song starts slow and ramps up fast, so I want the energy to match that gradual build and sudden explosion into the beat. These will shift around as I work, but they’re bookmarks that tell me which sections are filled. I also had it in mind to move the piece from daytime to nighttime as it progresses.

I like working in these small chunks first, then dialing in the timing so it matches the music. Keeping the music at the forefront as the driving element of these pieces is absolutely key. We cut to the beat, or at least make sure the actions on camera land on the beat. When a fan flies up, I cut on that motion and rise through the next shot with an intentional tilt up into the stage. A rapid zoom or pull-out works too; in one spot, we start on a painting and pull out quickly, right on the rhythm. Another jumps into an abstract shot just as the beat drops, then cuts in on one of those built-in movements—a rapid tilt up matched to the stage lights and lasers.

With everything in place, the edit is almost done. The last thing I do is go through and add motion transitions where they help enhance the movement I built in. If a zoom or a whip pan isn’t as pronounced as I want, a motion transition can amplify it, really driving a powerful zoom in and out of the next shot. I’ll add just a few, but otherwise the piece is in a good spot.

Check out the final video above, and I’ll make sure to post more stuff like this when the opportunity presents itself. Until next time!

#9042. Camera Traps Uncover Surprising Behavior in Rare Flat-Headed Cats

Camera Traps Uncover Surprising Behavior in Rare Flat-Headed Cats

A large-scale camera trap survey has revealed that the rarely seen flat-headed cat, traditionally thought to be nocturnal, also roams during the day.

The flat-headed cat (Prionailurus planiceps), named for its flattened forehead and elongated skull, is one of the world’s rarest and least-studied wild felines. It lives in fragmented habitats across Brunei, Indonesia, and Malaysia. For years, the species has been traditionally considered strictly nocturnal.

However, a new study published in Ecology and Evolution has challenged that understanding. Researchers used camera traps to monitor the proposed Lundu Mangrove Protected Forest in southwestern Sarawak, Malaysia, over a nearly three-year period between August 2021 and May 2024.

During the survey, the researchers recorded the flat-headed cat 59 times, revealing an unexpected pattern of activity. According to a report by Mongabay, the camera traps showed that the cats were active during both nighttime and daytime hours. Although activity peaked around midnight among flat-headed cats, it also extended into the late morning and afternoon.

The findings revealed “considerable daytime activity,” suggesting that the species’ activity patterns may be more flexible than previously believed. The cameras also recorded an adult female accompanied by a kitten, providing evidence of the species’ presence and possible reproductive activity in the study area.

“This was particularly encouraging because it provides evidence of the species’ presence alongside potential reproductive activity in the study area,” Ahmad Ampeng, the study’s lead author and a research officer at the Forest Department Sarawak, tells Mongabay.

The flat-headed cat is classified as endangered on the IUCN Red List. The species was also once considered possibly extinct in Thailand, until camera traps documented its presence last year, marking its first confirmed appearance there in nearly three decades.

#9040. Backlash Over ‘Robots’ Taking Photos at Christmas Lights Event

Backlash Over ‘Robots’ Taking Photos at Christmas Lights Event

A video of Christmas lights being switched on in Central London has provoked a debate about people’s picture-taking habits and the importance of living in the moment.

The video was shared by BBC London on November 4. It shows a sea of people, seemingly every single one of them with their phones aloft, filming in anticipation of the elaborate lights on Carnaby Street turning on and the fireworks that followed.

The comments were flooded with people disgusted that no one appeared to be taking in the moment, instead watching a real event that was unfolding right in front of them through the small screen of their phone.

“I’ve stopped filming most things like fireworks and concerts when I realized I haven’t watched a single one of them back,” says Sufian Ahmed. “It’s so much about being in the moment. Experiencing it with the person you’re next to. You lose all that when watching it through a narrow screen.”

Many compared it to an episode of the Black Mirror TV show, while others called out the people for being “robots.” Others pointed out the hypocrisy of social media users complaining about the video while watching it on their phone.

Previous studies have found that taking a photo of an event affects human memory. A 2018 psychological study suggested that shooting photos or videos gives people a false sense that they preserved a moment, when in actual fact it’s the camera that did it for them.

In 2013, researchers asked one group of people to tour an art museum without taking photos, while another group was assigned to take photos. Those who took photos were significantly worse at identifying items in the museum and recalled fewer details about the items they did remember than those who didn’t take photos.

Dr. Kaitlyn Regehr of University College London and the University of Toronto says public attitudes toward smartphones and technology are shifting.

“This is not the first year that people have attended events and watched those events through screens,” the smartphone academic tells the BBC.

“But what’s significant is that this year there’s a lot of critical public discourse happening. And that, I think, is really, really positive.

Dr. Regehr says the backlash could be down to “our discomfort with the amount of influence that big tech is playing on our lives.”

#9039. Has the couple in Jan van Eyck’s ‘Arnolfini Portrait’ been misidentified?

Reality check: the identity of the couple in The Arnolfini Portrait (1434) by Jan van Eyck is not the only contested element in the painting—the woman’s pregnancy, the event and the actuality of the room are also hotly disputed The National Gallery, London

Jan van Eyck’s Arnolfini Portrait (1434) has been a signature work in London’s National Gallery since it arrived at the museum in 1842. A few key facts about the dual portrait, showing a youngish man and his idealised wife, could be gleaned just by looking at the work’s prominent Latin inscription, which translates as “Jan van Eyck was here 1434”. Over the years, just about everything else associated with the painting, from its mysterious room to the obscure occasion, has been open to debate, other than the surname of the man—Arnolfini, connected to an extended family of wealthy merchants from Lucca active in 15th-century Bruges, where Van Eyck had his studio.

Now, on the occasion of the National Gallery’s exhibition Van Eyck: The Portraits (21 November-11 April 2027), which brings together all nine of the artist’s surviving panel portraits, the Berlin-based curator Stephan Kemperdick, writing in a catalogue essay, has planted a possible bombshell by suggesting that the man in the Arnolfini Portrait is Van Eyck himself, and that the woman standing next to him is the artist’s wife Margaret, the sitter in another Van Eyck portrait from 1439, which is on loan to the show from Bruges.

Kemperdick’s theory, presented in recent talks but published now for the first time, is not an entirely new one. In the late 1840s, the National Gallery’s future first director Charles Eastlake contended that the artist’s inscription, which he thought could be translated as “Jan van Eyck was this [one]”, meant that the painting was also a dual portrait of the artist and his wife. But in the early 1860s, the British art historian W. H. James Weale interpreted a reference in a 16th-century inventory to a certain “hernoul le fin” in the painting, which he regarded as the French version of the Italian surname Arnolfini. The connection between the couple and that family was thus set in stone, though scholars disagree, often vehemently, about which particular member of the Arnolfini clan is shown.

Kemperdick has revisited the inscription, which is unusually large and conspicuously places the artist’s name next to the male figure’s head. He argues this indicates a direct connection between Van Eyck and the man. He has also reconsidered the association between the “hernoul le fin” reference and the surname Arnolfini. Citing the early-modern categorisation of the late-medieval work as not a portrait at all, but rather a lewd genre painting, Kemperdick suggests that “hernoul le fin” is not the correct surname of the sitter, but a subsequent and mocking moniker used by later generations to misidentify the man as a “a deceived cheat”. Kemperdick also suggests that a reference to St Margaret in the bedstead statue near the woman’s head serves to identify her as Van Eyck’s wife.

Kemperdick is the curator of German, Netherlandish and French Paintings before 1600 at the Berlin Gemäldegalerie, which is noted for its Early Netherlandish holdings and has in its own collection a Van Eyck portrait (around 1435-38) of the very same man who appears in the National Gallery’s Arnolfini Portrait. The two will be shown together in the London exhibition.

Nicholas Flory, the co-curator of Van Eyck: The Portraits along with Emma Capron, the National Gallery’s curator of early Netherlandish and German painting, says that he and Capron find Kemperdick’s theory “interesting” but “speculative”, citing, among other reasons, that the woman in the Bruges portrait, whom we know to be Margaret based on the inscription, has greyish-blue eyes while the woman in the Arnolfini Portrait has brown eyes.

Other leading Van Eyck scholars also have their doubts. The German art historian Till-Holger Borchert—now the director of the Suermondt-Ludwig-Museum in Aachen and the former director of Musea Brugge in Bruges—is familiar with Kemperdick’s theory. “I’m not entirely sure I can concur,” he says. He thinks the early-16th-century inventory reference—associated with the painting’s owner at the time, Margaret of Austria, the governor of the Habsburg Netherlands—is a near iron-clad reference to the Arnolfinis. The Ghent University art historian Maximiliaan Martens, who has been involved in the lengthy restoration of Van Eyck’s Ghent Altarpiece, also “doesn’t see any reason to doubt” that the inventory reference is to the Arnolfinis.

The implications of Kemperdick’s theory are far-reaching. Another Van Eyck portrait at the National Gallery, from 1433, showing a much older man than the figure in the Arnolfini Portrait, is now tentatively identified by the London museum as a self-portrait. This, however, cannot be the case if Kemperdick’s theory is correct.

The exhibition Van Eyck: The Portraits will label the Berlin work with its previous and longstanding reference to the Arnolfinis, while the Gemäldegalerie, under Kemperick’s guidance, has recently renamed it Portrait of a Man with a Red Chaperon. And the debate about the couple promises to continue long after the show closes in April.

“I have thought for 30 years about this,” Martens says of the figures in the Arnolfini Portrait. He says he is still not sure if the man is Giovanni di Arrigo Arnolfini (who was apparently not married at the time the painting was made) or his cousin, Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini (whose wife had died before the painting was made).

Other aspects of the dual portrait that scholars continue to debate include whether the heavy-bellied woman is actually pregnant (Kemperdick and Martens think that may be possible, while Flory and Capron think she is just gathering up her heavy skirts), and whether the room itself is a real space or an imagined one (imagined, say Flory and Capron; real, says Martens).

Beyond who made it and when, the Arnolfini Portrait remains a mystery, which is in keeping for an artist whose date and place of birth, among other foundational knowledge, is also speculation. Asked to comment on the enigma associated with the Arnolfini Portrait, Borchert says: “Can you tell me anything about Van Eyck that isn’t enigmatic?”

#9038. 45% of US Independent Arts Publications Face Existential Crisis, Report Finds

In addition to declining funding, the survey identified a disturbing correlation between censorship concerns and financial precarity.

Nearly half of independent publications covering arts and culture in the United States said their business models will not be sustainable without “profound changes” to the current funding landscape, according to a report from Critical Minded and the Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation released this week.

The new survey notably identifies a disturbing correlation between censorship concerns, including external pressure from advertisers and sponsors, and financial precarity. The 41% of respondents who said they faced free-speech pressures or threats in the last two years were more likely to report funding declines, throwing into stark relief how what outlets choose to cover — or not — may determine whether they can pay staff and contributors, or keep the lights on altogether.

“Support for Arts and Culture Journalism: A Survey of Independent Publications in the United States” polled 141 independent outlets that cover the arts on issues impacting the field and strategies used to address them. The anonymized respondents are based in 34 states and the District of Columbia, with the highest concentration (38.2%) in the Northeast, and reach an average annual audience of about half a million.

A will (technically a "last will and testament") is a legal document that specifies how your assets should be distributed after your death. It must go through probate — a court-supervised process that validates the will, pays debts and taxes, and distributes assets to beneficiaries. A living trust (specifically a revocable living trust) is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. When you die, the successor trustee distributes those assets according to the trust terms — without court involvement.

You need both: A trust does not name guardians for minor children (only a will can do that), and a trust only controls assets that have been formally transferred into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — it directs any assets not in the trust at your death to pour into the trust, where they are distributed according to the trust terms. The pour-over will still goes through probate, but it ensures nothing falls through the cracks.

The term "living trust" almost always refers to a revocable living trust — one you can change, amend, or dissolve at any time during your lifetime. You remain the trustee, manage the assets as you always have, and pay taxes on trust income using your personal Social Security number. For income tax purposes, a revocable trust is invisible — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist.

An irrevocable trust is fundamentally different. Once established, you cannot easily modify it, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. This permanence provides two powerful advantages:

The federal estate tax exemption is $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples) in 2026, but this historically high exemption is scheduled to sunset after 2025, potentially dropping to approximately $7 million per person. FIRE households who have built $3 million to $10 million in net worth through decades of saving and investment growth should monitor this sunset closely. If the exemption drops, irrevocable trusts become relevant at much lower wealth levels.

For most FIRE households with $1 million to $5 million in net worth, a revocable living trust provides the right balance of control, flexibility, and probate avoidance. Irrevocable structures become compelling only when estate tax exposure is real or asset protection needs are elevated.

Estate planning is governed primarily by state law, and the value of a living trust versus a will varies significantly depending on where you live.

Nine states are community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. In these states, most assets acquired during marriage are owned 50/50 by both spouses regardless of whose name is on the title. At death, only the deceased spouse's half passes through their estate plan.

The remaining 41 states follow common law (also called "equitable distribution"). Ownership depends on whose name is on the title. This distinction affects how assets pass at death and whether a trust or will provides better spousal protection.

Use this framework to determine whether you need a trust, a will, or both:

A revocable living trust is strongly recommended if:

Remember that a trust only controls assets titled in the trust's name. After creating a trust, you must fund it by re-titling your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust. Unfunded trusts — trusts that exist on paper but hold no assets — provide zero benefit. The pour-over will catches stragglers, but relying entirely on the pour-over defeats the purpose because those assets still go through probate.

The most common estate planning mistake with trusts is failing to fund them. Creating a trust document costs $1,500 to $5,000, but if you never transfer your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust, it provides zero probate avoidance. After signing your trust, immediately re-title assets into the trust name. Your attorney should provide a funding checklist. An unfunded trust sitting in a drawer is an expensive piece of paper — not an estate plan.

Yes. A pour-over will catches any assets not transferred into your trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. A will is also the only legal document that can name guardians for minor children. Every trust-based estate plan should include a pour-over will.

A revocable living trust prepared by an estate planning attorney typically costs $1,500 to $5,000, depending on complexity and your location. This usually includes the trust document, pour-over will, powers of attorney, healthcare directives, and initial funding guidance. Online trust services cost $200 to $500 but may not address state-specific issues or complex situations.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as both the grantor (creator) and the trustee (manager). You maintain full control over all trust assets during your lifetime. You name a successor trustee who takes over only if you become incapacitated or die.

A revocable living trust does not reduce estate taxes — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist for income and estate tax purposes. However, a trust can be structured with provisions (such as an A/B trust or disclaimer trust) that maximize the use of both spouses' estate tax exemptions. For estate tax reduction, irrevocable trusts are the primary tool.

A revocable trust can be changed, amended, or dissolved at any time. You maintain full control. An irrevocable trust generally cannot be changed after creation, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. Revocable trusts provide probate avoidance and incapacity planning. Irrevocable trusts provide estate tax reduction and asset protection.

Without a trust, each state where you own real property requires a separate probate proceeding (called ancillary probate), multiplying costs and complexity. Transferring out-of-state property into a living trust eliminates ancillary probate entirely — the successor trustee can transfer or sell the property without court involvement in any state.

#9034. Special Edition: Jesus

Mona Chalabi, Anne Anlin Cheng and Patty Chang, Miles Greenberg, Betsy James Wyeth, and the hottest memes about the Nvidia honeypot.

Framed by their car’s windshield, and then again by my rearview mirror, a man and a woman who seem to be a couple look like they'd rather be anywhere but together. He’s behind the wheel, doing all the talking; she’s looking straight ahead, motionless like a marble statue. Gradually, her face wears a desperate expression that only grows more hopeless as he continues talking and gesticulating.

In the supermarket checkout line, I pick up a copy of TIME magazine for the first time in God knows how long, drawn to a painting of Jesus Christ on the cover. It’s a special edition promising to tell us “Who he was. Who he is. His miracles, his mission, his love.” I expect to see a lot of biblical sheep inside, but I don’t find any. I buy the issue as an artifact. I stopped believing in TIME magazine a long time ago.

Down the street, a place that pretended to be a legitimate art gallery for a couple of months, showing the worst possible commercial art, has finally given up, and now it’s selling fur coats. A man in a cowboy hat walks past two girls dancing for a social media video. The air is chilly, and I think of buying myself a leather jacket.

She looks at me with the most loving eyes as she holds a stack of perfectly folded laundry. She comforts me with her wide, auspicious smile, her jet-black hair, and her wrinkle-free, porcelain skin. I feel safe, accepted, and not judged. “Fast service, same day,” she promises because she’s just a model in an ad for a laundromat.

“As an adult and as a journalist, I have stared shamelessly.” That refusal to look away is precisely what data journalist, writer, and artist Mona Chalabi has built her deeply principled career on. Known best for her indelible data visualizations, from the obscenity of Jeff Bezos’s wealth to the Israeli government’s starvation of Palestinians in Gaza and the racial and gender biases in museum collections, the Pulitzer Prize-winning Iraqi-British journalist tackles the subject of wealth and economic inequality in America in her first book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are (2026). | Lakshmi Rivera Amin

#9033. Show of every Jan van Eyck portrait reveals many new sides to his works

Jan van Eyck’s Portrait of Margaret van Eyck (1439) is one of nine panel portraits the artist made that still survive, and all have been brought together in the National Gallery show Photo: National Gallery London; © Musea Brugge

There is a lot we do not know for certain about Jan van Eyck, including where and when he was born. What we do know is that his career—from the early 1420s until his death in 1441—helped launch the Early Netherlandish school, influencing the use of oil paint far beyond his native Low Countries and instilling a new and arguably everlasting value of verisimilitude in Western art.

But we stand to know a lot more about him this month, when London’s National Gallery brings together all nine of his surviving panel portraits along with his lone surviving drawing, also a portrait. The bijoux blockbuster show will give scholars a unique opportunity to compare scattered works of singular importance. Van Eyck: The Portraits—with a checklist that expands all the way to 13 through the addition of three works on paper by his followers—is built around some remarkable pairings.

Fresh from a conservation treatment completed in 2024, the National Gallery’s own Portrait of a Man (Self-Portrait?) (1433) will meet up with Portrait of Margaret van Eyck (1439), the artist’s wife, on loan from Bruges, where Van Eyck had his workshop when he was the court painter to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy.

The National Gallery’s Arnolfini Portrait (1434), Van Eyck’s enigmatic view of an elegantly dressed couple in an impressive reception room, will be shown for the first time with its related work from the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin clearly showing the same man, Portrait of a Man (Giovanni Arnolfini?) (around 1435-38).

Vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum is loaning Portrait of an Elderly Man (A Scholar?) (around 1438). It will be shown with the preparatory drawing from Dresden, in goldpoint and silverpoint on prepared paper, with its revealing notes on how to colour the painting itself.

Van Eyck’s devotional portraits, such as those in his groundbreaking Ghent Altarpiece and the Musée du Louvre’s recently treated Madonna of Chancellor Rolin (around 1435), are outside the scope of the National Gallery exhibition.

Some of the portraits have reverse imagery of fictive marble, and the museum is placing them in cases so visitors can view both sides. “We’re really excited to be able to show people how amazing the reverse is,” says Nicholas Flory, who is curating the show along with Emma Capron, the museum’s curator of early Netherlandish and German painting. Flory says the elaborate reverses suggest that “these objects were not designed for a single kind of specific space or to be flat against the wall”, but rather “to be interacted with”.

Newness abounds in the show. The Arnolfini Portrait had long had an ornate Gothic Revival frame until it was replaced in 2024 by a 15th-century gilded frame. Meanwhile, the Berlin work, showing its male figure in distinctive red chaperon headgear, completed a conservation treatment in 2023 that removed distorting yellow varnish. The result of that treatment, says Stephan Kemperdick, the curator of Netherlandish paintings before 1600 at the Gemäldegalerie, has been to “make the palette cooler”. Before, he says, the chaperon was “fire-engine red”, and the man’s face looked “suntanned”, whereas now, he says, the face is “pinkish or whiteish—a feature that distinguished people from the better classes in the 15th century”.

The London exhibition, which Kemperdick calls a “once-in-a-lifetime” event, is a culmination of sorts. Several Van Eyck works, including the Ghent Altarpiece, have undergone recent treatments, which Flory says has been “an impetus in Van Eyck scholarship”, and the National Gallery show reflects new research into Van Eyck’s technique, his original frames and inscriptions. Recent analysis of the National Gallery’s self-portrait, examined during its recent treatment, revealed how Van Eyck modulated the blueness of the background in the lower-right corner to “throw the sitter’s shoulder forward”, Flory says, creating a 3D effect.

Just out of view of the show itself, lurking in Kemperdick’s catalogue essay, is a possible bombshell: that the couple shown in the Arnolfini Portrait are not the titular Italian merchant and his wife at all, but rather Van Eyck and his wife. This would also mean that the Gemäldegalerie’s Portrait of a Man (Giovanni Arnolfini?) is also a self-portrait.

The Arnolfini Portrait is among the gallery’s most popular works, and the minuscule size of the show is in marked contrast with the likely museumgoer interest. However, Flory says the diminutive roster is, in fact, the big attraction.

“There was the possibility to expand it beyond Van Eyck and show his work in the context of his contemporaries,” Flory says. “But because he is such a monumental figure in the history of Western painting, and his portraits are so special, we really wanted to focus the exhibition on just Van Eyck himself.” Luckily, he adds, the remarkable loans, which have involved several museums sending some of their most precious works, mean “we got everything we were hoping for”.

• Jan van Eyck: The Portraits, National Gallery, London, 21 November-11 April 2027

A review of James Cahill’s book on the painter and the patron in “Beverly Hills Housewife,” the state of arts journalism, and why Tribal Nations are opposing a Congressional bill.

It’s a beautiful day to support indie publications! Last week, a survey conducted by Critical Minded and the Rabkin Foundation quantified the precarity of independent US-based art magazines amid a climate of censorship, corporate takeovers, and economic instability. And if that isn’t enough, Aaron Short shares a wry dispatch from the preview of the Art Dealers Association of America’s art fair in New York City — the tickets may have been $250 a pop, but at least there were unlimited dumplings and champagne to sweeten the deal?

#9031. PPAA creates twin houses in Mexico as an "argument for building less"

Mexican architecture studio Pérez Palacios Arquitectos Asociados has completed twin houses that combine concrete with glued-laminated timber in the forests of Valle de Bravo, Mexico.

The two houses – each measuring 500 square metres (5,382 square feet) – are collectively called Rejas and were designed for two brothers and their families, cohabitating on a 1.2-acre forested property in Avándaro, a couple of hours west of Mexico City.

“Avándaro is a landscape that’s been quietly overbuilt for decades, so the first decision on Rejas was actually a renunciation,” Pablo Pérez Palacios, founder of Pérez Palacios Arquitectos Asociados (PPAA), told Dezeen,

“Instead of designing a wall or a fence between the two brothers’ houses, we chose to regenerate the native forest that the site had partially lost, and let that stand as the boundary,” he said, explainging that decision set the tone for the rest of the project.

“The whole project is really an argument for building less, so the landscape has room to eventually reclaim the architecture.”

The site, with its regenerated forest, is steeply sloped toward the Avándaro reservoir, allowing PPAA to partially submerge each house.

From the driveway, the houses appear as one-storey structures, but the lower levels emerge on the other side as the terrain descends.

To navigate this, the houses sit on bases of concrete and local stone that anchor them into the slope, while timber roofs top the upper levels and open the spaces to the surrounding trees.

The houses were designed to interact with the landscape, and have almost identical plans, though their place in the landscape differs.

Public spaces are on the upper level, with a kitchen, dining and living room in a glass box within the larger, rectangular platform.

A covered terrace comprises the remainder of the level with designated seating and outdoor cooking areas that are framed with planters.

Below, five bedrooms with ensuite bathrooms and a lounge area sit within the forest floor, cool and contained within the boxy volume.

“The deliberate positioning of the openings eliminates any possibility of facing windows – no window in one house looks toward the other. Each dwelling establishes its own relationship with the natural surroundings as if the other did not exist.”

The studio pulled the service areas for both houses into separate buildings placed along the edge of the property to free the centre of the plot for the houses and their relationships with the landscape.

Designed to patina with the landscape, the minimalist material palette relies on stone and concrete to give mass and solidity to the base and mass timber to be both the structure and spatial character of the upper level.

The pairing allows the materials to complement one another, juxtaposing lightness and weight.

“This tension between the stone base that anchors and the glulam roof that liberates is neither an aesthetic operation nor a reference to any vernacular tradition,” the studio said.

“It is a proposition about how to inhabit: what protects and what opens, what remains and what breathes, what belongs to the ground and what belongs to the air.”

Long known for concrete construction like this subtractive house in Los Angeles, PPAA has been expanding recently into mass timber design with projects like a rotating cross-laminated timber pavilion in Mexico City and Mexico’s first “all-wood” mass timber structure in Querétaro.

Architecture: PPAADesign Team: Pablo Pérez Palacios, Emilio Calvo, Miguel Vargas, Jonathan Reséndiz, Adriana Hernández Interiors: Mariana Morales

#9030. All the Award-Winning Photos From Nature Photographer of the Year 2026

All the Award-Winning Photos From Nature Photographer of the Year 2026

The Nature Photographer of the Year 2026 winners have been unveiled, showcasing the world’s best nature, wildlife, and landscape photography.

This year’s competition received 27,108 entries from photographers in nearly 100 countries, a record-breaking number for the longtime photo contest.

Finnish photographer Hannu Ahonen bested stiff competition to earn the title of Nature Photographer of the Year. Ahonen’s award-winning photo, “The One that Left and the One that Stayed,” is an extraordinary image of a water lily leaf positioned alongside its icy duplicate.

“It is not often that a photograph of a plant is crowned the overall winner of a major photography competition, but the jury could not overlook this fascinating image by Hannu Ahonen,” says jury chair Theo Bosboom. “First and foremost, the photograph captures a unique situation: a water lily leaf with an almost perfect black-and-white replica of it lying next to it in the water.”

Ahonen’s winning photo tells a compelling and unusual story. The living water lily leaf is positioned on the left, while the ice that formed on top of it and slipped off sits delicately to the side, blown away slightly by the breeze. Even the veins from the leaf are visible in the icy shell.

Nature Photographer of the Year adds that the photo reveals the “marvelous beauty of nature” while embodying its transient character. The sheet of ice will soon melt away, joining the water that keeps the lily alive in the first place. It’s a symbolic photo at a time when climate change is impacting all life on Earth, especially its ice.

“The winter ice had arrived, but it remained snowless for a long time. Some of the pond’s lily pad leaves began to crumble on top of the ice. The wind carried a few of them away, revealing delicate, frosty ornaments left behind. I eagerly captured this natural phenomenon, something I had never witnessed before,” Ahonen explains.

Ahonen has an inspiring story. He has ADHD and lives in a wilderness home in Finland with no carbon footprint. Rarely venturing more than a couple of miles from his home, he spends much of his time behind the camera in his yard, using photography as a spiritual escape and creative outlet.

Alongside the overall winner, Ahonen, the competition’s jury also selected winners across nearly a dozen categories. There are also special prizes for youth photographers and an accomplished portfolio. Ahonen took the top spot in the Plants and Fungi category, so that category is not included below.

French photographer Lucas Mugnier-Lavorel won this year’s Birds category for his environmental portrait of a Magellanic woodpecker in Patagonia.

“Environmental portraits of wildlife can make us feel closer to the animals despite being farther away from them, when done right. This image of a Magellanic woodpecker in its gorgeous habitat was a perfect example. It stood out from thousands of submissions because of its understated sense of place, beauty, simplicity, and timing,” says judge Steffen Foerster.

“Overall, it was a very successful reminder of how the portrayal of nature in its literal state can still be the most powerful of photographic expressions,” Foerster concludes.

British photographer Paul Goldstein’s foggy photo of a giraffe earned the top prize in the Mammals category.

“Quiet images can be easy to overlook in the fiercely competitive mammal category, one of the largest in NPOTY. This ethereal image of a giraffe peeking out of the mist revealed its strengths gradually. Initially a little disorienting, it offered just enough of a visual puzzle to keep the viewer engaged until the image resolved,” Foerster explains.

Judges tapped Marcus Kuan’s macro photo of a surprisingly rich and diverse little ecosystem alongside a pitcher plant in the Other Animals category. The Singaporean photographer impressed the panel with his composition and lighting.

“The lighting, colors, and unexpected gathering of species immediately caught our attention. Kuan beautifully captured a world where crustaceans, amphibians, and carnivorous plants cross paths,” explains jury member Louis Guillot.

“As judges, we were drawn to the possibilities unfolding within this single frame. Could the pitchers be digesting invertebrates? Might the frog be exploring a potential egg-laying site, while the crab continues its daily search for food among the plants?” Guillot continues.

Photographer J Fritz Rumpf from the United States won this year’s Landscape category with a silhouetted photo of Iguazú Falls in Argentina.

“What immediately caught our attention was the incredible light and atmosphere in this photo. The longer we looked, the more fascinating it became. There is so much to discover: the last light of day illuminating the mist rising from Iguazú Falls, the silhouettes of trees and rocks, the birds circling above, the sunlight streaming through an opening in the rock at the center, and the subtle waterfall on the left,” says jury member Ilse Koks.

Another American photographer, Matt Pérez, won the Underwater category with a striking photo of a turtle beneath a collection of newt eggs.

“Pérez’s photograph immediately drew us in. As a jury, we wanted to linger over it, exploring the details and wondering what we were seeing,” remarks Guillot. “Newt egg masses decorate the submerged branches like baubles on a Christmas tree, framing the scene and guiding our eyes towards the pond turtle with its piercing yellow eyes.”

Guillot adds that the scene looks “otherworldly,” which is a very apt description.

Chinese photographer Xuzhong Liu’s abstract drone shot of a winding landscape ticks all the right boxes. It has interesting patterns, striking colors, and a very pleasing composition.

Liu captured the image in a wetland area in China and says the scene strongly reminded him of peach blossoms he had previously photographed—hence the title, “Peach Blossoms in the Snow.”

“This photograph has everything that can make a drone shot interesting and fascinating. First and foremost, there are beautiful shapes and subtle colours, but there is also a sense of alienation. What am I actually looking at, and what is the scale of the landscape in the photograph?” asks the chair of the judging panel, Theo Bosboom.

Czech photographer Petr Bambousek’s winning photo depicts a sobering scene of a Malayan sun bear resting inside a garbage incinerator.

“The winning image stood out for its striking depiction of the impact human activity has on local wildlife,” explains jury member Lana Tannir. “The sleeping Malayan sun bear inside a garbage incinerator creates a powerful visual contrast, showing how habitat loss and human waste increasingly force wild animals into close contact with human environments.”

Tannir says Bambousek’s photo is “unexpected and unsettling.”

Hungarian photographer László Tóth won the Black and White category for his striking, high-contrast, abstract photo.

“This photo really stood out to us. At first, we were not quite sure what we were looking at. It sparked some wonderful discussions among the jury and made us look even closer,” says Ilse Koks.

As for what the photo actually depicts, it’s a thin layer of snow on top of a frozen lake, shaped by the wind.

This photo might be familiar to PetaPixel readers. Norwegian photographer Audun Rikardsen recently won an award for a similar underwater portrait of a polar bear peering down through a hole in the ice.

“Just when we thought we had seen about every kind of polar bear image there is, along comes this shot taken from inside a hole in the ice looking up at the bear,” says Steffen Foerster. “Once you realize what is happening, you start thinking about how this shot could possibly have been taken. Then it dawns on you that it seems almost impossible, no matter how.”

This special category, “De Lage Landen” (which translates to “The Low Countries”), celebrates photos captured in the low-lying region of northwestern Europe, including the Netherlands, where Nature Photographer of the Year is based. This year’s winning photo is by Hungarian photographer Enikő Kálovics.

“The winning image stood out for its ability to transform a familiar landscape into something dreamlike and unexpected,” says Lana Tannir. “The combination of the tiny lacewings, the autumn forest, and the purplish night sky creates a delicate, atmospheric interpretation of the nature of ‘De Lage Landen.'”

American photographer Parham Pourahmad, who was also recently celebrated in the 2027 North American Nature Photography Association (NANPA) Showcase, won this year’s Youth category with a lovely monochromatic photo of a coyote beneath a large tree.

“In ‘Tree of Life’, Pourahmad captured a striking scene that could comfortably hold its own in the adult categories,” says Guillot. “Black and white was an excellent choice, defining the coyote’s silhouette and revealing the majestic oak’s intricate network of branches. Even within this wider scene, the coyote’s downward gaze is clear. Pourahmad explained that it was searching for rodent prey, a small detail that brings the photograph to life.”

Pourahmad has also been named Youth Photographer of the Year.

The Fred Hazelhoff Award celebrates a portfolio of nature photos, rather than a single image. This year’s portfolio winner is German photographer Simone Baumeister.

“In the portfolio category, the bar is set considerably higher for participating photographers than in the individual categories. Whilst a single fantastic photograph is sufficient there, in the portfolio category you need a whole series of outstanding images that not only complement one another but also fit together well in terms of style and theme. Simone Baumeister has succeeded brilliantly in this with her portfolio on eagle owls in the city,” says jury chair Theo Bosboom.

Baumeister has been fascinated by owls for as long as she has been interested in nature photography. The eagle owl’s story is a positive one, in contrast to the plight of many species across the globe. The species, once on the brink of extinction in Germany, has made an incredible recovery. Its resurgence is thanks largely to major conservation efforts and extensive reintroduction programs.

“It was perched in twilight on a church, right below the street lamps, moving cars, and a string of people passing by, with music blaring from a pub right on the church square. Not a soul took notice of the impressive bird with a wingspan of 1.7 meters flying up the steeple, sitting enthroned right within everybody’s view,” the photographer says of the first time she saw an eagle owl in a city.

Ever since then, she has been consistently excited by eagle owls and keen to photograph them in many different places. Observing and photographing them in various cities inevitably morphed into a dedicated project.

Alongside the category and special award winners above, the judges also selected runners-up and highly commended photos, all of which can be seen on the Nature Photographer of the Year website and below.

Entries for the Nature Photographer of the Year 2027 open on November 20, 2026.

#9029. Advance Your Creative Practice With a Graduate Degree From the University of Louisville

All MFA and MA students receive generous scholarships, with additional support for research, creative projects, and travel.

With substantial scholarships, exceptional facilities, accomplished faculty, and private studios, students pursuing an MFA in Studio Art and Design at the University of Louisville have the resources and creative freedom to develop their artistic practice within a dynamic, supportive community.

The rigorous 60-credit MFA program encourages experimentation, critical inquiry, and interdisciplinary exploration. Students may pursue interdisciplinary practices or concentrate on individual media, including ceramics, drawing, glass, painting, photography, printmaking, sculpture, design, new media, and installation.

Located in Louisville's Portland arts district, the MFA program occupies a dedicated, newly renovated warehouse featuring individual graduate studios, state-of-the-art production facilities, laboratories, a seminar room, and an exhibition gallery. This distinctive environment provides students with the space, resources, and opportunities to develop ambitious creative projects.

The Hite Institute also offers a 31-credit-hour MA in Art History or Curatorial Studies. Combining critical theory, art historical research, contemporary art, and hands-on exhibition experience, the program prepares students for careers in museums, galleries, curatorial practice, arts administration, and art writing, as well as further academic study.

Founded in 1946, the endowed Hite Institute of Art + Design has built a distinctive identity grounded in its avant-garde origins and oriented to creative experimentation and critical inquiry. Its accomplished faculty of practicing artists, designers, and scholars encourages students to expand their creative and intellectual horizons while engaging with contemporary cultural, social, and environmental issues.

Both graduate programs maintain small, selective cohorts, allowing for close faculty mentorship, individualized attention, and meaningful collaboration. Students benefit from the Hite Institute's extensive resources, including six galleries, outstanding glass and additive manufacturing facilities, partnerships with museums and cultural institutions, an active alumni network, and visiting lectures by internationally recognized artists, curators, and arts professionals.

In addition to guaranteed scholarships, graduate students may qualify for teaching assistantships, internships, and additional awards that provide valuable professional experience and support their creative and scholarly development.

Applications for Fall 2027 admission are due January 15, 2027.

#9028. Shaw Contract Design Awards name top interiors of 2026

A Japanese office intended to evoke a tree canopy, and a revived US concert hall are among the interior design projects to win Best of Globe at this year’s Shaw Contract Design Awards.

The upgrade of an athletics clubhouse in the US, a legal workplace in the UK and a large three-story office in India also took the top prize in the annual award programme, now in its 21st year.

Held annually by flooring manufacturer Shaw Contract, the Shaw Contract Design Awards celebrate interior design projects that “spark creativity, connect communities and contribute to a better, more sustainable world”.

This year’s winning projects were selected from nearly 550 global submissions by an international jury of architects and designers, with interior design students also joining as part of Shaw’s commitment to supporting the next generation of design talent.

According to the jury, the 2026 winners were unified by “a clear design narrative, an understanding of local context, varied and inclusive user experiences, responsible material strategies and a meaningful relationship between design intent and completed space” – despite their varying scales and styles.

“Throughout the global judging session, the jury returned to a central question: whether each project’s stated intent was visible and understandable in the completed design,” explained Shaw Contract.

“The panel distinguished between attractive spaces and projects that used planning, materials, detail and experience to communicate a clear and consequential idea.”

The St Louis Symphony Orchestra Powell Hall in the US, overhauled by Christner Architects, was one of the winners.

According to Shaw Contract, the jury selected it for its sensitive balance of old and new elements, as well as the important social role it plays in the city, thanks to improved accessibility and audience facilities.

Also in the US is the winning Missouri Athletic Club project, completed by HOK. The scheme involved revamping an existing clubhouse to better suit the needs of its current members.

HOK’s design was commended for adding “a new layer to the club’s heritage rather than treating the past as a fixed visual theme”, according to the brand, introducing a contemporary layout and aesthetic.

The third winner was We Labo 25F, a small workspace in Japan that embodies the principles of biophilic design – the use of natural features such as plants to improve the wellbeing of building occupants.

Its architect, Okamura, was praised for incorporating greenery as more than just “a decorative layer” and creating an interior that mimics working beneath a tree canopy.

The office was also selected in recognition of its adaptable interiors and circular design features, including furniture made from tsunami debris.

We Labo 25F was one of three workplaces to win Best of Globe, alongside Diageo by M Moser Associates in India and DLA Piper by Sheppard Robson Architects in the UK.

Diageo spans 7,700 square metres and accommodates 300 employees across each of its three floors, accommodating its owner’s expansion from Bengaluru to Gurugram.

It was selected by the jury for its “richly layered and carefully crafted” interiors, which combine a wide range of workspaces with shared hospitality areas. M Moser Associates dedicated more than half of the building to community spaces.

Finally, DLA Piper by Sheppard Robson Architects is a large workplace for a legal company. It was designed to cater to different work styles.

According to Shaw Contract, it won the prize for providing a broad range of workspaces suited to different needs, as well as wellbeing, dining and meeting areas.

The jury particularly enjoyed how materials had been applied in a way that adds “warmth and richness into areas that might traditionally be treated as purely corporate”.

The Best of Globe winners are selected from the programme’s Best of Region winners. Winners receive global media exposure and a donation to a charity of their choice.

Shaw Contract’s ambition for the award programme is to encourage discourse within the international creative community.

To learn more about Shaw Contract and the awards programme, visit its website here.

#9027. After Months of Delays, the Sony FX5 Is Finally Shipping to Customers

After Months of Delays, the Sony FX5 Is Finally Shipping to Customers

This is not a drill. The Sony FX5 really has launched.

Last month, after numerous delays, Sony said the highly anticipated FX5 cinema camera would finally launch on November 15. As Sony Alpha Rumors reports, Sony actually delivered, and preordered cameras have begun shipping to customers. Multiple Sony Alpha Rumors commenters confirmed they have received their orders from retailers including Adorama and B&H.

Video creator Brandon Washington took to Instagram to share that his preorder arrived, with numerous commenters chiming in that they have gotten their hands on the FX5 as well, including someone who walked into local stores without a preorder and picked up a unit.

That said, some who preordered have not yet received their cameras, so it’s unclear how many orders have been fulfilled versus how many customers are still waiting. It is, frankly, impossible to know because both Adorama and B&H are treating new FX5 orders as “preorders,” meaning the camera is not actively in stock yet. Meanwhile, the FX5 is not available to order directly through Sony in the U.S.

To say the FX5’s launch has been tumultuous would be an understatement. The camera was announced on July 22, and at the time, Sony said it would begin shipping just a few weeks later in “mid-August.”

When the planned release date arrived in August, Sony said the FX5 was delayed by at least a month. One month became two and then three. In early October, PetaPixel reported that the delay may have been tied to an issue with the rear LCD. Sony itself has never officially explained the delay.

In any event, the Sony FX5 has finally arrived. While it may take some time before all preorders are fulfilled, this is undeniably great news for videographers and creators. The Sony FX5 has certainly impressed us at PetaPixel so far, and we’re looking forward to doing a comprehensive review of the camera as soon as possible.

As PetaPixel wrote in July, there’s reason to believe the FX5 is Sony’s most important cinema camera to date. And now, finally, it’s here. It sure seems like Sony has a winner on its hands.
