#9026. Draconian Trump Executive Order Could Strip Art Orgs of Nonprofit Status

The order under consideration would strip all nonprofit organizations with alleged “terrorist ties” of their tax-exempt status.

After the Wall Street Journal reported earlier this month that the White House is considering an executive order that would strip nonprofits deemed to have alleged "terrorist ties" of their tax-exempt status, many arts and culture organizations are bracing for what could be a series of politically targeted attacks from the Trump administration.

According to the report, officials are reviewing Section 501(p)(2)(C) of the United States Internal Revenue Code, which authorizes the president to label nonprofits that are allegedly "supporting or engaging in terrorist activity." Organizations tagged with the label would have their tax-exempt status immediately suspended, spelling a potentially devastating blow to their operations.

The White House has not made an official confirmation or announcement of the measure, with a spokesperson telling Hyperallergic that "any policy announcements will come directly from the President," and "discussions about potential decisions or their impacts are otherwise baseless speculation."

#9025. Caá Porá Arquitectura and Jerome Haferd Studio design drum-like performance centre for Ecuador

Ecuadorian studio Caá Porá Arquitectura has teamed up with US-based Jerome Haferd Studio and engineer Juan Sebastián Pérez for the Bombódromo performance centre in Carchi, Ecuador.

The building will feature a central venue that has massive bamboo support elements based on local drums.

The campus will include dozens of buildings centred around a massive auditorium in the province of Carchi, north of Quito, sited along the Chota River in an Andean valley.

Masterplanned by Caá Porá Arquitectura, the campus was designed for local government to celebrate Afro-Ecuadorian culture.

Based on this, the central performance centre has a design based on the bomba, a drum used by local people.

“The inspiration for a lot of the design language was kind of to bridge African and Andean kind of design languages and ancestral aesthetics,” Jerome Haferd told Dezeen.

“That is embodied in the bomba drum, which is a unique instrument that is made by the people in this region, who we worked with very closely to come up with the design concept for the master plan.”

“[The bomba] was adapted and generated out of materials local to this valley in Ecuador, and so it’s really a hybrid between the Andean mountains and Africa.”

The main performance space, designed to hold more than 10,000, will have massive bundles of laminated bamboo supporting a roof system 30 metres in diameter.

These bundled columns have been designed to feature laminated bamboo and timber elements, reflecting the construction of the bomba drum and local construction methods more generally.

Acoustic fabric will hang from the wooden rafters of the semi-enclosed performance space.

A series of stone buildings will flank the main performance space, forming the back-of-house facilities.

An outdoor area will feature a tiered gathering space tucked into the low-lying trees around the river and provide the main viewing platforms for the performances.

As many as eight outbuildings will feature on the campus, including classrooms, a restaurant and artisan kiosks.

These structures will be built with metal roofs and rammed-earth walls, furthering the connection to local building techniques.

“The result is a radical, place-based reinterpretation of how a performing arts venue can respond to a unique cultural context while accommodating flexible uses,” said the team, which worked with local group Fundación Casa Oshun for the community outreach.

The project is expected to break ground in 2027.

Recently, a team including SANAA, Caá Porá Arquitectura, Estudio A0 and Jerome Haferd Studio was selected to design the National Museum of Ecuador in Quito, after the original design was cancelled following community backlash.

#9024. Caira Is Jumping on the Vibe-Coded Camera Train

Caira Is Jumping on the Vibe-Coded Camera Train

Camera Intelligence, the company behind the controversial Caira camera, is leaning into the current trend of vibe-coded camera hacks by making it a dedicated feature of its smartphone-mounted Micro Four Thirds camera system.

To call the Caira controversial is not a hot take: it’s one of the few cameras on PixelMeter that have an equal number of recommended, mixed, and panned reviews. The experience is highly subjective.

“I’ll give the Caira this: No one else is really making anything like it,” Chris Niccolls wrote in his review from earlier this year.

“I’m left with a concern about who would actually enjoy using the Caira camera. Advanced photographers will not enjoy the problematic handling, the generative AI features, and the fiddly control scheme, but this camera was never intended for them anyway. I worry that casual crowds will not appreciate the benefits of buying, carrying, and learning about interchangeable lenses, and see much benefit in the purchase of this product over their smartphones. Content creators might want to dabble with the different optics and some manual controls, plus they will find the separate functionality of the phone apart from the camera useful, but they generally already have DJI Pocket Osmo or Sony ZV cameras with mobile apps.”

From its inception, the Caira camera has been cozy with AI. In fact, it was one of the most panned features of the camera when it was in beta — Google’s Nano Banana image generator was built directly into the system, allowing users to generatively edit photos directly in the camera. Before the camera launched, Camera Intelligence reined in the capabilities of the system in response to the blowback.

“When we first announced the generative editing feature in October, it was an extremely raw, early, novel, and nebulous concept. We were not expecting to get everything perfectly right. But, it was being considered from a point of view that many people outside the camera industry find it challenging and overwhelming to navigate and maximize the benefits of editing tools like Lightroom and Photoshop,” Camera Intelligence’s CEO, Vishal Kumar, told PetaPixel.

While AI was significantly pulled back, it’s clear that Camera Intelligence’s goals for Caira are heavily influenced by it. That is reinforced today as the company is fully embracing vibe-coding camera hacks, a trend that has gotten very popular over the last couple of months. Think Magic Lantern, but for any camera and at the whim of the photographer.

“Something big is happening in the camera industry right now. Photographers are using AI tools like Claude Code and ChatGPT to hack their own cameras and add features the manufacturer never shipped. Many people are vibe coding these modifications without permission or a safety net, and some are bricking expensive cameras in the process,” Kumar says.

“At Camera Intelligence, we’ve been waiting for a moment like this and want to embrace and encourage this development. We’ve always had ambitions to provide access to our operating system that runs on the Caira (did you know that ‘Caira”‘ stands for ‘computational artificial intelligence camera’?). We’re opening up Caira, our Micro Four Thirds camera that attaches to an iPhone, through our new ‘Creative Sandbox’. It’s a new, safe development environment inside Camera Intelligence OS where our users can build their own features for the camera using their own AI coding tools.”

It’s hard to tell if this was something Camera Intelligence always envisioned as a possibility or if it’s just an example of the company jumping on the latest trend, but it is taking the capability seriously. It is hosting a Holiday Camera Hack in its London office in December, which is a one-day hackathon for up to 20 photographers, video creators, and engineers. Applications for that are open.

#9023. Tate Turns Julio Le Parc Into Instagram Art

The show elides the artist’s political motivations, instead cheerfully encouraging visitors to “let these mesmerizing works engage your senses.”

LONDON — In Paris, in the years leading up to the massive social upheavals of 1968, Julio Le Parc was making the first of his Game Rooms. These were collections of works that aimed to playfully destabilize the viewer’s experience, such as seats with springs that challenged the act of sitting, areas of uneven tile floors, and patterned discs designed to be manually spun. But for Le Parc, as well as the progressive collective Groupe de Recherche d’Art Visuel (GRAV) that he co-founded, the works were about far more than entertainment. Indeed, he hoped that cultivating the audience’s active participation would not only disrupt what he saw as the hierarchical and passive nature of the museum, but also effect a political awakening outside of it.

A recreation of one of the Game Rooms appears in the exhibition Julio Le Parc: Light. Colour. Action., which was “developed in close dialogue with the artist,” before his death earlier this year at the age of 97. Though the current world, as in 1960s Paris, grapples with mounting social and political tensions, one is unlikely to describe today’s art museum experience as “passive.” Indeed, outgoing Tate Modern Interim Director Catherine Wood notes in the exhibition catalog’s foreword, “At a time of heightened popularity for exhibitions touting immersive and interactive experiences, celebrating Julio Le Parc’s seven-decade career with a monographic exhibition at Tate Modern feels especially meaningful and urgent.”

#9022. British Museum and Victoria and Albert Museum extend loan of Asante regalia to the Manhyia Palace Museum in Ghana

Nicholas Cullinan, the director of the British Museum, visits the Asantehene Otumfuo Osei Tutu II in Kumasi, the historic capital of the Asante Empire and capital of today's Ashanti Region in Ghana

Asante regalia gold objects on loan from the British Museum and Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) will remain on show in Kumasi, Ghana until 2030 following the extension of loan agreements by the two UK museums. The British Museum has loaned 15 objects while the V&A lent 17 pieces, almost all of which were looted during military operations in the late 19th century.

The British Museum and the V&A signed a loan agreement in 2024 with Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, the 16th Asantehene (King of the Asante), to return the gold regalia to the Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi, the historic capital of what was then the Asante (Ashanti) empire. The loans will be renewed for a further three years at the end of the current term in April 2027. The two UK museums are legally unable to deaccession so the objects are being returned as long-term loans.

“The rollover of the loan agreement was always likely and from both the British Museum’s and Manhyia Palace Museum’s point of view, this has been a successful partnership with increased visitors, training and expansion at Manhyia. There is nonetheless enduring frustration from many in Ghana, both in Asante and beyond, that this is only a loan,” says Barnaby Phillips, author of The African Kingdom of Gold: Britain and the Asante Treasure.

The loan renewal announcement followed a recent visit to Kumasi by Nicholas Cullinan, the director of the British Museum, following an invitation by the Asantehene.

The gold regalia associated with the Asante royal court is on display in the Manhyia Palace Museum's Homecoming exhibition. Items shown include a small gold ornament in the form of a lute-harp (sankuo), one of the cast gold objects presented in 1817 to British diplomat Thomas Bowdich during his trip to Kumasi.

“The British Museum has about 220 pieces of Asante gold regalia and the Manhyia Palace Museum has been involved in the selection of objects [for loan]. There has been considerable input regarding what goes back to Ghana,” adds Phillips.

The idea of a loans deal, first discussed in the 1970s, was revived when the Asantehene visited London in May 2023 to attend the coronation of King Charles III.

The museum is investigating how the English-made jug turned up in West Africa before being seized during the 19th-century Anglo-Ashanti wars

The 32 items held in the collections of the two UK museums were taken during wars in the 19th century

#9021. “Mighty Miniatures” Features Over 300 Tiny Artworks From Indigenous Communities Across the Western Hemisphere

Opening November 21 at the National Museum of the American Indian in New York, this exhibition includes masterpieces created over a span of nearly two centuries.

“Mighty Miniatures,” an exhibition celebrating the intricate art of miniatures, is on view at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of the American Indian in New York from Saturday, November 21 through Friday, August 20, 2027. Curated by Anya Montiel (Tohono O’odham descent), the exhibition features over 300 pieces of art that showcase the skill of Indigenous weavers, sculptors, carvers and other artists that work on a miniscule scale.

The exhibition includes tiny masterpieces created over a span of nearly two centuries by artists from Indigenous communities from North and South America, as well as Hawai'i and the Caribbean. The small works reflect worldviews and cultural expressions, encouraging play and transferring intergenerational knowledge.

“‘Mighty Miniatures’ brings together some of the smallest works in the museum collection, reaching across the Western Hemisphere and spanning nearly 200 years,” Montiel said. “It is amazing to see how these miniatures have been made with such skill, ingenuity, and detail. This exhibition is a celebration of Indigenous artistry on a small scale and the artists who create them.”

Left: Nahua doll’s chair, no date. Wood, yarn. 0.7 x 0.5 in. (14/4064); right: Tohono O’odham I’itoi ki: (Man-in-the-Maze) miniature basket, ca. 2000. Arizona. Horsehair. 4 x 2.6 in. 26/8865

The exhibition is divided into six sections:

Left: Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) canoe model, no date. Minnesota, Birchbark, sinew, paint. 0.5 x 2.4 x 1.1 in. (20/4941); right: Floyd Kingeekuk Sr. (Siberian Yupik, 1933–2006), ringed seal figure, 1975. Savoonga, Alaska. Ivory, ink. 0.9 x 4.1 x 1.2 in. (27/684)

A family-friendly opening program is scheduled for Saturday, Dec. 12, 11 AM–4 PM. Multi-disciplinary artist Lance Cardinal (Cree), a finalist on the TV show Best In Miniature, will lead visitors in mini drum making sessions. Gallery tours by Montiel will illuminate the stories behind the objects and discuss how the exhibition came together.

#9020. How iPhone Duo’s Unlock With Front Camera Works (and How It’s Different Than Face ID)

How iPhone Duo’s Unlock With Front Camera Works (and How It’s Different Than Face ID)

The newest iOS 27 developer beta partially addresses one of the iPhone Duo’s biggest shortcomings: its lack of Face ID.

When PetaPixel reviewed the iPhone Duo, scoring it a 7.5, Jaron Schneider knocked Apple’s debut foldable for its reliance on relatively slow, inconsistent Touch ID. While Apple’s recent smartphones have all used Face ID to unlock quickly, the iPhone Duo sticks with Touch ID. It’s finicky, and users must hold the phone in just the right way to unlock it. Even when it works as expected, it’s not quite as swift as Face ID.

“I have found that Touch ID is slower than Face ID for unlocking the phone. It got to the point where I was so grateful that I have an Apple Watch because I could set it to automatically unlock it when it sensed I was wearing the watch. Unlock with Watch is also, somehow, faster than using Touch ID. It removed a lot of the friction I was butting up against with Touch ID, but it requires a Watch,” Schneider wrote of his Apple Watch-powered workaround.

However, with today’s launch of the iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple has begun testing a new feature: Unlock with Front Camera.

To be clear, this is not Face ID. The iPhone Duo still lacks the necessary hardware to offer the iPhone’s typical unlocking method. However, Unlock with Front Camera is set up in a similar way, requiring users to look at the front camera and turn their head from side to side. Like Face ID, it is also fast and works at off-angles.

I have been using an iPhone Duo review unit for the past few weeks as part of a long-term follow-up review and have been forced to rely on Touch ID on numerous occasions, often finding it frustrating. I installed the new developer beta on the Duo, set up Unlock with Front Camera, and am very much on board with it.

Again, it’s not a perfect Face ID replacement. It requires the user to use Touch ID every so often, for starters, about every 45 minutes. Just as other iPhone users occasionally need to enter their passcode for certain tasks or after a restart, iPhone Duo users will still need Touch ID even with this new feature.

Unlock with Front Camera does seem to work in poor lighting conditions, although I have not been able to test it yet in total darkness. Given the front camera’s lack of an infrared sensor, I expect some challenges.

Face ID relies on the iPhone’s TrueDepth sensor to quickly and securely confirm the user’s identity against existing robust data. Without Face ID and TrueDepth, the iPhone Duo doesn’t promise the same level of security or performance. Even so, Apple is clearly confident that Unlock with Front Camera is sufficiently secure, at the very least.

Unlock with Front Camera promises at least some of Face ID’s convenience, which is ultimately more important to most users than Apple’s absolute top-notch security. The iPhone Duo still stores facial data privately and securely to confirm (or deny) a match between the user attempting to unlock the phone and the initial setup imagery.

The Duo can definitely tell the difference between me and a picture of me. When I attempted to fool the Duo, it not only didn’t fall for my cleverly laid trap, but it also locked the device and required me to use Touch ID again. This is also its response when someone else tries to unlock my phone. If something doesn’t jibe, users must either use Touch ID again or enter their passcode.

It also works only with the front-facing camera, not the under-display one on the inner screen. That’s not a huge issue, but it’s worth noting.

So no, the iPhone Duo doesn’t suddenly have Face ID thanks to a software update, but it does have something that is at least better than what we had and addresses a very common complaint lodged against Apple’s new phone.

I will continue my long-term testing of the iPhone Duo, using it as my only smartphone. It has not been without its shortcomings, but Apple said today that there are now more than 200,000 apps that natively support the Duo. Between that and Unlock with Front Camera, the Duo genuinely keeps getting better.

#9019. Sumayya Vally to design Dubai art foundation around the "memory of a house"

South African architect Sumayya Vally is designing a permanent home for the Elie Khouri Art Foundation (EKAF), which will be located within a renovated villa in Dubai.

Set to be built in the Jumeirah 1 development in Dubai, the foundation’s home will be located in a former villa, which will be dramatically overhauled by Vally – principal of architecture studio Counterspace.

“I think of buildings as having many lives,” said Vally. “At EKAF, we begin with a house that has already held a world within it. Its doors, cornices, balustrades, and particular ways of receiving people and separating rooms contain the traces of another life,” she continued.

“I am interested in what happens when we take these intimate geometries and give them a new public scale: when the architecture of a room becomes the architecture of a city-facing facade, and the memory of a house becomes the beginnings of an institution.”

Although few details of the design have been revealed, a render shows what appears to be a three-storey building with a light pink textured facade.

Lines across the facade appear to suggest fragments of the previous building, with recognisable shapes including doorways visible. Geometric holes punched in the facade will reveal activities taking place inside.

EKAF was established by Lebanese-French businessman Elie Khouri and its permanent home is planned to open in 2028. The foundation will contain gallery space to show its permanent collection and will also include space for temporary exhibits.

“I hope that artists, designers, researchers and makers from the region will bring other imaginations into the work, and that the institution will continue to acquire forms and meanings we cannot yet anticipate,” added Vally.

Designer of the Serpentine Pavilion in 2021, Vally was named emerging architect of the year at Dezeen Awards in 2023 and one of Time magazine’s 100 leaders of the future in 2021.

#9018. Restitution Claim on $180M Van Gogh Shakes Up Sotheby's Marquee Week

Heirs of the Jewish publisher Samuel Fischer, who once owned the painting, are requesting it be withdrawn from auction.

Heirs of a prominent Jewish publishing family have called on Sotheby's to withdraw a rare Vincent van Gogh painting highlighted in the marquee auction sales in New York City this week, claiming that the work had been sold under duress amid Nazi persecution in Europe.

The heirs allege that the family member who owned the painting, which Sotheby's valued at a record-breaking $180 million, sold it because of Nazi-imposed restrictions on what emigrant Jews were allowed to take with them at the time.

Sotheby's confirmed to Hyperallergic that the painting is still slated to go under the hammer this Wednesday, November 18, and that it was aware of the heirs' concerns and “takes provenance and restitution matters extremely seriously and has undertaken extensive research into the [painting's] ownership history.”

#9016. Martin Puryear’s Liberatory Violence

A concern with liberation and revolution runs throughout his exhibition at the High Museum.

ATLANTA — Despite my best efforts to be anything else, I am a writer, and not even the Marines-like insanity of Bard’s interdisciplinary MFA or my day job in the library could erase that from me. Every object instantly becomes a word I see on a perfectly white page, a symbol made up of assorted shapes like “bicycle” (object that carried me from my home to the High Museum of Art) or “press pass” (object that allows me into the High Museum of Art), a compulsion that is always at its worst when viewing sculpture in the page-white tomb of a museum.

I was grateful for that compulsion, however, when I viewed Martin Puryear’s Nexus. Writing, underneath its surface, is extremely violent, exceptionally bloody, and annihilatory in scope. It is almost impossible to describe the reality of this fact on the page, and I have struggled even further to articulate this vocally to others, even other writers. So when walking into Nexus and “Bask” (1976) was there, lying as still and deadly as a knife on its white plinth, I smiled in surprised relief and my body physically relaxed. Puryear is noted for his use of natural materials — wood, rawhide, fiber — and his attention to traditional practices like basket weaving, boatmaking, tanning, and structure building from peoples around the world, which obscures the sculptures’ violence under that tricky word, “natural.”

#9015. Five little-known stage designs from the archives of Zaha Hadid

Photography by Luke Hayes unless stated otherwise

The unsung set designs of Zaha Hadid take centre stage in the latest exhibition curated by her foundation in London. In this roundup, we spotlight five standout objects that were uncovered from her archives for the show.

Named Zaha Hadid: Architecture of Performance, the exhibition is the Zaha Hadid Foundation‘s first collection-based show dedicated to the architect’s portfolio of stage and set designs.

It coincides with the reopening of the foundation’s home in Hadid’s former office – a former Victorian schoolhouse at 10 Bowling Green Lane in Clerkenwell, following a refurbishment by Studio KA coinciding with the 10th anniversary of Hadid’s passing.

The exhibition was curated by the foundation’s senior researcher Catherine Howe and design historian Libby Sellers as guest curator, and contains five projects illustrated through a mix of archival models, drawings, video footage and even costume.

Together, these offer insight into the evolution of Hadid’s signature complex geometries and digital design techniques, through the lens of sets for dance, opera and pop music.

According to curator Howe, the exhibition exemplifies how Hadid “didn’t want to be fixed” in her work, and how “she wanted to work across so many media”.

Howe added that the exhibition came about serendipitously, after the foundation had kept discovering records of these unsung projects while unpacking boxes.

“We open a lot of boxes,” she told Dezeen during a tour of the exhibition. “Sometimes it’s fortuitous, or it’s that there’s a big box and we need to move it, and we kept noticing all these amazing projects that hadn’t really been talked about.”

“Of course, everyone talks about her incredible buildings, but I think the interdisciplinarity of some of these projects was just being forgotten about, and we said ‘we need to do something on performance’.”

The foundation’s chairman, Rana Hadid, who is also the niece of Hadid, told Dezeen the reopening of the foundation was a “very emotional” moment for her, but suggested the exhibition only marks the beginning of discovering treasures in the foundation’s archive, which is estimated to contain 300,000 items.

“[Hadid’s] archive is so extraordinary, it’s limitless paintings, drawings, sketchbooks, digital material, personal material, it goes way beyond architecture,” Rana Hadid explained.

“It’s really about studying the process of her thinking, and using all that to help younger generations learn more about the process, the experimentation, the way you can start an idea and move forward with it, use technologies to be able to build it.”

The Zaha Hadid Foundation is an independent charity founded by Hadid in 2013. The Zaha Hadid: Architecture of Performance exhibition is on until 27 March 2027.

The foundation’s reopening programme also includes a video artwork by artist LionHeart and a timeline visualisation of Hadid’s life by data journalist Mona Chalabi.

Read on for five stand-out exhibits from the Zaha Hadid: Architecture of Performance exhibition.

Hadid created this model for her design for the staging of Mozart’s Così fan tutte opera, presented at Frank Gehry’s Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles in 2014.

Her dynamic stage design featured a spiralling white platform, engineered with sections that could rise and fall to help echo the shifting relationships of performers in the opera.

It had a curvature that mirrors many of her buildings, including the iconic Heydar Aliyev Centre in Baku, completed two years prior.

Another model featured in the exhibition is one Hadid created when designing the set for the Pet Shop Boys’ Nightlife World Tour, which took place between 1999 and 2000.

The design comprised an interconnected, reconfigurable system of ramps that could be tailored to suit different venues while maintaining the overall aesthetic. It also incorporated projection surfaces, transforming the stage into a multimedia environment.

According to the foundation, it was Hadid’s “first commission for a major pop concert”.

This collection of digital drawings depicts the stage design that Hadid created for the Metapolis Ballet in 1999, and embodies the abstract design language for which the architect was best known.

These ultimately became a trio of lightweight bridge structures that were moved, reconfigured and even worn by dancers across the stage. It is exhibited alongside a costume, which Hadid also designed for the ballet.

This trio of models were developed by Hadid for her pavilion at an event in Groningen called What a Wonderful World! Music Videos in Architecture in 1990.

It responded to a brief that asked for explorations into how the cultural phenomenon of music videos could be translated from screen to public space.

Hadid’s final design featured an uncharacteristically bright colour palette and a grid-like structure with shifting floors and angular walkways, and proposed “how architecture could shape the experience of viewing itself”, the foundation said.

The final pavilion was exhibited alongside contributions by her fellow ‘deconstructivist’ architects, including Rem Koolhaas, Bernard Tschumi, Peter Eisenman, and Coop Himmelb(l)au.

This abstract sketch of an unnamed architectural project, originally developed by Hadid for Hamburg, later formed the basis of a dance performance called d1 by British choreographer Rosemary Butcher.

The project, which was Hadid’s first dedicated to performance, saw the sketch transformed into a monochromatic network of lines on a floor, across which dancers moved as though “navigating a cityscape”.

Zaha Hadid: Architecture of Performance takes place from 3 November 2026 to Saturday 27 March 2027. For more events in architecture and design, visit Dezeen Events Guide.

#9014. What Does Frida Kahlo Mean Today?

A new documentary poses this question across socio-cultural contexts, steering clear of whitewashing the artist’s personal history.

These days, Frida Kahlo isn’t free. She is the plastic cosmetic bag in an Ulta carousel. She is a throw pillow in a World Market bin. Her name and image might be the most commodified of the 20th century, so ubiquitous that she feels emptied of meaning. Or is she?

Relying primarily on the testimony of Mexican voices, Frida: The Girl That Just Doesn’t Go Away, a new documentary by Trisha Ziff, poses this question across a colorful spectrum of socio-cultural contexts, steering clear of whitewashing the artist’s personal history. “I learned about Communism from Frida’s bookshelf,” shares actress and activist Ofelia Medina, who visited Kahlo’s home on a sixth-grade field trip.

“Frida gave me strength, she gave me a life and a job,” explains Juana López Sánchez, an Indigenous artisan whose livelihood is selling hand-crafted Frida dolls in Mexico City.

#9013. 'It is an unusual model, but I am an unusual person': Shafeena Yusuff Ali on her Abu Dhabi foundation and gallery

Shafeena Yusuff Ali, who has master’s degrees in art history, business administration and social impact, set up Rizq Art Initiative in 2023 Courtesy Rizq Art Initiative

If the art world is an orchestra of players, Shafeena Yusuff Ali is attempting a one-woman band. Born in Abu Dhabi to the Keralan billionaire M.A. Yusuff Ali, whose Indian-Emirati conglomerate LuLu Group spans retail, hospitality and real estate, she considers among her roles: collector, dealer, art historian, writer, entrepreneur and adviser to corporate and private collections.

It was upon acquiring work for her family’s London hotel that Yusuff Ali began envisioning a career within art. A trio of successive master’s degrees in art history, business administration and social impact led her to establish Rizq Art Initiative in 2023, an Abu Dhabi-based organisation that includes a commercial gallery, an artist and curator residency, an education platform, an off-site exhibitions programme and an advisory. The organisation is presently in the process of separating into a for-profit commercial gallery and a non-profit foundation.

Vivek Vilasini’s Housing Dreams (Walls) (2014). Yusuff Ali has acquired a large number of works by the Indian artist Courtesy Rizq Art Initiative

“It is an unusual model, but I think I am an unusual person,” she says. “Notmany gallerists have three postgraduate degrees, and carry both business and academic backgrounds. I understand how industries work and I have also written an art historical paper on each work in my collection”.

Rizq, which in Arabic means “provision” or “sustenance”, was established to kickstart a nascent scene by plugging overlooked gaps in the local art ecosystem. “The biggest challenge facing the Abu Dhabi art scene is a lack of nuanced peripheral actors,” Yusuff Ali says. “Critics, fabricators, experimental spaces, warehousing and storage. For an art ecosystem to work you need all these elements to work in coherence.”

Informed by Yusuff Ali’s ties to both India and the UAE, Rizq focuses on artists from the Global South, including young Emiratis Shamsa Almansoori and Reem Al Mubarak, and the Keralan watercolourist Anupama Alias Ani. Of just five commercial galleries in Abu Dhabi “we are the only one focusing on artists from the global majority”, she says.“This is important in a city where most inhabitants are from regions the art world doesn’t necessarily cater to.” During Frieze Abu Dhabi (18-22 November), the gallery is staging a solo show by Al Mubarak.

Beyond its Abu Dhabi gallery, Rizq also programmes offsite exhibitions, including a satellite show for the sixth edition of the Kochi Biennale in Kerala, contributing to a growing dialogue between the art worlds of South Asia and the Gulf.

Yussuf Ali's heritage also informs what she buys: areas of interest include lesser-known South Asian Modernists, such as the Keralan painter K.C.S. Paniker, as well as pioneering artists of the UAE like Hassan Sharif. Perhaps the artist whose work she has collected most widely is Vivek Vilasini, the only Indian member of the Flying House, a 2000s experimental art collective in Dubai that has hugely influenced today’s contemporary art scene in the UAE. “Vivek is a friend,” Yusuff Ali says. “It is remarkable that an Indian artist in the UAE has played such a central role in defining the nation’s art history.”

As for Abu Dhabi, Yusuff Ali believes in the long term, and understands that the local market is “only just beginning to grow”. Presently her private funds keep Rizq’s gallery afloat, but she is quick to point out that she speaks the language of business alongside art. “I have established a proof of concept and spent the past three years demonstrating measurable impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “I am confident that the next time we speak, we will have brought enough patrons on board to become profitable.”

The Art Newspaper: What was the first work you bought?

Shafeena Yusuff Ali: The first significant work was a Mona Saudi sculpture, Mother and Child (1981), before she passed away. I bought it when I was pregnant—and at a generationally different price. When I was buying it I fully realised it was special.

A painting by one of the forgotten masters of Kerala, N.K.P. Muthukoya.

If you could own any work from a museum what would it be?

I’d like to hang a work by Amrita Sher-Gil alongside one by Princess Fahrelnissa Zeid. My life bridges South Asia and the Middle East and these two women are strikingly similar in how they lived painful but luxurious lives.

What do you recommend doing outside the fair?

November is perfect biking weather. Walk around the city—don’t drive. And get a boat to one of the outer islands. They can be really magical.

What is your least favourite thing about art fairs?

Sometimes it gets too homogenous—the same seven galleries showing the same seven artists.

What should people know before coming to Frieze Abu Dhabi?

The culture here is quite shy, and highly relationship based. Newcomers might struggle if they lack patience.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November

#9012. Latinx Artists Are the New Visionaries

Without guarantees of commercial or institutional rewards, their work stems from a shared conviction: We have rich cultures to offer, and we will tell our stories by any means necessary.

Latinx communities are facing one of the most aggressive series of attacks in recent history, with many families enduring the pain of separation, persecution, and dehumanization. But if you’ve been paying attention to Latinx arts and culture, you’ll see that as we are being told to hide and disappear, artists are stepping into newfound confidence, showcasing the full value and complexity of our identities. The work of these new visionaries is a rallying cry: Now is the time to write, create, and make art boldly — together.

Over the past several years, I have documented the work of Latinx creatives across public art, fashion, and independent filmmaking, and I believe we have every reason to feel unabashedly optimistic. Across these fields, artists are choosing to create work that is deeply rooted in their communities, drawing directly from vernacular traditions, oral histories, and family memories that were once pushed to the margins. They are using culture to reclaim heritage and reframe the narrative. This marks a distinct departure from older paradigms, where artists were taught — or forced — to believe that conforming to mainstream, assimilationist models was the only path to success. While they recognize there are no guarantees of commercial or institutional rewards, their work stems from a shared conviction: We have rich cultures to offer, and we will tell our stories by any means necessary.

Sometimes, their methods involve elevating vernacular and popular culture to expand traditional aesthetic repertoires. We see this in contemporary fashion with designers like Willy Chavarria and Raul Lopez (Luar), who draw from working-class aesthetics, immigrant youth, and urban street culture. Most importantly, these designers openly credit their sources of inspiration, making clear that Mexican-American communities and neighborhoods and Black and Brown queer nightlife are fashion-forward in and of themselves. They frequently use street-cast Black and Brown models to communicate a richer, more inclusive vision beyond traditional, Eurocentric runways.

In other cases, artists reassess their communities' histories to directly challenge historical marginalization, as seen in the work of Gina Gwen Palacios in Brownsville, Texas. As SpaceX expands across the region, treating the land as empty of people and culture and ripe for corporate speculation, Palacios centers the rich legacy of Mexican-American communities and their direct links to the present. Through paintings that highlight her family’s legacy as fieldworkers alongside the underrepresented landscape of South Texas, Palacios elevates everyday elements such as nopales and mesquite trees to tell stories of migration, hard labor, and policing.

Against the settler-colonial myths propagated by SpaceX pundits, artist-led projects in the area, such as Boca Chica, Corazón Grande, have focused on crowdsourcing archival materials from residents to uplift their deep roots in the region. This effort reaffirms Boca Chica Beach’s identity as "the people’s beach," directly challenging claims that Brownsville and Rio Grande Valley communities are devoid of people and value, and merely sites for space launches, by centering residents' memories and their continued symbolic and living ties to the land.

The political significance of these types of projects cannot be overstated. While Guadalupe Rosales's landmark archival initiative Veteranas and Rucas has garnered considerable recognition in art circles, similar crowdsourced, post-custodial digital archives are emerging across Latinx communities nationwide. Examples include Nuevayorkinos, Documenting the Nameplate, Rhizomes: Mexican American Art Since 1848, and, of course, Boca Chica, Corazón Grande. By inviting community contributions, these platforms deliver the empowering message that everyone's history is inherently worthy of analysis and documentation.

This spirit is also evident in New York City’s public art, where artists are Latinizing the cityscape through projects that draw on marginalized elements of history, such as Afro-Indigenous heritage and the city’s Latinx and multicultural history, challenging the erasure of their presence across the city’s memorial and monument landscape. Melissa Calderón, the first Latina to create a permanent public monument in the city, paid homage to Roberto Clemente with “Para Roberto” (2019), the first monument of its kind in the Bronx. Maria Magdalena Campos Pons’s “Procession of Angels for Radical Love and Unity” (2024) reframed New York City’s history from the perspective of its Black and brown residents in a performance filled with Orisha Santeria references. That same year, Edra Soto’s “Graft” (2024–25) took over the Doris C. Freedman Plaza in Central Park, inaugurating a sculptural installation drawing on Caribbean and Puerto Rican vernacular architecture. Think also of David Rios’s “Get Carried Away, You have the Right” (2023), drawing on Afro-Taino futuristic images in his installation at Amtrak, and Shellyne Rodriguez’s “Phoenix Ladder: Monument to the People of the Bronx” (2025), a reproduction of a Bronx building evoking the borough’s strength and rebuilding after the 1970s fires.

It is true that many of these artists remain marginalized, navigating a chronic lack of opportunities and resources. Consider the last time you saw a film by award-winning independent Latinx directors like Cecilia Aldarondo or Diana Peralta on a mainstream streaming home screen or in a theater. Yet when we look at the work itself — its courage, its artistry, and its local impact — the movement is undeniably transformative. It demonstrates that Latinx communities are resilient and that art and culture are powerful tools of empowerment and continuity.

This realization is vital not just for us, but for society at large. Appreciating Latinx art offers a clear path beyond the polarized, distorted representations that have dominated public discourse for so long. The narratives Latinx artists uplift are the very ones everyone must champion as we navigate the rapid rise of AI technology and the growth of violent capitalism. Artists in the Rio Grande Valley, for example, are fiercely defending the intrinsic value of their environment and history, reminding us that community and culture are ultimately priceless. Others are also confronting traditional histories and value hierarchies within creative industries while redefining what is considered fashionable, memorable, and significant.

Most importantly, artists’ visions have the potential to generate change in all of us. This work actively transforms the lives of future generations: raised with powerful models of resistance against dehumanization and persecution, their imaginations will remain free.

Arlene Dávila's new book, Visualizing Latinx: Creative Practices in Fashion, Film, and Beyond (2026), is now out through Duke University Press.

#9011. Not a Hotel Architects converts brutalist Tokyo warehouse into own office and headquarters

Japanese company Not a Hotel‘s in-house architecture team has turned a 1967 warehouse into a workspace divided by glass partitions and filled with design classics, including an entire Jean Prouvé house.

The former logistics warehouse has a brutalist design and spacious interior with seven-metre-tall ceilings.

To create zones that could house different departments for the Not a Hotel (Nota) company, which is known for its striking hotel designs, the architects added three-metre-high glass partitions that divide the floor plan into three rows.

These were then divided into multiple smaller rooms that have different functions.

While creating the new interior, the in-house team, called Not a Hotel Architects, decided to keep the building’s existing structure and make it a defining feature of the design.

“The project embraced the raw, brutalist beauty of the existing structure – retaining its steel frame and exposed concrete surfaces,” Not a Hotel architect Kei Shiho told Dezeen.

The building will function as the office and headquarters for Not a Hotel, as well as a location that could be used by the owners of its Nigo House – a hotel built into a cliff overlooking Tokyo Bay and designed by artist Nigo.

“We wanted the Nota office to not just be a place for our employees but two other things: a foundational base for the brand’s vision and identity, as well as a place to host the Nigo Lounge for owners of The Nigo House,” Shiho said.

As a result, the office features a mix of both unusual Nigo designs and design classics, with the large spaces enabling the architects to play around with the interior.

“The high ceilings created a great canvas to experiment with interior design, including exhibiting a bit of Nigo’s rare goods collection in USM Haller boxes up to the ceiling as well as installing the Jean Prouvé demountable house,” Shiho said.

In the Harumi Lounge, a 15-metre-long table with a decorative wooden tabletop sits underneath the seven-metre-tall ceiling. Translucent curtains can be closed on both sides to create a calmer environment and shield it from the workplaces next door.

An original demountable house by architect Prouvé has its own room and can be used for work or meetings.

“Its inclusion serves as a daily reminder and educational tool for the architectural team regarding material longevity and functional beauty,” Shiho explained.

The Nigo Lounge, which is near the office entrance, features three walls clad with 352 USM Haller cabinets filled with design and art pieces.

Another room holds Nota’s library of physical architecture samples inside 96 custom Globe-Trotter trunks, which function as a materials library that is searchable via QR codes.

The design pieces on display in the headquarters were chosen as a callback to things that inspired the launch of the company, which has a strong design focus.

“Our founder Shinji Hamauzu was a vintage furniture collector, and he started Not a Hotel with the idea that he wanted to build properties that could be a place to exhibit masterpieces of design,” Shiho said.

“So the main showpieces in the office are all things related to our brand and our creative community, as well as our inspirations: many pieces by the late designer Virgil Abloh, vintage furniture from Prouvé, Perriand, and Jeanneret.”

The project has been shortlisted in the large workplace interiors category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards.

Not a Hotel recently released designs for a giant Poké Ball guest room and is working with Nigo and Pharrell on a new district in Tokyo.

#9010. What Mary Lovelace O'Neal Left Behind

"Requiem" is a fitting self-elegy for the painter, precisely because nothing about it feels mournful.

Upon her death in May 2026, the abstract painter Mary Lovelace O’Neal left behind a monumental body of work. Her oeuvre includes signature large blackened canvases, marked by fluid, ecstatic gestures in neon paint that resemble the glowing afterimages of a moving flame. O’Neal’s first posthumous exhibition, Requiem, is a fitting self-elegy for the painter precisely because nothing about it feels mournful.

The work could not be more vital, and in it one feels the artist’s energetic and intuitive handling of paint as a kind of physical charge. O’Neal’s compositions transmit a powerful sense of presence and force, as though inviting viewers into the vicarious experience of an artist grappling with the formal concerns of color and line before transcending them.

The result is an almost oceanic feeling, one I imagine is equally profound in the making of a painting as staggering as the intense, cascading standout “Requiem for a Daffodil” (1997). The black, fingerlike marks that protrude from the surrounding deep navy seem to be reaching for the floral clusters and reeds in the painting’s top half, like a perpetual grasping at splendor in the shadows.

Though non-representational, these works continually approach figuration, filled with partial outlines of human and animal forms. These half-figures peer through their dark surroundings, like the pink mass in the center of “What’s Time to a Pig” (c. 1990s), and are caught in a constant state of emergence. Like an act of divine creation, O’Neal captures the transformation of raw material into something seemingly miraculous through the hands of a master craftsman.

During this formative and fruitful period between the 1970s and 1990s, when her visual language and iconoclastic artistic sensibility crystallized, O’Neal was also coming into her own as an artist. She was a groundbreaking student, becoming the first Black woman to receive an MFA from Columbia University in 1969, and in 1985, she became the first African American professor to receive tenure in UC Berkeley’s Department of Art Practice.

The back room offers a rich sketch of the painter’s life as it intersected with both world history and art history. Born in Jackson, Mississippi, in 1942, Jim Crow was fully in place in the American South during the artist’s childhood.  She attended Howard University in 1960 alongside David Driskell and Lois Mailou Jones, dated the activist Stokely Carmichael, and was an activist in her own right.

The archival materials reveal the cultural and political concerns of O’Neal’s time. It’s all the more remarkable that she navigated these constraints while retaining the verve and genuine, delightful strangeness these paintings must have necessitated. “Untitled” (n.d.) gets at the humor and irreverence of O’Neal’s style. An Uncle Sam-like figure, half-covered in chalky white paint, evokes a satirical Ralph Bakshi cartoon, with many identifying features erased. It has a winking quality. Though political in nature, it foregrounds O’Neal’s formal concerns, which circle mainly around the possibilities of certain pigments (like the enveloping darkness of lampblack contrasted with punchy neons) and the permeable boundary between abstraction and figuration. It is this formal rigor that made O’Neal trailblazing in more ways than one –– both as a Black American shattering institutional barriers and as a woman painter making important interventions into the inherited, lionized artistic movements of the Color Field, Abstract Expressionism, and Minimalism.

Mary Lovelace O'Neal, "Race Woman Series #7" (1992-93), mixed media on canvas (left); Mary Lovelace O'Neal, "Untitled" (n.d.), mixed media and oil on canvas

“Race Woman Series #7” (1992–93) dramatizes the tension between the structural or compositional and the political, suggesting that it was an enduring preoccupation for the artist. A dazed face vaguely springs up from a prominent green being, which could just be read as an indecipherable scrawl, while a white specter at the top of the canvas drips over it. O’Neal’s use of color is frenetic and instinctive, resulting in a painting that is too varied to slot into a clear interpretation. Like the Klannish chiaroscuro of Norman Lewis’ “Alabama” (1960), the legibility of “Race Woman Series #7” relies on the light its instructive title sheds on it.

But unlike Lewis, when we search for correlation between O’Neal’s caption and the canvas, we are pulled deeper into her self-reflexive, numinous and unrepeatable idiom, which makes its own intuitive sense and, anyway, seeks to go beyond sense-making into the terrain of near-mystical experience.

Mary Lovelace O’Neal: Requiem continues at Boesky Gallery (509 West 24th Street, Chelsea, Manhattan) through December 19. The exhibition is organized by the gallery.

#9009. Talking Art and Data With Mona Chalabi

The award-winning journalist and artist talks about her first book. Plus, Carolina A. Miranda on two new Guadalupe Rosales tomes out this fall.

Mona Chalabi is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist, and as much as it shows across her incredible body of visual data reporting, she has always kept her eye on another prize entirely. I sat down with her earlier this fall at Christopher Park across from the Stonewall Inn, a site of protest and resistance, to talk about her new book and her career as a whole.

The culmination of six years of research, interviews, and illustration, Ten Lives breaks the silence around class in her characteristic visual style. To me, it’s a reflection of her principled approach to journalism and storytelling that feel utterly lost in a world where self-promotion, access, and branding can matter more than the work itself. Chalabi brings a refreshing integrity and playful approach to reporting unflinchingly on the genocide in Palestine, the horrors of the healthcare system, and massive wealth inequality. While she insists her work isn’t “fine art,” it’s perhaps the purest example of what art should do: challenge our ways of seeing. She’s also uncommonly funny, humble, and perceptive. (Can you tell I’m a fan?)

Class is also at the center of photographer Mark Alice Durant’s memoiristic book, which critic Melissa Holbrook Pierson likens to Rainer Maria Rilke’s Letters to a Young Poet for our dystopian world of 2026. Other books in this edition similarly respond to the Orwellian state of art and power. Nitasha Dhillon and Amin Husain, both scholars and activists, have organized protests against the Museum of Modern Art in 2021, the Whitney Biennial in 2019, and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi in 2015, among other instances of artwashing. They penned a joint review of Italian curator and organizer Marco Baravalle’s book The Battleground of Art: Radical Curating in the Crisis of Neoliberalism, a toolkit for seeing through the mainstream art world’s undermining of political movements and building sustainable alternatives.

Critic Carolina A. Miranda, meanwhile, takes up two new books by East Los Angeles artist Guadalupe Rosales, who came up in a community of Chicano kids raised in the 1990s amid uprisings and political action. Miranda writes that the anthology Rosales edited, as well as her blended memoir and photo book, perfectly encapsulate “the ways she engages the stories of others even as she tells her own.” A wise observation to carry with us as we face the week ahead; more of the latest in art book reviews and news below.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books

#9008. Public toilets in Paris by Chartier-Corbasson "elevate the ordinary"

Photography by Romain Meffre & Yves Marchand

French studio Chartier-Corbasson Architectes has transformed a neglected underground passage beneath the Trocadero Gardens in Paris into a public restroom, using an industrial-feeling palette of stainless and weathered steel.

The project forms part of the ongoing OnE masterplan, a competition-winning scheme to develop the public spaces and gardens around the Eiffel Tower that was awarded to Paris-based Chartier-Corbasson Architectes and London studio Gustafson Porter + Bowman in 2019.

The public toilets occupy a tunnel through the Trocadero Gardens that was originally designed for the 1937 Universal Exposition by Roger Lardat, framed by distinctive openings in bush-hammered concrete and lined by flint walls that were etched with graffiti by US soldiers at the end of the second world war.

The tunnel had long been closed to the public, used instead as a storage area for the city’s cleaning services. For its renovation, which has been shortlisted in the Heritage project category of Dezeen Awards 2026, Chartier-Corbasson Architectes looked to highlight its thoughtful, utilitarian design while giving it a new purpose.

“Far from being a mere functional adaptation, the project, entirely off-site, transforms a closed, neglected, and invisible space into a high-value, integrated, and dignified public amenity situated in a busy urban environment,” explained the studio.

“By restoring meaning and form to a previously purely utilitarian space, this project demonstrates that architecture can elevate even the most ordinary uses, while having a significant impact on the city, its users, and its collective memory.”

The distinctive pink-toned bush-hammered entrances at either end of the tunnel have been carefully restored, and now frame a series of new Corten steel gates that incorporate sculptural seating elements at either end.

The original domed skylights that illuminate these entrance spaces have been updated with custom-made glass blocks, while below, their form is mirrored in a series of circular stainless-steel sinks.

The majority of the toilets occupy a row of stainless-steel cubicles inserted between the flint-lined walls of the central passage, creating a two-way route with doors that open on alternating sides.

As much as possible, the existing structure was adapted with minimal intervention, demonstrated by a series of cubicles that have been tucked into a series of curved niches at one of the tunnel’s entrances and simply fronted with stainless-steel doors.

“The direct reuse of the underground space, without expansion or alteration, demonstrates a restrained and intelligent approach to urban transformation,” said the studio.

“The intervention focuses on a clear material contrast: the systematic use of stainless steel highlights the original flint walls and concrete, further enhanced by strategic artificial lighting,” it added.

As part of the project, Chartier-Corbasson Architectes introduced natural ventilation into the subterranean spaces and also created new stainless-steel gutters to help manage water infiltration from above.

Given its setting in a high-traffic public park, the new elements were predominantly constructed off-site to minimise disruption and on-site waste.

Other projects that have recently sought to elevate public toilet design include a toilet block in London by Studio Weave, which is clad in contrasting panels of stone salvaged from a demolished office building, and the 17 Tokyo Toilets designed by famous architects.

Photography by Romain Meffre & Yves Marchand

#9007. Why Is the Whitney Museum Selling a De Kooning Painting?

“Yellow River” (1958) was deaccessioned and will be auctioned at Christie's just three years after it was gifted to the museum in 2023.

Looking to cash in on marquee week in New York, the Whitney Museum of American Art has consigned a Willem de Kooning painting from its collection to Christie's for its 20th-century evening sale tomorrow, November 17. Once a promised gift to the museum, de Kooning's “Yellow River” (1958) is expected to fetch up to $18 million.

The practice of museum deaccessioning has long been a subject of controversy. In 2022, the Association of Art Museum Directors (AAMD) loosened its policy to allow institutions to apply funds from the sale of deaccessioned art toward the “direct care” of their collections.

A lot description for “Yellow River” on Christie's website notes that the proceeds will benefit the Whitney's collection. The Whitney has not yet responded to Hyperallergic's request for comment, but a museum spokesperson told Artnet News that deaccessioning is “a component of the Whitney’s collections strategic plan, allowing the museum to thoughtfully evaluate and refine its holdings in support of its long-term collection priorities.”

The de Kooning painting going under that hammer had a rooted connection to the Whitney before it was bequeathed to the museum in 2023. Postwar art collector, attorney, and museum trustee David Solinger, who would go on to become the museum's first president beyond the Whitney family in 1966, purchased the work from de Kooning's sold-out exhibition at Sidney Janis Gallery in 1959.

“Yellow River” emerged from a series of “highway" paintings representing the artist's shift from cacophonous urban compositions to more airy landscapes, designating the freeway as a conduit connecting New York City to the Hudson River Valley and Long Island's South Fork. In vibrant warm yellow, earthy brown tones, and stretches of deep blue, de Kooning's decisive gestures direct viewers across overlapping paths and visual rest stops throughout the canvas.

“I love to be on those highways,” de Kooning said to British critic and curator David Sylvester about the expansive roads during a BBC interview in 1960. “And they are really not very pretty, but the big embankments and the shoulders of the roads and the curves are flawless.”

“Yellow River” hung at the foot of Solinger's bed for some time, serving as a testament to Solinger's fascination with the artist. His wife, Betty Ann Besch Solinger, took ownership of the work after Solinger passed in 1996, and in 2011, she designated the work as a promised gift to the Whitney in honor of her late husband. It officially entered the Whitney's holdings in 2023, the same year that the museum deaccessioned seven works, including an Edward Hopper landscape, and sent them to auction to benefit the collection.

Opening November 21 at the National Museum of the American Indian in New York, this exhibition includes masterpieces created over a span of nearly two centuries.

#9006. Tonkin Liu creates pair of glulam buildings for craftspeople restoring York Minster

London architecture studio Tonkin Liu has created two timber buildings on either side of York Minster, which contain facilities for workers restoring the Gothic cathedral.

Named The Centre of Excellence for Heritage Craft Skills, the buildings include the rectangular Heritage Quad and the triangular Technology Hub, both of which give working stone masons views of the Grade I-listed York Minster.

“These are the first two buildings to be built with historical precedent in a hundred years; it was important that they responded to the setting and heralded a new chapter for heritage craft,” Tonkin Liu co-founder Mike Tonkin told Dezeen.

“The restoration of York Minster needed to be accelerated because climate change is increasing its degradation,” he continued. “The two new buildings will speed up the conservation by four decades within the next century.”

Working with preservation body Historic England and local planning authorities, Tonkin Liu retained, repurposed and extended a series of existing structures near York’s medieval city walls to form the Heritage Quad.

Its facilities, which contain workshops and education spaces for stonemasons and accommodation for apprentices, are united by glued-laminated timber (glulam) and a plywood roof that extends to partially cover a central courtyard.

Its distinctive roof channels water into rainwater tanks, rounding over the courtyard to give working masons a framed view of York Minster, and tilting up at the northern end to give passersby views into the workshops.

On the other side of the cathedral, the steel-and-glulam-constructed Technology Hub houses digital technology tools for stone cutting.

Triangular in plan, the hub features rows of arched windows rising from its photovoltaic-covered roof.

“Planning restricted the upper height within the surrounding buildings, and cutting equipment and gantry cranes set the lower structural height limit,” said Tonkin.

“The need to allow views of the Minster and light into the surrounding buildings led to parabolic fan vaults that fill the workshop with light.”

Both the Heritage Quad and the Technology Hub were constructed from glulam, setting them apart from their historic neighbour.

“The buildings are fabricated in timber – stone is reserved for the Minster,” said Tonkin.

However, Tonkin Liu drew upon the cathedral’s use of light and geometry when designing two structures.

“The two buildings work within the ecclesiastical tradition that celebrates structure, geometry and light,” said Tonkin. “Both buildings have a physical and symbolic relationship to the Minster.”

“The roof of Heritage Quad rises between the square and the circle, forming an arch that gives the masons a clear view of the Minster – the verticality of the expressed structure works with the tradition of the Minster’s perpendicular Gothic character,” he continued.

“The Technology Hub’s triangular plan is set back from the boundary wall to maintain views of the Minster from the surrounding houses,” added Tonkin. “The wooden vaults find strength through form, as in the Minster, and trusses align with the existing walls and consequently radiate towards the transept of the Minster.”

The Centre of Excellence for Heritage Craft Skills is shortlisted in the mixed-use category of this year’s Dezeen Awards.

Other projects completed by Tonkin Liu that have featured on Dezeen include a biometric tower in Manchester’s Civic Quarter and a swing bridge at London’s Crystal Palace Park, which gives access to an island filled with 19th-century concrete dinosaur models.

#9005. Frieze Abu Dhabi’s Global Futures section to reflect the 'turbulence and violence of our times'

“I looked at projects that reflected the turbulence of our times, the violence of our times,” says Tarini Malik, the curator of Frieze Abu Dhabi’s Global Futures section Sarah Bates

Abdullah Al Saadi devises an alphabet from sweet potatoes; Ala Younis’s mosaics make monuments from old, nondescript buildings; Mohammed Joha assembles cardboard and textiles as collages addressing displacement.

Disparate as these works seem, they are being shown in dialogue with one another in the Global Futures section at Frieze Abu Dhabi, where they will be presented as unique systems of knowledge that preserve memory and lived experience.

Curated by Tarini Malik, the section features solo presentations by artists from a range of artistic and cultural backgrounds. In some ways, the section builds upon conversations from other parts of the fair. Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi, for instance, will investigate historic routes of migration, trade and cultural exchange across the Indian Ocean. Global Futures appears to attempt this within a contemporary context.

“The process of putting together Global Futures actually came together quite beautifully and organically,” Malik says. “We started with a number of proposals, looking at projects that felt so apt to this moment. We thought about what it means to have a fair, what it means to have this international constellation of galleries at this moment in Abu Dhabi. What are the conversations happening within the cultural sphere that are prevalent to this moment?”

With Taymour Grahne Projects, the Kuwaiti artist Ala Younis will present 11 works from her Climate Conditions series. The mosaic panels, crafted out of hand-cut stones and mounted on metal frames, depict old office buildings, municipal structures and other places in Abu Dhabi that are often overlooked. Younis first unveiled the series in her 2025 solo exhibition at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery. The project materialised after a three-year stay in the Emirati capital. Knowing the city’s propensity for rapid change, she sought to document and commemorate the structures as she saw them. In rendering their likeness in mosaics, Younis alludes to the Roman tiles that have outlasted the structures they once decorated. The title of the project refers to how the structures interact with the environment—their wood and metal bits expanding and contracting to changes in humidity and temperature.

The Mexican artist Tania Candiani, on the other hand, looks underground for a more sprawling and rhizomatic type of structure. Her Root Systems, presented by Galeria Vermelho, charts networks of plant roots in embroidery, unearthing a subterranean language with its own systems of exchange and communication.

“These projects established two very different but sort of complementary points of departure,” Malik says. “They look at these ideas of migration, of ecology, of transformation—shared across different temporalities and across different structures.”

These themes, Malik says, resonate across the other presentations in Global Futures.

Through his Naked Sweet Potato series, Abdullah Al Saadi transcribes his personal engagement with the landscape of his native Khor Fakkan. Studying the different shapes and textures of sweet potatoes, the Emirati artist renders a language from the vegetable. He makes jewellery from it and he uses it to revisit his childhood, to transcribe his excursions to the UAE countryside. Where Candiani lays bare the universal language of roots, Al Saadi’s Naked Sweet Potato introduces an idiosyncratic and deeply personal lexicon to the conversation. The series includes drawings, paintings, sculptures and engravings, as well as collected materials. First shown at the UAE National Pavilion during the 2011 edition of the Venice Biennale, Naked Sweet Potato will be presented at Global Futures by Aisha Alabbar Gallery.

With Zawyeh Gallery, the Palestinian artist Mohammed Joha will exhibit No Shelter, building upon the series he is presenting at this year’s Venice Biennale (until 22 November). His canvases feature stratified layers of discarded textiles, paper and cardboard that come together as vibrant, abstracted landscapes.

The artist, who is based in France, began the series as he watched the destruction of his native Gaza from afar. His work comes as a poignant expression of heartache, the shredded materials evoking the devastation of Gaza and the forced displacement of its population. The way they come together in colourful compositions, however, simultaneously stands up against the violence, insisting on reconstruction in the face of ruin.

“I looked at projects that reflected the turbulence of our times, the violence of our times,” Malik says. “Things can feel unsettled and art opens up a dialogue for us to understand one another.”

The Indian-born artist Arshi Irshad Ahmadzai, showing at Global Futures with the Mumbai-based gallery Chatterjee & Lal, will be showing her series Azal se Abad tak, which includes drawings and paintings on cloth. The works investigate how different cultures have articulated the concept of eternity.

The Ghanaian artist Godfried Donkor will present paintings, collages and embroidery with Gallery 1957. He draws from an eclectic range of inspirations for his works, including comic book superheroes, boxing athletes as well as mythological figures.

Finally, Marfa’ Projects will exhibit works by the Lebanese artist Seta Manoukian. A celebrated figure of the late 1960s Beirut art scene, Manoukian’s paintings are a stunning, often otherwordly depiction of life during the Lebanese Civil War. The works Manoukian produced after emigrating to Los Angeles in the late 1980s can be regarded as attempts at establishing stability and certainty in the aftermath of the conflict. These include works from her T-Shape series, which will be exhibited at the fair.

“We have work from her Rose series to her Rock series, as well as one of her early more figurative paintings,” Malik says. “In a constellation of around five or six works, we’re trying to build something that feels like a journey through the life of a really iconic artist.”

All in all, the Global Futures section, Malik says, seeks to draw connections between the exhibiting artists in a way that does not reduce the “specificity of where these artists are from and what they’re talking about”.

“I think we’ve chosen works together that really represent [a given] body of work by that artist in the best way possible,” Malik says. “It was really about building shared connections […] while also thinking about how they intersect in the UAE and in this rapidly transforming city.”

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November

Yoto is winning the low-screen moment by holding back. Its designers explain how they balanced a vocal community with a clear mission.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I’ve been obsessed with Yoto since 2019, when a friend introduced me to the tactile, lo-fi audio player for kids. My children have used it daily ever since, and it’s one of the most interesting brands out there. It arrived just as parents were looking for an alternative to endless high-stimulation screens, and it has grown from a community-led, Kickstarter-style product with its foibles into a polished, self-assured brand that still listens closely to its community.

So when I heard a new generation was on its way, I asked to speak to the design team behind the biggest shake-up of its physical design yet. It’s a fairly tricky proposition: a product used by children but invested in by parents, with a clear mission and a feature set that’s still evolving. The new players have a mischievous new look, a green dial (big news in the world of Yoto) and a few other added features. Most importantly, the design team and Yoto chose not to lean any harder on the screen’s capabilities. For families trying to rely less on screens, that’s a crucial decision.

Below is my conversation with Jack Godfrey Wood of design studio Heirloom, covering the design mission, how the players were prototyped and tested, and the challenge of designing for a product with such a clear purpose and such a vocal community.

We knew people there. One of our colleagues worked on the original Kickstarter version, the wooden cube with the two blue dials, and two of our team designed the later generations at another company. When we started Heirloom, we took on the current fourth-gen players, so our team has been involved in and out from the beginning. It made sense straight away, because we all had that Fisher-Price cassette deck as kids and this felt like this generation’s version. Once Tom and Ben showed us the community they’d built, I knew it would work.

There were technical aims and design aims. Yoto wanted more storage, more battery and more internal robustness, and they wanted the player to be splashproof. That meant a lot of work on keeping dust and liquid out. Inside, the downloads are faster, there’s more storage and the sound is better, so they’ve fixed the things I wanted fixed as a parent. Our job was to make the players fit better in kids’ hands, travel better, and be easier to hold, carry and drop without anything breaking.

Sign up to the design newsletter from Creative Bloq, brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of graphic design, branding, typography and more.

Where did your design decisions come from?

Both the community and our own experience, plus writing some rules. Yoto’s core goal is “kids in control and parents in charge”. We also knew we didn’t want addictive, distracting moments. Both screens have more resolution than before, but we kept everything in pixel world, because to us that’s Yoto. It’s a fun menu, not a distracting screen. We could have added motion, like a character that waves at you if nothing happens for 15 minutes, but we felt the community would say that was wrong.

Does Yoto’s approach feel different to other consumer tech clients?

Yes. Yoto’s goal isn’t to keep eyeballs on the screen. It’s how often the player gets used and whether it adds value to a child’s and a family’s life. It’s a very clear moral code, which makes design decisions easier. A lot of the pixel work we did is artful, precise and beautiful, but we kept it happily lo-fi and didn’t turn it into another Apple product.

Yoto wanted the backup content stored in each player to be available on the player itself. That way, if you can’t find the card, your kids can still listen to what they like, and you don’t have to get your phone out at 9pm when nobody’s going to bed. The hard part was doing that without turning the screen into an iPod or an iPad.

It was our way of giving kids access to what they want without overwhelming them with 200 cards. Daily radio and podcasts have moved onto it, along with 20 favourites. It populates automatically, but parents can set up day and night versions in the app. At night, all 20 can be sleep or relaxation content. In the daytime, you can have Elton John and Harry Potter. It also means your favourites are there wherever you go, which is really good for holidays. We still love cards, though. In all our research, they’re still the main way younger kids want to use it.

For one of the players, up to 10 to 15 concepts across a few different areas. When we gave the more pebbly form to some children, it was obvious how naturally it fitted their hands and how much they wanted to hold on to it, so we presented that one with a strong recommendation. For the other, we looked at five or six directions, but Yoto wanted it to feel like a continuation of the previous products. The concept was quite singular, and we spent a lot of time on the detailing: where the dials sit, how sharp they should be, and so on.

What did you change about the dials and finish?

The dials used to be crisp. We softened them so kids can reach them from different angles, and made them slightly longer for more grip. The smart button isn’t in the middle, which most designers would do. Because it’s a kids’ product, kids can use it from the front as they hold it.

How do you work with such an opinionated community?

Because we’re external to Yoto, they do most of the community work and the feedback is funnelled to us through the Yoto team. We’re forthright about what we think is right within Yoto’s mission, and we don’t try to do everything people ask for. The challenge is that the community is always ageing up, but we also have to look after new families who’ve never used Yoto. A new user shouldn’t have to learn anything, and an existing user shouldn’t be thrown off because every feature suddenly does something else. The community’s feedback is great because it comes from hard-won experience, not assumptions.

By keeping the mischief, fun and wonder, and the underdog spirit, rather than suddenly feeling like a big corporation. My favourite bits are the hidden details. There are little faces between the dials, and the charging cable has four tiny Yoto logos, one of which is winking. No one’s going to talk about it, but one day someone will spot it and get a little flutter of appreciation.

Georgia has worked on Creative Bloq since 2018, and has been the site's Editor since 2023. With a specialism in branding and design, Georgia is also Programme Director of CB's award scheme – the Brand Impact Awards. As well as immersing herself with the industry through attending events like Adobe Max and the D&AD Awards and steering the site's content streams, Georgia has an eye on new commercial opportunities and ensuring they reflect the needs and interests of creatives.
