#9003. YSG creates Bali wellness hotel with DJ station

Australian studio YSG has converted a former private vacation residence into a boutique hotel in Bali focused on playful spaces and Indonesian music and culture.

The Moon Gang Bali hotel is located among the rice fields on the northern outskirts of Ubud and includes five interconnected suites, outdoor terraces and a lounge surrounding a central courtyard.

According to its Australian hoteliers, the hotel was inspired by “our feverish obsession with Indonesian music and culture” and its offerings include an all-day spa and a “DIY DJ station” stacked with Indonesian and Japanese city pop records curated by DJ Midnight Runners.

YSG was similarly influenced by Indonesian and Japanese design for the hotel’s spaces, which feature bamboo and timber structures and lava stone tiling.

“Once a private vacation residence in severe disrepair, the concrete bunker was radically transformed into a modern-day Babylon infused with cosmic references and hybrid Japanese architectural elements, including the spa’s sliding bamboo doors depicting lunar phases,” the studio said.

The hotel is only accessible via motorbike or on foot, according to the team, and is located along an alleyway.

Guests enter on the far side of the courtyard pool, while the suites and common areas enclose the space on three sides.

The suites were designed with “dreamers, misfits and wanderers in mind”, according to the hotel, and each is outfitted with an assortment of objects by local studios set against walls clad in recycled earth-based finishes.

Locally made objects throughout the hotel include counter and stools manufactured from recycled plastic bottle tops by Weedoo Plastics, pool lounge chairs handwoven from upcycled materials by BYO Living and wall sconces made of local seseh wood and green-coloured resin by AA Practice.

YSG also made efforts to source construction materials locally while working on the project, as the studio noted it was difficult to transport them to the secluded site.

This included crushing terracotta tiles and breeze blocks and repurposing them as flooding riffraff to help with drainage, and joinery designed to be assembled on site.

The studio also addressed significant water damage to the complex and replaced rotten wooden walls, portions of the roof and concrete flooring.

The project also included adding a second-storey suite made of bamboo with an oversized skylight.

Other details include a black-and-white checkered tile relief that surrounds the pool’s edge, as a nod to the Saput Poleng cloths wrapped around holy objects as part of local customs.

YSG previously converted a warehouse into a co-working space in Sydney and brought 1970s elements to a local cafe.

#9002. Licht Kunst Licht illuminates Cologne Cathedral’s historic facade with "largely invisible" lights

Lighting design studio Licht Kunst Licht has used more than 700 surface-mounted LED luminaires to transform nighttime views of the world’s tallest cathedral without drilling a single hole in its delicate stonework.

Licht Kunst Licht (LKL) collaborated with RheinEnergie and the Dombauhütte Köln restoration workshop to develop a lighting concept for Cologne‘s historic cathedral, which is also Germany’s most visited landmark.

Prior to the intervention, it was primarily illuminated using floodlights placed atop nearby buildings. These 1,000-watt metal halide lamps consumed a great deal of energy and, according to LKL, flooded the building in an unflattering neutral white light.

LKL replaced this broad-brush approach with discreet, warm-spectrum LED fixtures, illuminating the building’s Gothic features by providing subtle backlighting combined with vertical grazing light to enliven the ornate facades.

“The central concept ‘light follows architecture’ replaces indiscriminate floodlighting with targeted illumination,” the studio explained.

“Instead of flattening the facade, light is directed to articulate depth, rhythm and verticality. The outcome is a sculptural night presence while the luminaires remain largely invisible by day.”

The project’s key innovation was the development of bespoke, multifunctional lighting poles that are covertly integrated into the structure using custom clamps to protect the stonework. The aim was to render the fixtures “largely invisible” during the day and allow them to be dismantled without impacting the historic structure.

Each pole contains a glare-free light module used to provide facade or circulation lighting that is fully dimmable and can be adapted to events, seasons and ecological needs.

According to lighting designer and LKL project lead Philipp Schmitz, a lack of detailed architectural plans necessitated an extensive study of the facades to ensure the intricate Gothic details were suitably illuminated.

“Because digital simulations were insufficient for such a complex, heterogeneous structure, we conducted years of extensive on-site lighting tests, experimenting with optics, angles and positions to achieve the desired effects through empirical observation,” he pointed out.

Only 10 per cent of the light now comes from fixtures located away from the building, compared to 80 per cent previously. This reduces unwanted light scatter and improves precision, while long-wave light reduces disruption to nocturnal species.

A series of minimalist stainless-steel lighting pylons on the cathedral plaza now illuminate entrances and highlight selected facade elements.

Sustainability was a key consideration throughout the project, with overall energy consumption reduced by 80 per cent while delivering improved visual quality, according to LKL.

Cologne Cathedral is the seat of the Archbishop of Cologne and is a renowned monument of German Catholicism and Gothic architecture.

Construction began in 1248 but was halted around 1560 and then restarted in the 19th century, with the building finally completed to its original medieval plan in 1880. The cathedral, which was briefly the world’s tallest building upon its completion, went on to be declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996.

Dezeen readers crowned LKL’s scheme lighting design of the year in the public vote at this year’s Dezeen Awards. The project is now in the running to be crowned overall winner by a jury of leading industry figures including Norman Foster, Michael Anastassiades and Jaime Hayon.

This may be the best stoopid idea for a Christmas gift I’ve seen.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Struggling to find a Christmas or Black Friday prezzie for the person who owns every novelty mug on Earth? Why not gift a palm-sized robot programmed to endure a relentless existential crisis on your desk?! Ladies and gentlemen – here is the Butter Bot.

Following a successful 2024 Kickstarter and two years of intensive engineering, creative tech studio CircuitMess is finally shipping its officially licensed Rick and Morty Butter Bot. And yes, theoretically, it will be able to pass you the butter. Better yet, it rolls around on rubber caterpillar tracks delivering deadpan commentary about the futility of its own existence. Yes please!

However, even though this grumpy little companion looks like the product of some of the best 3D printers out there, it will set you back $349. Yeah, it's for the ultra-fans only.

Inspired by a two-second gag from the intro of an Rick and Morty episode, Butter Bot started life as a cult Kickstarter project backed by 2,715 eager fans ($441,349 pledged). CircuitMess spent two years, and three electronics revisions plus custom steel moulds, turning that animated gag into a real, palm-sized AI desk robot.

And yes, of course this includes AI. Under the hood, it packs an onboard AI camera, dual microphones, edge sensors, and a remote controller featuring a live first-person video feed. Because its voice, face, and object recognition run on-device, it should recognise its owner, identify random desk clutter, read out phone notifications, tell jokes, control your TV, and – crucially – ferry sticks of butter across the table (though how the hell this is done is currently a mystery to me).

Left alone, it roams your workspace, avoids table edges, and loudly questions its own purpose. Pick it up and it panics; shake it and it disapproves; press the controller’s 'Poke' button and you’ll visibly irritate it.

Tinkerers can also snap on six modular add-ons, including an air-quality sensor, motion-sensing intruder alarm, and LED light show. O you can reprogram its open-source brain from scratch using C++ or CircuitBlocks (I'll leave that to the people in the know).

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Available worldwide now at circuitmess.com for $349, it’s a wonderfully over-engineered piece of pop-culture hardware that can turn existential dread into festive cheer. If you can afford it!

#9000. Access to Shanghai Grand Opera House staircase restricted to paid ticket holders

Photography by Kaia Wang, Yumeng Zhu, Tian Fangfang, Chen Hao

The Snøhetta-designed Shanghai Grand Opera House has introduced a paid ticketing system for visitors wanting to access the signature spiral staircase and rooftop viewing platform at the recently opened building in Shanghai.

When Dezeen visited the site, we observed a temporary barricade separating the free-to-access ground-level public space from the spiral staircase leading up to the roof. Access to the staircase and roof now costs 50 yuan (£5.60) per person.

Since opening, access to the architectural feature has been restricted, with visitors now required to pre-book tickets online to access it between 10:30 am and 2:30 pm. According to the booking site, people with tickets to see a performance inside the opera house are still required to purchase a ticket, and the fee includes accident insurance.

Asked about the apparent change in access requirements, Snøhetta said that demand meant that “visitor management is necessary” and that “access arrangements will continue to develop”.

“As with any major cultural institution, operational procedures continue to evolve during the opening period as the Opera House team gains experience with visitor patterns, capacity needs, and the building’s day-to-day use,” the studio told Dezeen.

“Given the exceptional public interest and the limited capacity of the roof and public stairs, visitor management is necessary to ensure a safe and enjoyable experience for everyone,” it continued.

“Access arrangements will continue to develop with operational experience, but the intention remains the same: to create a building that can be widely enjoyed by the public while balancing accessibility, safety, and the visitor experience.”

Following news that a fee had been introduced, the phrase “is it worth spending 50 yuan to visit Shanghai Grand Opera House” trended on Chinese social media.

Some commenters questioned whether charging to visit the attraction was justifiable, while others sympathised with the need for crowd control. Others shared tips on how to take the best photos of the building without paying the entrance fee.

Visitors Dezeen spoke to at the site were concerned about both the fee and the temporary barriers.

“I don’t think it’s worth the money,” Mr Qiu, who paid to climb the stairs, told Dezeen. “Basically you pay to climb a giant stair. If you want good photos of the stairs, best to take from afar, which you can do for free,”

Ms Ye, who didn’t pay the entry fee, told Dezeen that she was really disappointed that the barricade was in her photos.

“I don’t know what the point of the barricade is – to separate the paid and unpaid? Or for better crowd circulation? But at least they need to put some effort into designing it to match the beauty of the building,” she said.

“It really is an eyesore for the photos.”

The building, and its accessible roof, are often compared to Oslo Opera House, which was also designed by Snøhetta and is topped with a walkable roof. According to the studio, both projects were designed to “reduce thresholds wherever possible”.

“Buildings like opera houses inevitably create thresholds through walls, doors, and ticketed programs,” said Snøhetta co-founder Kjetil Thorsen at the time of the Shanghai Grand Opera House opening.

“We see it as our responsibility to challenge those thresholds and make the building as much a civic destination as a performance venue. People should be able to enjoy the building without attending a performance. It should become part of everyday life, a place to spend time, meet others, and experience the city,” he continued.

“A successful landmark is not only recognised by visitors, it is also embraced by the people who live around it and make it part of their everyday lives.”

Several other cultural projects in China have been built with publicly accessible roofs. However, the accessibility presented in concepts has often been restricted when the buildings open.

Also in Shanghai, the Start Museum, designed by French architect Jean Nouvel and opened in 2022, features a public roof that can be used for displaying large-scale artwork. However, the space has rarely been used.

The Amateur Architecture Studio-designed Fuchun Cultural Museum Complex is defined by a continuous undulating roof to resemble the experience of climbing the local Fuchun Mountain. However, the roof didn’t open to the public for four years and is now only open to public visits for one hour a day, three days a week.

#8999. Anxiety Tattoos: How Ink Therapy Can Help Ease Mental Health Struggles

Tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

The act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

For many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

But here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

Psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

There’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

One 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

However, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos showed no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

The relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It says, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

In a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings showed that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.

So you just got a tattoo — congrats! Time to focus on aftercare. If you want your tattoo to age gracefully, the next few weeks are extra important to…

There are a number of reasons a new or old tattoo can itch. Infections, allergic reactions, and preexisting skin conditions are just a few possible…

#8997. Minimal merges small van and electric bike in Pedal 4 delivery vehicle

British start-up Minimal has designed an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van in the Pedal 4, now operating in London with delivery companies Royal Mail and Evri.

Shortlisted in the consumer product design category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, Pedal 4 was built to take up less room on the roads and evade traffic even on London’s crowded and complex streets.

The four-wheeled, pedal-assist cargo vehicle has a footprint not much larger than a bike – three metres by one metre – and is able to go down pedestrianised roads and use cycle infrastructure, according to Minimal.

At the same time, it boasts 2.5 cubic metres of cargo space and in London trials made 36 per cent more deliveries per hour than vans.

“Electric vans solve the emissions problem, but not the access problem,” said Minimal CEO and co-founder Patrick Bion. “They still sit in the same traffic, fight for the same kerb space and need a driver with a licence.”

“They weren’t built for the job they’re doing,” he added. “We designed Pedal 4 around that job: a full round of deliveries, through streets a van can’t get down, ridden by anyone who can ride a bike.”

Minimal considers the Pedal 4 to be not just an electrified van or scaled-up bicycle, but a vehicle engineered specifically for delivery with an aesthetic drawn directly from its functional architecture.

It has a four-wheeled base for stability and independent double-wishbone suspension at the front and a rubber torsion axle suspension system at the rear to help keep it level around corners, even when its cargo box is full.

The team removed the traditional bike chain, minimised fasteners and reduced part counts with the aim of making the vehicle both rugged enough for its task and easily serviceable.

They wanted the vehicle’s aesthetic to come directly from its functional architecture – an exposed zinc-coated carbon steel frame with satin black metal covers.

“Pedal 4 has to do a van’s job every day for years, so it can’t be fragile, fussy or expensive,” said Minimal product design engineer Sean Heany. “Our biggest wins came from deleting parts, not adding features.”

“By rethinking the geometry, we cut part count and fastenings, which made the vehicle tougher, quicker to fix and cheaper to build in our London microfactory.”

The Pedal 4 includes two slots for swappable batteries, which lift out to charge outside of the vehicle and together give a range of 60 kilometres.

In the UK, the vehicle is classed as a heavy-duty electrically power-assisted cycle (EPAC) and can be driven without a licence, which Minimal says widens the pool of people who can do the job.

However, Minimal believes that the future of logistics lies in autonomous and worker-driven vehicles working side by side. To that end, each Pedal 4 is equipped with the company’s FleetOS fleet management software, which tracks its route and vehicle performance.

Minimal says that the data collected will be used to make the next round of design changes and inform the company’s autonomous vehicle programme. Recently, it has launched Bot, a UK- and EU-focused delivery robot.

“Pedal 4 is where our autonomy work starts,” said Heaney. “Every vehicle is connected, and more than 100,000 kilometres of real delivery data has taught us what city logistics actually demands.”

“The same principles carry over: fewer parts, lower cost, built for uptime. They are what make autonomy work economically, not just technically.”

Pedal 4 has been engineered for, tested on and now launched on London’s streets through partners Royal Mail and Evri, but Heaney says the same vehicles and software are built to scale across Europe. The company plans to launch in the US in 2027.

“London is one of the hardest places in the world to deliver, which makes it the best place to start,” said Heaney. “If Pedal 4 works on London’s streets, it can work anywhere.”

“Cities can’t keep moving goods the way they did last century,” he continued. “We need new ways of moving things that make our cities, our environment and our everyday lives better.”

Other recent new electric vehicle typologies include the Amble One – a doorless electric buggy in the vein of a golf cart – and a three-wheeler called Trinity designed for urban travel.

#8996. Curator Christiane Paul Helped Write the History of Net Art. She’s Doing It Again with a New Survey at the Whitney.

Editor’s Note: This story is part of Newsmakers, a new ARTnews series where we interview the movers and shakers who are making change in the art world.

Rare are the times when a New York museum has turned over an entire floor to a presentation of digital art. That makes “artport: A History of Internet Art,” opening at the Whitney Museum on Saturday, an outlier in the institution’s programming—and something of a major occasion.

The titular artport is an online gallery launched in 2001 by curator Christiane Paul, who has since gone on to commission plenty of works in the intervening 25 years, by artists ranging from JODI to Mimi Ọnụọha. Officially indexed as part of the Whitney collection since 2015, artport continues to commission artists. The most recent was Jazsalyn, who, for one work staged earlier this year, proposed what she called “Black Metatheories” as means of forming something alternative to AI and called on users to respond to a range of prompts, including one that reads: “Consider blackness. How does life persist within the spectrum of impossible possibility?” Related Articles Frieze's Kristell Chadé Discusses Why the Fair Has 'Never Been About Adding Points on a Map' Newsmakers: Studio Ma's Christiana Moss on Building Museums for a Hotter, More Expensive World

Artport’s offerings live on the Whitney’s website. Generally, however, they have not been show in the Whitney’s galleries, something that will change with Paul’s exhibition opening this week, which features more than works associated with artport. The show is yet another digital art–focused exhibition from one of the great thinkers on the subject. She literally wrote the book on digital art in 2003, and is currently in the process of writing a follow-up to it.

ARTnews spoke with Paul, a curator of digital art at the Whitney, to learn more about artport’s history and how she created such an ambitious show. This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

ARTnews: Artport was founded in 2001, but it didn’t become a part of the Whitney’s collection until 2015. More than 10 years later, what is its place at the Whitney today?

Christiane Paul: I would not say it’s changed much. The original thinking, which we kept intact, was: It’s kind of weird to lock down net art in a collection. And that is why we decided to commission the works under non-exclusive licenses. But what changed in 2015 was really that we wanted to acknowledge the artist’s status in all of this. By making it officially its own little umbrella collection within the permanent collection, all of the artists gained lifetime membership status, and are now treated the same way as collection artists—that wasn’t the case before.

Also, the works are of course more integrated into the collection database. Before, when you searched, everything was there on artport, but it did not necessarily appear in collection searches, which also became problematic when we added more physical works by some of the artists—for example, a sculpture by Auriea Harvey [whose work was commissioned by artport in 2023]—to the collection. You would find the sculpture, but not the rest of her work.

When artport commissions an artist—let’s say, for its “On the Hour” series, which stages projects on the Whitney’s website at designated times—who is the commissioner, the Whitney or artport?

The commissioner is always the Whitney Museum, and I invite artists to submit a proposal. What we don’t do is show existing work. We did a series from 2009 to 2023, “Sunrise Sunset,” that marked sunrise and sunset through a 30-second intervention into whitney.org that played on all pages. I found the format highly intriguing, because it’s so net art to disrupt, particularly an institutional website. While it was very beautiful and poetic, there also was a concern: This was sunrise and sunset, New York time only. That prompted us to change it to make it into hourly interventions.

My invitations to “On the Hour” are often based on two criteria. First of all, who are artists who can really work with that kind of seriality intervention, in terms of vignettes? I think it’s also a great way to give younger artists a chance to do something for the museum. In general, artport has always paid a lot of attention to emerging artists, but due to the format, this lends itself to being a little more experimental.

What did you look for when you started commissioning artists? How did you know an artist was good for artport?

The main goal of artport was always to show the breadth of practice in the in the online field. When artport was launched in 2001, of course, there already was a history of net art. I mean, depending on if you’re counting by accessibility to the public, the internet launched in 1993. Artistic practice in this space started around that time and really took off in the mid-’90s. So, by the time I started, there was already a backlog of the artists who were creating the language of the field: Mark Napier, Tina La Porta, Martin Wattenberg, Marek Walczak, Amy Alexander. I was rapidly moving through those people at the time. Then I was following who was doing significant work in that area.

Certainly, when you started artport, institutions had already begun paying attention to net art. Documenta X in 1997 had a net art section, and Lawrence Rinder organized a net art portion of the 2000 Whitney Biennial. You did something similar for the 2002 edition, and Rhizome partnered with the New Museum in 2003. But it seems like we’re in a very different moment now, where net art can even be the subject of major exhibitions like the artport one. What does it mean, now, to bring net art into museum walls?

I would once again say my approach has not changed that much. There’s more technological support for doing these types of shows, so the infrastructural possibilities and budget certainly did change. But since the ’90s, there has been this discussion of: “Oh, this should only be seen online.” I always thought that was such an ironic misunderstanding because online is not on your couch in your house. Online is everywhere! We’re online in the museum. People are on their phones. Everything is networked.

You’re definitely changing the context [by showing it in a museum], but it’s important to see this art in the context of other art forms, and that was very important to me. The challenge that an exhibition like this poses is: How do you make the work easily accessible within a gallery space while also maintaining its net-ness? On the one hand, it’s about not overwhelming people with dozens and dozens of screens, which we do still have in this exhibition. But we’re also changing formats quite a bit, and at the same time, we’re not sucking out what the online environment is really about.

The way I approached it with this exhibition was to use an open floor and a landscape of browser windows as a design conceit. There are floating walls held up by poles. There’s also a lot of cabling, as you can imagine. The walls or panels suggest open browser windows on which the screens are presented. They’re not segregating works into rooms—they’re all the web, where you might switch from one tab to another. Some works have been translated into more of an installation, like Andy Deck’s Screening Circle [2006], for example, which you use online, with different people contributing to it. You use your mouse to choose pixels and create an icon within this screening circle. And in the gallery, you will see it projected onto a platform with actually four tablets for input, so four people can use it simultaneously. It will switch between them and also bring in the online work.

There are also works that have components of paintings or prints, like Michael Mandiberg, for example. They did an endurance performance, Life Study [2018], where, over the course of four years, they filmed themself doing paintings of their assistants. We’re not only showing the work and its archive, but also some of the paintings.

The exhibition is titled “artport: A History of Internet Art,” which suggests that it is a history of net art, and that there are others still to be told. What is the history you’re telling?

Julia Kaganskiy puts it nicely in her essay for the catalog. There are timestamps that are demarcating the concerns, attitudes, social norms, and media environments that have shaped our collective lives. I think any type of net art that one would have picked beyond artport from the ’90s until today would somehow tell that history. Of course, the history that artport tells is a very specific one in that there are certain choices of artists, and they tell that history in a specific way, through their personal lens. If it were a completely different roster of artists, those timestamps marking these shifts would still be there, but the story would be told slightly differently.

There’s also a new performance by the artist duo Operator: the third act of their ongoing “Human Unreadable” project, begun in 2022.

Operator has, for the past four years, created the series “Human Unreadable,” which is a generative choreography on the blockchain. It’s open source, so that people can use to do their own performances. In Act I, they translated sequences that were created by the choreography into large-scale black and white images that were sold as NFTs. In Act II, collectors could reveal the movement sequence that had generated the image. From the start, the work raised the question: How much of the body survives translation into code? In Act III, we have bodies without the mediation of the screen performing the first 100 tokens choreographic sequences. It really is a multimedia theater piece that also includes spoken word, and it is really about our relationships to technological systems, the artist’s personal story, and negotiating ambition and technology in your life. And its two matinees are live streamed: I think we now have 18 partner institutions. The live stream is not simply “Oh, here is a camera that shows you what’s happening at the Whitney.” It is more of an artwork in and of itself, with moving cameras and modifications, almost a little bit more like Nam June Paik’s Good Morning, Mr. Orwell minus the technological difficulties. [Laughs.]

A lot of younger viewers who encounter this exhibition may not entirely understand everything involved in creating the early net art surveyed here—for example, the splash pages produced for artport between 2001 and 2006, which rely on a technology that is generally out of use in our current internet. How will you contextualize those pieces for viewers less familiar with them?

There were 57 splash pages—they were done monthly—and I am only showing the ones where artists created standalone projects rather than just a splash page or gate page for their work, because that kind of browsing is better done at home. The intention is to get lost in an artist’s work and website, and that would really distract from the focus of the exhibition. That being said, we are explaining the functionality of splash pages and what they were in the section text. But I hope the art of that time, and the environment of the web at the time, really translates—to me, that is actually the most significant part of the exhibition. There are these really nice connections across the floor between these early works and later ones that show you how really our attitudes towards self-representation, identity, surveillance data processing have shifted over time.

There’s an early work by Jillian McDonald that was made 20 years before deepfakes. It’s about fan culture—she inserted herself into the film Buffalo ’66 with Vincent Gallo. I have it right across from works by Tina La Porta, who did voyeur_web [2001] at a time when live casting was so popular. People would put up webcams in their homes, in their kitchens, in their bedrooms, as this kind of gesture of returning the gaze, something that people wouldn’t do anymore today. It’s a completely different attitude that gets reflected in Maya Man‘s A Realistic Day in My Life Living in New York City [2024–25], which takes this highly stylized TikTok culture of a supposedly realistic day that is completely performed and provides a counterpoint to what voyeur_web did.

The freedom that some of this early net artists had is amazing. It’s just not possible anymore, with so much of the internet became commodified, capitalized, and cleaner.

What really struck me in reviving some of the older pieces was that the first generation of net artists really used the web as material, in terms of scraping and reprocessing. The access they had, you don’t have that anymore with the corporate lockdown.

And you had to have a certain degree of technical know-how, too. I was rereading a 2015 interview you did with the artist Marisa Olson for Rhizome in which you said you were dubious that net art still existed. Do you still feel that way?

I would slightly revise my framing. [Laughs.] What I was really getting at was that in the ’90s or early 2000s, you really had a category of net artists. Those were people who really worked with the web, and that was it—that was their practice. And I think with so-called post-internet, post-digital art, this crossed over into more material form, even though the internet was still at the core of the practice. In the sense of the net artist who does work online, and that is the practice, period? I think that is much harder to find today. You still have net art, and a lot of it. I mean, Maya Man, Chia Amisola are younger artists who are really doing net art in the spirit of the online environment, but Maya also does very material works. Artists have been branching out more: They may be doing work on the web and in sculpture painting across the board. You might argue that has changed in contemporary art in general, which has become less medium-specific. But there is still net art.

#8995. European Beauty Standards: Impact on Self-Image and Diversity

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins says about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of big butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal issues and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

Two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins says about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

“She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins says this concept can lend to beauty standards.

When it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins says you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in new people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

Coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins says change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins says, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.

Picture this: you've just landed in Honolulu after a long transcontinental flight. You've got four days on Maui planned, and then a few nights on Kauai before heading home. The problem? Those interisland flights add up fast — Hawaiian Airlines will gladly charge you $150–$250 *per person* for a 20-to-40-minute hop between islands. For a family of four, that's easily $600–$1,000 in airfare just to island-hop, on top of everything else you've already spent to get to Hawaii. Now imagine paying 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person instead — miles you transferred from your American Express Membership Rewards account at a 1:1 ratio just a day or two before booking. Suddenly, that $150–$250 ticket costs you points worth less than a nice dinner. At 3.3 cents per point on the high end, you're extracting extraordinary value from miles that most people leave sitting in an account doing nothing. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about finding pricing inefficiencies in loyalty programs. Hawaiian Airlines prices these interisland segments on a dynamic award chart — but because these are short, regional hops operated almost entirely on 717s and A321s between islands most people aren't cross-shopping for redemptions, the program hasn't inflated the price the way major international carriers have. The sweet spot holds. The math is simple and satisfying: a cash ticket from Honolulu (HNL) to Kahului, Maui (OGG) or Lihue, Kauai (LIH) typically runs $100–$250. You're redeeming 7,500 miles to cover that cost, which means you're getting **1.3 to 3.3 cents per point** in value — above what most programs deliver on domestic redemptions. And because Hawaiian charges **zero fuel surcharges** on its own-operated flights, every mile goes toward the ticket price, not toward fees. For the FI-minded traveler who planned a multi-island Hawaii trip anyway, this redemption doesn't just save money — it reframes how you think about points. These aren't bonuses. They're a currency, and knowing where to spend them is the skill.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: HawaiianMiles prices interisland flights at a flat 7,500 miles in economy, and that price is shockingly stable relative to what these tickets actually cost in cash.

Here's why this works as a pricing inefficiency. Hawaiian Airlines operates a near-monopoly on interisland travel in Hawaii. There's limited true competition for these routes (go! Mokulele operates turboprops on some routes, but Hawaiian dominates the jet service). Because cash demand is inelastic — visitors need to get between islands — Hawaiian charges a premium in cash. But the HawaiianMiles award program hasn't kept pace with those cash price increases in the same aggressive way that programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles have. The result: 7,500 miles per segment, consistently, while cash prices climb.

Now let's talk about how you actually get those miles into your account.

The primary transfer path the ChooseFI community uses is American Express Membership Rewards → HawaiianMiles at a 1:1 ratio. If you have the Amex Gold, Platinum, or a no-annual-fee Amex Everyday card earning MR points, you can transfer directly to Hawaiian. Transfer speed is 1–2 days — not instant, so plan accordingly and don't wait until the last minute.

Two other paths exist if you're working with different currencies:

One critical nuance: HawaiianMiles are earned primarily through flying, not credit card spend. Hawaiian does have a co-branded credit card, but it's not a top earner for most people's daily spend. This means your primary accumulation strategy is transfer partners — Amex MR and Bilt are your best levers.

Another key detail: Hawaiian miles never expire. This matters because you can slowly accumulate miles across multiple statement cycles, transfer when you're ready to book, and not feel rushed. There's no expiration clock running against you.

Finally, the no fuel surcharges policy is a genuine differentiator. Many programs — particularly those involving European carriers — tack on $300–$600 in surcharges that gut your redemption's net value. HawaiianMiles charges no fuel surcharges on Hawaiian-operated flights. Your 7,500 miles covers the flight. Taxes and fees on interisland tickets are minimal, often just a few dollars. What you see is what you get.

Go to hawaiianairlines.com and use the 'Book' tool, selecting 'Reward Travel' as your travel type. Enter your route — for example, HNL to OGG (Honolulu to Kahului, Maui) or HNL to LIH (Honolulu to Lihue, Kauai). Plug in your desired travel date and search. You're looking for economy award space priced at 7,500 miles. Availability on interisland routes is almost always wide open — this is one of the best availability scores (5/5) of any sweet spot in this guide series, but it costs nothing to confirm before you transfer.

If you don't have a HawaiianMiles account, create one at hawaiianairlines.com — it takes about two minutes and is free. Note your HawaiianMiles number. You'll need it for the transfer step.

From Amex Membership Rewards: Log into your Amex account, navigate to 'Membership Rewards,' select 'Transfer Points,' and choose Hawaiian Airlines HawaiianMiles as the destination. Enter your HawaiianMiles number and the number of miles you want to transfer (at minimum, 7,500 per person you're booking). Transfers process in 1–2 days.

From Bilt Rewards: Log into your Bilt app or biltrewards.com, navigate to 'Redeem,' select 'Transfer to Airline Partner,' and choose Hawaiian Airlines at 1:1. Same 1–2 day transfer window.

From Marriott Bonvoy: Use this only as a last resort due to the 3:1 ratio. Navigate to Bonvoy's transfer portal and select HawaiianMiles. Allow up to 5 days.

Once your miles land (check your HawaiianMiles account balance), return to hawaiianairlines.com, log in, and re-run your award search. Select the flight you want, confirm the 7,500-mile price, and proceed through checkout. Taxes on interisland awards are typically just a few dollars — no fuel surcharges apply.

HawaiianMiles opens its booking window 330 days out. If you're planning a Hawaii trip far in advance and have specific flight times in mind, you can search and book early. That said, given the excellent availability on these routes, booking 2–4 weeks out is usually fine.

This is rare for interisland routes, but if it happens, try: searching adjacent dates, looking at different departure times on the same route, or checking alternate routing (e.g., OGG to LIH instead of HNL to LIH directly). Interisland availability doesn't fluctuate the way transatlantic business class does.

Let's make this concrete. You're planning a two-week Hawaii trip for two people. You've booked your Honolulu arrival flight separately, and now you need to connect the dots between islands: Honolulu (HNL) to Kahului, Maui (OGG) mid-trip, and then Maui (OGG) to Lihue, Kauai (LIH) before heading home.

The cash price check: Pull up hawaiianairlines.com and look at what these tickets retail for. On a typical mid-trip travel day, the HNL→OGG segment is priced at $189 per person. The OGG→LIH hop runs $149 per person. For two travelers, that's $676 in cash — before you've bought a single plate of shave ice.

The points price: Each segment costs 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person in economy. Two passengers, two flights: 30,000 HawaiianMiles total, plus roughly $10–$20 in taxes and fees across both bookings. No fuel surcharges.

The CPP calculation: You're replacing $676 in cash spending with 30,000 miles. That's 2.25 cents per point — well above the 0.8–1.2 cpp you'd expect on typical HawaiianMiles redemptions, and solidly within the 1.3–3.3 cpp sweet spot range for this redemption.

What the experience looks like: Hawaiian's interisland product is no-frills — these are 20-to-40-minute flights on Boeing 717s. You won't get a meal or premium service. But you will get a reliable, on-time carrier, clean aircraft, and the undeniable satisfaction of hopping between two of the most beautiful island destinations on Earth without opening your wallet at the gate.

For the ChooseFI traveler, the win isn't the in-flight experience — it's the mental accounting shift. You budgeted for interisland flights; now that budget goes to a sunset sailing charter or a snorkeling excursion instead. The points paid for the planes. The cash funds the memories.

Do: Transfer Points in the Right Batch Size HawaiianMiles doesn't allow you to transfer partial miles back out, so calculate exactly how many you need before initiating a transfer. For two passengers on two flights, that's 30,000 miles. Transfer exactly that amount — or a small buffer — rather than dumping your entire MR balance into a program you may not use frequently.

Do: Use Amex MR or Bilt as Your Primary Earning Strategy Since HawaiianMiles are earned primarily through flying, your accumulation plan should center on transferable currencies. The Amex Gold Card (4x on dining and groceries) and Amex Platinum (5x on flights) are elite MR earners. Bilt's no-annual-fee card earning on rent is underused by the ChooseFI community for exactly this kind of transfer.

Do: Search for Availability Before You Transfer This is worth repeating as a pro tip because new points travelers make this mistake constantly. Transfer speeds are 1–2 days for Amex MR and Bilt. Don't transfer points and then discover the flight you wanted is sold out. Always confirm availability first, then transfer, then book immediately once miles land.

Avoid: Using Marriott Bonvoy for This Transfer At a 3:1 ratio, you'd spend 22,500 Bonvoy points for a 7,500-mile award. Bonvoy points are worth approximately 0.7–0.9 cpp on their own best redemptions. The math doesn't hold here — save your Bonvoy points for hotel redemptions.

Do: Consider the Merger Context Hawaiian Airlines is in the process of merging with Alaska Airlines, and HawaiianMiles may eventually transition into Alaska Mileage Plan. Pay attention to program announcements. This could change transfer partners, award pricing, or program structure. The current sweet spot exists now — book it while the program operates under its current rules.

Avoid: Waiting for a 'Better' Redemption on These Miles HawaiianMiles are a limited-use currency. They're excellent for interisland and mainland-to-Hawaii flights, but they don't transfer to other airlines and don't unlock international business class sweet spots. If you've got miles in this program, use them for exactly what they're designed for — Hawaiian flights — rather than letting them sit hoping for a better opportunity that may never come.

Do: Book Multiple Segments in a Single Trip If you're doing a true multi-island itinerary, every interisland hop is 7,500 miles. Three islands means two hops — 15,000 miles per person. Plan your island sequence to minimize backtracking, and book all segments at once once your miles transfer.

Most visitors to Hawaii stick to one island because interisland flights add $100-$400+ per person to the trip cost. By using points for these short hops, you unlock a fundamentally different Hawaii experience — island-hopping from Oahu to Maui to the Big Island to Kauai without the airfare costs stacking up. This is a multiplier strategy: you are not just saving on one flight, you are enabling an entirely different type of trip. Combining a points-funded mainland-to-Hawaii flight with points-funded interisland hops creates a nearly free (in cash) multi-island Hawaiian vacation.

Decide which islands you want to visit and in what order. The most common combinations are Oahu + Maui, Oahu + Big Island, or a three-island itinerary. Map out how many interisland hops you need so you know the total points required.

Check Hawaiian Airlines (7,500 miles each way), Southwest (variable, typically 4,000-8,000 points), and United (5,000-7,500 miles) for each interisland segment. Southwest often offers the best flexibility with no change fees and no blackout dates.

For Hawaiian Airlines, transfer Amex Membership Rewards. For Southwest, earn Rapid Rewards directly or transfer from Chase (transfer to Southwest is currently limited). For United segments, transfer from Chase or use Turkish Miles&Smiles for even lower pricing.

Book each interisland hop as a separate one-way award. This gives you maximum flexibility to mix airlines and optimize pricing per segment. One-way awards have no penalty compared to round trips on these short routes.

Align your interisland hops with your arrival and departure flights. Arrive on one island and depart from a different one (open-jaw booking) to avoid backtracking. For example, arrive Honolulu, hop to Maui, depart Maui to the mainland.

Hawaiian Airlines has the most extensive interisland network and offers the most daily frequencies. Southwest Airlines also operates key interisland routes (Honolulu-Maui, Honolulu-Kona, Honolulu-Lihue). United flies select interisland segments as well. Each airline has different award pricing and transfer partner access.

Hawaiian Airlines interisland awards typically price at 7,500 HawaiianMiles each way. Southwest varies by cash fare but generally costs 4,000-8,000 Rapid Rewards points each way for interisland hops. United interisland segments can be booked for 5,000-7,500 miles using various Star Alliance partner programs.

Yes, especially when booking multiple hops. A family of four making two interisland hops at $150 each way would spend $1,200 in cash. Converting that to points frees up significant cash for accommodations, activities, and dining. The per-point value (1.5-2.5 cents) is reasonable, and the trip flexibility gained is substantial.

A popular strategy is to fly into Honolulu (Oahu), hop to Maui for beaches and Haleakala, then continue to the Big Island (Kona) for volcanoes and snorkeling, and optionally finish on Kauai for dramatic scenery. Each hop is 30-60 minutes. Allow 2-3 days minimum per island.

This redemption was built for families and couples planning a multi-island Hawaii vacation — full stop. If you're visiting multiple islands (which most Hawaii first-timers and repeat visitors do), you're already mentally budgeting for interisland flights. This sweet spot simply redirects that cash budget back into your pocket and replaces it with points.

Families get a 5/5 Family Friendly score here for good reason: availability is wide open, booking is simple, and the economics scale beautifully. Four people, two hops = 60,000 miles to cover potentially $1,200+ in interisland airfare. That's an extraordinary displacement of vacation cash.

Beginners are explicitly welcomed by this redemption's design. There's no partner airline complexity, no fuel surcharge math to calculate, no routing rules to decode. You search on Hawaiian's website, you transfer points, you book. The 5/5 Beginner Friendly and Easy to Book scores reflect that this is genuinely one of the simplest award redemptions you can execute.

Minimum points needed: 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person per segment. For a solo traveler doing two hops, that's 15,000 miles. For a family of four doing two hops, that's 60,000 miles.

This is NOT for: Travelers who don't have an Amex MR or Bilt account and no path to earning HawaiianMiles quickly. It's also not ideal for travelers who only need a single interisland flight — the opportunity cost of setting up the transfer relationship for 7,500 miles may not be worth it unless you're already accumulating MR points for other redemptions.

This redemption earns a **Beginner** rating — and it genuinely deserves it. In a world of waitlists, fuel surcharges, routing rules, and phone-only bookings, Hawaiian interisland awards are refreshingly clean. **What makes it easy:** Award availability is consistently excellent (5/5). The booking portal is functional and user-friendly. There are no fuel surcharges to calculate. Miles never expire, so there's no pressure. You can complete the entire redemption — from transfer initiation to confirmed booking — in about 48 hours. **The one genuine friction point:** Earning HawaiianMiles isn't as straightforward as earning Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex MR. Hawaiian doesn't have a widely-used co-branded credit card for most people's everyday spend. This means you're dependent on transfer partners, and the Amex MR and Bilt paths are your primary options. If you don't have either, this redemption becomes harder to access. **Tip 1:** Start with an Amex card that earns Membership Rewards — the Amex Gold is the ChooseFI community favorite for everyday earning. Once you're accumulating MR points, you have a direct path to Hawaiian via a 1:1 transfer. **Tip 2:** Always search award availability before transferring. It takes 30 seconds and protects you from the one mistake that could derail an otherwise smooth booking. **Tip 3:** Don't overthink the merger situation. Hawaiian and Alaska remain separate programs today. Book what's in front of you. If you can earn Amex MR points, you can execute this redemption. It's the perfect first award booking for a ChooseFI member who wants to see how the system works without risking complexity.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Interisland awards are the key that unlocks multi-island Hawaii vacations without the stacking airfare costs that keep most travelers on a single island. At 7,500-10,000 miles per hop, the points cost is modest, and the trip transformation is significant. Whether you use Hawaiian Airlines miles, Southwest Rapid Rewards, or United partner programs, the strategy is the same: let points handle the short hops so your cash stays in your pocket for experiences. Combined with a points-funded mainland-to-Hawaii flight, interisland awards make a multi-island Hawaiian vacation one of the most achievable aspirational trips in travel rewards.

#8993. Steven Holl designs The Sculpture Watch as a tribute to Álvaro Siza

Photography by Nuno Sousa Dias unless stated

American architect Steven Holl has designed a colourful watch for Swiss watch brand Cauny that was informed by conversations with Portuguese architect Álvaro Siza.

Named The Sculpture Watch, the timepiece has a dial that includes four intersecting blocks of colour within a circular case that resembles a watch designed by Siza for Cauny.

According to Holl, his watch was designed to be a dialogue between the two architects and was directly informed by a compliment the Portuguese architect once gave him.

“On July 25, 2018, I gave a summer lecture in at the Porto Academy,” Holl told Dezeen. “Siza came to my talk and came up to me after and said ‘Steven, you use colour like Matisse, I must try in my next project’.”

“Siza is the greatest living architect,” he continued. “I will never forget that afternoon. This watch is an homage to Alvaro Siza,”

The Sculpture Watch has a three-dimensional dial with the red, green, yellow and blue colour blocks raised on top of each other.

It was intended as a direct translation of Holl’s watercolour paintings that were complimented by Siza. Holl is well known for his painting and begins the majority of his architecture projects with a small watercolour sketch.

“Watercolor painting, integral to my design process for architecture, inspires this timepiece,” said Holl.

“The colour volumes on the dial are made of brass; well-tested in watchmaking and best to allow Cauny to reproduce the watercolours.”

“My approach to colour is conceptual,” he continued.

“I try to engage colour in the idea driving the design, like the ‘projected colour’ from unseen surfaces in the DE Shaw trading floor, or the complimentary colours in the ‘seven bottles of light’ in our Chapel of St. Ignatius, which is analogous to the Jesuit spiritual exercises.”

Holl also reflected on how colour can reflect the passing of time.

“Time is marked in a personal way, with each moment its own polychrome experience,” he said.

“Colour turns time’s passage into both a visual and temporal experience. The fragility and variation of colour remind us that time is a human experience of duration.”

The Sculpture Watch is the fifth piece created for Cauny in its The Architects of Time Series. Following Siza, who designed the first timepiece in the collection, architects Rafael Moneo, Eduardo Souto Moura and Tadao Ando have designed watches for the brand.

Numerous high-profile architects have turned their hands to watch design and we recently rounded up six watches designed by Pritzker Architecture Prize-winning architects.

#8992. After Exile, Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara’s Prison Drawings Arrive in New York

In one of Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara’s prison drawings, swans skim a swimming pool inside a cell. In another, a clownish figure peers over the prison wall, perched with apparent ease on barbed wire. The Cuban artist and leader of the San Isidro Movement made thousands of such works in Guanajay, a maximum-security prison outside Havana, where he served time after his arrest on July 11, 2021, amid anti-government protests across the island. His release this year, after international outcry over creative freedom, was contingent on exile to the United States. A small selection of those works makes up “Tocar el cielo,” their first public showing, now at the New York gallery Foreign & Domestic (curated by Alexander Meurice, and on view through December 13). Related Articles After Days of Uncertainty, Cuban Artist Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara Arrives in Miami Jailed Dissident Artist Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara Pens Appeal to 'People of Conscience' On Two-Year Anniversary of Arrest: 'Every Young Cuban Is a Political Prisoner'

Art that emerges from incarceration tends to speak first in material, with scarcity making resourcefulness something like a protagonist. Otero Alcántara recounted drawing on drink cartons and cigarette packs, and smuggling in colored ink that ended up on other prisoners’ skin, when bodies were canvas enough. Who gets to make art inside, and who can get supplies to them, comes with its own politics. But he describes his five years in prison as one long performance, an “involuntary artistic gesture,” and the show reflects rather than transcribes the specifics of injustice. It’s an oblique testimony to how, bereft of sky or savior, the mind can slip its confines.

ARTnews spoke with Otero Alcántara via email about his experience making art in prison, and settling into his second life in Miami. The following conversation has been translated from Spanish and condensed for publication.

ARTnews: How is your spirit these days? What has surprised you most about settling into life here?

Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara: I think it’s been a shock. It’s unsettling, and it scares me a little.

People outside Cuba could connect with my work, but it grew out of life in the neighborhood, out of my connection with the people there. Above all, it came from knowing that neighborhood called Cuba, that neighborhood called Havana, where I was like a fish in water.

In New York, I’m getting to know other ways of thinking, other ways of doing things. I’m learning how art relates to people here and how people relate to art. There’s the language barrier, too. In my own practice, I want art to disappear into the social fabric, into people’s lives. I want it to have a real effect on the person walking down the street.

I feel like an embryo, like I’m learning from scratch how art and people relate to one another. So yes, it scares me. I’d call it a difficult process, but it’s a living process.

Can you tell me about making art in prison? How did you get supplies, and when did you work? What did materials typically cost you?

I started making art the moment I set foot in prison. They put me in a punishment cell, and I spent about two or three months there. Before prison, I was detained more than 50 times in three years. Even if they only held me for two or three days, I always made something in the cell. At first, I didn’t have the materials I had later. When I finished a drink my family had brought me, I’d keep the carton and draw on it. I used cigarette packs too. I’d stitch them together to make a surface I could draw on.

Once the materials from home ran out, my friends sent me more. When I called, all those friends of mine—Yanelys Núñez, Claudia Genlui, Coco Fusco, Camila Lobón, Anamely Ramos—picked up the phone. That was an act of resistance and an act of friendship. They took money they could have spent on food or on things they needed and used it to send me good art supplies, really good ones, all the way to Cuba, into the prison where I was being held.

That’s what I mean by cultural resistance. For my friends, it meant keeping the art alive and keeping the artist alive. They taught me how good it is to have a friend, and how good it is to be one.

Can you tell me about the recurring figure in the prison cell works? You’ve depicted him as a clown. Who does he represent? Who, or what, is the joke?

The clown keeps coming back in my work. When I look back at everything I made in prison, from beginning to end, I can see that the figures in those first drawings and paintings really were clowns. Over time, all that was left of the clown was the nose and traces of this strange makeup that gradually broke down. The colors started to bleed into one another. I feel that had something to do with how I was changing, how I was growing older in prison. At one point, even the paper tears. I tear it. I don’t know if it was hatred, if I was channeling hatred through my hands, or frustration. I don’t know why it was a clown.

As for the question about the joke, I remember being on hunger strike once, in a group of prisoners that included several men who’d protested on July 11. We’d become friends in there. They were getting sentences of ten years, eight years, five years. It literally seemed like a joke.

To me, the whole thing felt like a circus, like watching a show, only this show had real consequences for people’s lives. So if there’s a joke in it, if there’s an irony, that’s where I see it. They put up this whole circus tent. What happens under it affects so many people’s lives, and none of it makes any sense.What was it like to go years without seeing your whole reflection?

In prison, there was a tiny mirror. Mirrors are prized possessions in there. You hold yours out and someone in another cell, maybe three or six feet away, holds his out too. And there, in that little piece of mirror, you can see the other man’s face. You can see when a guard is coming.

If your mirror is only four inches across, all you ever see of yourself is a piece of your face. You never see your whole body. You go into prison looking one way and come out looking another. The first time I stood in front of a full-length mirror again, it was like coming back to see someone and finding myself face to face with a new person.

I think that found its way into my work. I have a series of self-portraits where my features start to disappear. They’re smudges, scratches, moods. Most of the work I made in prison was like that. I painted states of mind.

The only portraits that came close to being realistic were the ones I made of my friends. It was all about memory. I wanted to keep existing in my friends’ minds, and I wanted to remember them, too.Two of your works involve faith: a cross, and beside it a pile of idols sinking into an abyss. What is the relationship between your art and faith?

My art has a lot to do with faith and religion. For me, those are two different things. Both are tied to being Cuban. And for as long as I can remember, people have had faith that the system would fall, that the dictatorship would come to an end, that life would get better.

In Cuba, you have very little power to change the reality you live in. There’s no democracy, and the system makes you feel like you can’t fend for yourself. On the island, you’re always waiting for somebody on the outside to save you. And by “save you,” I mean a cousin or a brother sending you money. It’s like having faith in a god who lives somewhere out there, some kind of extraterrestrial being who’s going to keep you going on the island. You put your faith in finding a girlfriend or a boyfriend who has money, or in a foreigner coming along, marrying you and taking you away. The system is so rigid that you have very little room to change your own circumstances.

Before prison, I made performances that drew on images of the Virgin Mary and the saints. What interests me is how these objects change the way people behave, how they shape a culture, and how those in power use them to manipulate people.

Prison is maybe one of the last places where you lose whatever say you still had over your own life. Your future is in the hands of a prosecutor or whoever else gets to decide. It’s like living in a jungle where a lion decides which animal it wants to eat that day, and you pray it won’t be you.

Confinement also brings you face-to-face with yourself. You get in touch with something more visceral in yourself, something more animal. And all you’re left with is the faith that tomorrow might be better.

That reminds me of a story about a friend of mine in prison. He’d been waiting a year or so for his trial, and he was getting desperate. Nothing had been proven against him.

One day he used the five minutes a week they gave him on the phone to call his lawyer. He said, “Hey, tell me something. Any news?”

His lawyer said, “Don’t worry. Last night I dreamed they were going to let you go.”

In another work, a maze fills the cell. Is it a way out or another kind of trap?

I think the labyrinth has to do with how you feel in prison. When you’re in prison, you really have no way out. But there’s also the question of what you can do with that one small space. You have to turn it into your own amusement park. For me, the labyrinth is about the thousand ways you have to reinvent one space to survive in it.

There’s also something about getting lost so you can find yourself again, and finding yourself only to get lost again. As time goes by, you get tangled up in nostalgia, in sadness, in forgetting. You feel whole places in your mind starting to disappear, and you find yourself holding on to the memory of them.

Your practice is so community-driven. How did you keep that part of yourself alive in solitary?

The place where I lived was called Pasillo 20, Corridor 20. It was in the maximum-security section at Guanajay, cut off from most of the other prisoners. For five years, I lived among about 20 men.

Some of the men painted or drew. I started what I called the San Isidro Grants. For two or three months, as long as my money lasted, I gave some money to men who painted and bought them materials so they could keep painting. I brought in art history books and gave them away.

I also made work outside the prison while I was still inside. One piece that mattered a lot to me was Momento Cero, which I made with Coco Fusco. People counted down the days I had left in prison. There was also Fe de vida. During the Havana Biennial, we invited curators and artists to come to visit me in prison. Reaching out to people outside was connected to what I was doing with the men I lived with, finding ways to make room for community, kindness and love in a place that was so violent.

You arrived in the United States at a moment when artists here are facing censorship and funding cuts on a scale I haven’t seen in my lifetime. What has it been like to land in this context?

First of all, I feel like I haven’t quite landed here yet. I mean that physically, in my body, but also in my thinking and how I see things as an artist. What I can say is that the little I’ve seen and heard here doesn’t come close to the lack of freedom in Cuba.

Now I’ve come to a country I hope will be a place of passage for me. When you speak from New York, your words carry more legitimacy than if you’re speaking from, say, Havana or Haiti. I don’t know why the world gives that so much weight. Well, yes, I do know why.

Coming here, I can see that this country is going through a transition, a crisis. There’s conflict in the relationships between institutions, art, and artists. I think this is a moment when artists have to take responsibility. We can use art to resist, to change things, and to put forward a vision of a better world.

Do you see any parallels between what you experienced in Cuba and what’s happening here, or do you see them as fundamentally different?

The danger in drawing a parallel is that someone can always say, “Look what happens to people in Cuba. That doesn’t happen to you here. You’ve got me to thank for that, so you have to do what I say.” That’s where populism comes in. If you understand which freedoms an American artist enjoys and what artists elsewhere have to live without, you have a starting point. You can defend the ground you’ve gained and recognize when someone is using those freedoms to blackmail you.

We need to keep those differences in view. That’s how we recognize what we’ve already won as a nation and keep fighting for the freedoms we still need.

How have Cubans on the island and in the diaspora responded to the politics of your release and to your ability to keep making art in prison?

I think my art and the art of my generation, the work of the San Isidro Movement and others, have had an impact on Cuba, both on the island and in the diaspora. It’s only been five years since July 11, 2021, and people already recognize the part that my work, and the art we made together in San Isidro, played in the spirit of rebellion that emerged in 2018, 2019, 2020 and 2021.

For me, those five years in prison are one big work of art, one long performance. I call it “an involuntary artistic gesture.” The dictatorship acts on my body against my will, and what it does to me provokes an aesthetic response in other people.

The other thing that matters is social media and everything that played out there when I arrived in the United States. What struck me was how it exposed some bad habits that have taken hold in the way Cubans use social media. I’m talking about people acting irresponsibly. Some influencers have learned how to make money on YouTube, Facebook and Instagram. Controversy brings in viewers, and viewers bring in money.

What matters most to me is what I’ve experienced walking the streets of Miami. From 99 percent of the people I’ve met, if not 100 percent, what I’ve felt is affection. I’ve felt love.

When you think about what art is for and what an artist owes the world, has your view changed since prison?

I think art is one of the tools we have as human beings to transform society and culture. And when I say culture, I mean it in the broadest sense, right down to the way we behave. Those in power know what art can do. They use it when it serves their interests. When it doesn’t, they go after it. They try to put art itself in prison.

Art is one of the teeth on the gear that keeps society moving. And the artist is the one who thinks, who proposes something, who puts their own body on the line. So, I think the artist bears the greatest responsibility.

An artist’s responsibility extends to humanity as a whole. There’s a commitment to humanism there: understanding that you have power and, more than that, a responsibility. Because if you don’t use your art to help people, someone else will use it for purposes that don’t help them.

When you picture your studio, or your next show, a year from now, what do you see?

A year from now, I’d love the work I brought out of Guanajay to have found homes in archives, museums and private collections. I want someone standing there to get a sense of what one human being lived through in confinement. I was a Cuban in prison. I was also a human being locked up. Someone in a prison anywhere in the world could go through what I went through, you know? For my studio, what I want is room to work and room to try things. There are sculptures I want to propose, ideas I couldn’t develop in Cuba because of the repression.

I also hope I’ll have helped more Americans understand something about Cuba. Our two peoples are so close, yet there’s still a romantic view of Cuba here, and that has consequences for us Cubans. Fidel Castro was a dictator. We’ve lived under a dictatorship for more than 60 years.

More than anything, I’d like people in the arts here to understand our work and make room for it in the stories and images that are part of everyday American life. What happens on that island finds echoes in so many other places.

#8991. These IEMs get the Most Beautiful Earphones Award for 2026, but will their crowd-pleasing tuning win you over?
