## The Moment You Recline Into ANA "The Room" The flight attendant slides your suite door closed. You're somewhere over the Pacific, 35,000 feet above the ocean, enclosed in what ANA calls "The Room" — a fully private, floor-to-ceiling enclosed business class suite on a Boeing 777-300ER. The seat converts to a fully flat 78-inch bed. There's direct aisle access. The service is famously meticulous. And you're flying from New York to Tokyo in a product that rivals first class on most other carriers. This is not a fantasy. This is what 90,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles buys you on ANA's JFK → NRT route. ### The Math That Should Stop You Cold A one-way business class ticket on ANA between New York and Tokyo typically retails for **$6,000 to $12,000 in cash**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin trans-Pacific fares are genuinely that expensive, which is precisely why the ChooseFI community treats travel rewards as a core pillar of the FI lifestyle — you're unlocking experiences that would otherwise require years of extra saving. At 90,000 Virgin Atlantic miles for that same seat, your points are delivering **6.7 to 13.3 cents per point (CPP)** in value. To put that in context: most points are considered "good" redemptions at 1.5–2 CPP. This redemption is 4 to 9 times that benchmark. This is what a true sweet spot looks like. ### Why the Gap Exists Virgin Atlantic prices its ANA partner awards using a **fixed award chart** — a relic of the old loyalty program era when airlines published static pricing tables rather than dynamic, revenue-based pricing. ANA's own Mileage Club program charges 75,000–90,000 miles for the same route. Virgin Atlantic's chart prices it at 90,000, but — and here's the critical part — **with zero fuel surcharges on partner-operated flights**. What you see is what you pay. The result is one of the most compelling premium cabin redemptions in all of loyalty programs. The ChooseFI community's founding principle is that every dollar has a job. When 90,000 transferable points can do the job of $12,000 in cash, that's not just travel rewards — that's an asymmetric opportunity you'd be leaving on the table.

One of the highest cents-per-mile redemptions in all of travel rewards

Here's the aha moment: Virgin Atlantic is selling you access to ANA's inventory at a price ANA itself doesn't offer domestically in the same way. That's the inefficiency. And it's hiding in plain sight.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club maintains a fixed award chart for partner flights. This is increasingly rare in a world where airlines have moved to dynamic, revenue-linked pricing. Because the chart is fixed, Virgin Atlantic charges 90,000 miles for ANA business class between North America and Japan — regardless of whether that seat would cost $6,000 or $12,000 in cash on the day you're flying.

When cash prices spike (holiday season, cherry blossom season, Golden Week), your points cost stays the same. That's not the case when you book directly through ANA Mileage Club, where pricing can vary, or through programs that have adopted dynamic pricing altogether.

This detail alone makes or breaks the redemption. Virgin Atlantic levies high fuel surcharges on its own metal (Virgin-operated flights). Book a Virgin Atlantic-operated long-haul in business class and you might pay $500–$800 in fees on top of your miles.

But when you book partner-operated flights through Virgin Atlantic — specifically ANA — those surcharges drop to zero. You pay government taxes only, typically $50–$100 on a trans-Pacific itinerary. That's it. No fuel surcharge games.

This redemption is accessible because Virgin Atlantic Flying Club accepts transfers from the two most popular transferable points currencies in the ChooseFI ecosystem:

All transfers are instant. This matters because ANA business class availability on partner programs is scarce, and when you find a seat, you need to move fast. You cannot afford to wait 3–5 days for points to post.

Here's a non-obvious but critical piece of tradecraft: you do not search for ANA award availability on Virgin Atlantic's website. Virgin Atlantic's search engine is limited for partner award space. Instead, you search on United.com, because United and ANA are both Star Alliance members and United shows ANA partner award availability accurately in its search results.

Find the space on United.com, confirm the flight numbers and dates, then call or use the online booking tool at flyingclub.virginatlantic.com to complete the booking.

Virgin Atlantic miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. This means as long as you earn or redeem even one mile every three years, your balance stays alive. Keep that in mind as you accumulate — a small card transaction through the program every couple of years is all it takes to protect a hard-earned balance.

Virgin Atlantic maintains a fixed partner award chart that prices ANA business class at 90,000 miles regardless of demand or seasonality. ANA's own dynamic pricing can push award costs significantly higher during peak periods. This redemption is built for the couple or solo traveler who has been building a transferable points balance and is ready to make Japan the centerpiece of a bucket-list trip. If you've been diligently earning Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards and you want to experience what a truly premium long-haul flight feels like — without paying $8,000–$12,000 out of pocket — this is your redemption.

It's particularly well-suited to the FI-minded traveler who values experience over stuff. You're not flying business class because you can't manage without it. You're flying it because 90,000 points delivering $8,000–$12,000 in value is one of the most efficient uses of a points balance available anywhere in loyalty programs today.

For the ChooseFI traveler who has optimized their earning strategy and is ready to deploy a meaningful points balance on a once-in-a-decade trip, this is one of the most compelling redemptions on the board.

## Why This Redemption Is Rated Moderate This isn't a beginner redemption, but it's absolutely within reach for someone who understands the basics of transferable points programs. Here's what makes it moderate rather than easy — and how to handle each challenge. ### Challenge 1: Finding Available Award Space ANA business class partner award seats are genuinely scarce. ANA doesn't release large blocks of partner availability, and what they do release on prime routes like JFK–NRT goes quickly. This is the single biggest obstacle. **The fix:** Search at exactly 331 days out, use United.com for the most accurate availability search, and have flexibility in your travel dates by at least one week in either direction. ### Challenge 2: The Multi-Program Booking Process You're searching on one airline's website (United), transferring points from a bank program (Chase/Amex) to a third airline's loyalty program (Virgin Atlantic), and then booking through that third airline's portal. It's a three-step process across three platforms. **The fix:** Follow the step-by-step process above methodically. Don't rush. Confirm availability before touching your points. ### Challenge 3: Points Accumulation 90,000 miles is a meaningful balance — but it's achievable. Chase Sapphire Reserve's welcome bonus alone can get you most of the way there. This earns a 4 out of 5 on the "Easy to Earn" scale for good reason. ### The Bottom Line If you've successfully transferred points and booked an award before, you can do this. The learning curve is real but short. The reward — flying ANA "The Room" over the Pacific for $60 in fees — makes every minute of research worthwhile.

#8949. Hickey Stages: Understanding and Managing Love Bites Effectively

Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti. If you’ve ever scrambled for scarves or turtlenecks, welcome to the kissing booth of knowledge! Join us as we navigate the lifecycle of hickeys, from their eye-catching start to their subtle fade, and learn how to speed up their departure.

A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck. This intense suction causes the tiny blood vessels under the skin, a.k.a. capillaries, to burst and release blood into the surrounding tissues. The immediate result? An unmistakable red or purple mark that gradually shifts to a darker shade as it heals.

From a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing. They showcase the skin’s sensitivity and the body’s rapid response to minor vascular injury. Not so romantic when you think about it scientifically, right? But hey, it’s all part of the human experience of showing affection — or something like that.

When you get a hickey, your body starts a healing process that resembles how it deals with other bruises. Here’s a more detailed look at each stage of a hickey’s life cycle.

Immediately after the passionate moment, a hickey appears on the skin, screaming in shades of bright red or deep purple. This initial coloration is due to blood from the ruptured capillaries pooling beneath the skin’s surface in response to the suction. It’s your skin’s way of signaling that there’s been some minor internal damage in that area.

As the hickey begins to heal, it undergoes a whole wardrobe of color transformations, showcasing your body’s metabolic process at work.

Initially, the hickey darkens as the blood begins to oxidize. Then, after a few days, the body starts to break down and reabsorb the blood, so it turns lighter — going from blue to green to brown and, finally, mellow yellow. This rainbow journey reflects the breakdown of hemoglobin, the iron-containing substance in the blood, into biliverdin and bilirubin.

Finally, your hickey starts to ghost you. Over a week or two, depending on factors like your skin type, overall health, how severe the hickey was., and how your body rides the healing waves, the last traces of your hickey fade into nothing.

During this stage, the body’s immune system clears away the remaining by-products of the broken-down blood. White blood cells swoop in like a cleanup crew at a festival, gobbling up and digesting the debris in a process called phagocytosis, while increased blood flow to the area helps to flush out the remnants.

Need a hickey gone yesterday? Here’s how to help your hickey heal. Start with a cold pack — grab a spoon from the freezer or a chilled gel pack and gently press it against your hickey. This will help reduce any swelling and scatter the blood pooling under your skin, which can help minimize that bold bruise.

After using cold treatment for the first 48 hours, it’s time to turn up the heat. Switch to warm compresses to get the blood flowing smoothly again. A few minutes a few times a day invites more circulation to the hickey zone, helping you hustle through healing and clear out the blood remnants more swiftly.

You can also try a dab of comfrey ointment. Research shows it may reduce bruise size and coloration for some peeps.

Caught off guard? A little concealer or foundation over the hickey makes it less noticeable.

Not into makeup? Scarves and high-necked shirts are also great accessories for your camouflage arsenal.

Typically, a hickey will last anywhere from 5 days to 2 weeks, depending on its severity and your body’s healing capabilities.

Communication is key! Let your partner know your feelings about receiving a hickey — some might find it fun, while others may prefer to keep their necks clear.

While generally harmless, hickeys can sometimes lead to complications like skin infections or, very rarely, blood clots. It’s best to keep the affection gentle to avoid any issues.

Hickeys are nothing more than bruises in disguise. They start as bright red to purple love stamps and gradually fade over several days to a couple of weeks. Speed up the process with heat and cold packs or a splodge of comfrey cream.

Remember, the best approach to handling hickeys — like all aspects of relationships — is communication and care. So go forth, love responsibly, and keep a scarf handy, just in case!

#8948. Polestar Formula 2030 concept car "screams performance"

Swedish electric-vehicle brand Polestar has unveiled the Formula 2030 concept car featuring interchangeable, customisable dashboard buttons.

The first Polestar concept created under the direction of head of design Philipp Römers, the Formula 2030 is intended to herald the design direction of the company’s production cars in the coming years.

It takes the form of a low-slung sports car with proportions that Römers said “scream performance”.

With signature “Dual Blade” headlights, the front of the car previews the face of the next-generation Polestar 2, a saloon scheduled to launch in 2027.

Meanwhile, the tail of the Formula 2030 mirrors the upcoming Polestar 7 crossover SUV, moving away from the continuous rear lightbar that has become widespread among electric cars in favour of separate “Single Blade” lights.

Unlike Polestar’s most recently released production vehicles, the Polestar 4 and Polestar 5, the Formula 2030 also has a conventional rear windscreen.

“Design should always reflect the values and mission of a brand and that is exactly what we did with Polestar Formula 2030 concept,” said Römers, who joined Polestar from Audi in January 2025.

“It is a physical embodiment of how we apply Polestar’s core values of design, performance and sustainability to the next production cars.”

At 1.35 metres tall, 4.68 metres long and 2.02 metres wide, the Formula 2030 has a very low roofline but a broad stance.

Its styling was intended to project power, with a long bonnet, wraparound windscreen, short overhangs, muscular haunches and substantial 22-inch wheels.

Other sporty design elements include a deep front splitter and a single vertical windscreen wiper.

The Formula 2030 showcases a newly developed paint colour called Nitrogen, with accents of gold dotted throughout the car.

Inside, the design echoes efforts in recent concept cars from other carmakers to emphasise the driving experience.

The cockpit features a curved screen band mounted above the steering wheel, presenting information to the driver.

Another screen is integrated into the centre console, which slopes gently up to the dashboard.

A sliding “drive mode selector” on the centre console would allow the car to alternate between three modes – Performance, Normal and Autonomous – changing the angle of the central screen, seating and steering wheel to allow for a more passive or active driving position.

The Formula 2030 embraces a wider trend in car design back towards incorporating physical buttons, rather than only touchscreens.

Also occupying the central console is an interface of eight large mechanical controls. These can be configured to the user’s preferences, with choices between different types of buttons and switches capable of being programmed for specific functions.

In a modest nod to sustainability, the seat backs are made from a bio-based composite combining European flax and bio-based polypropylene, while the insides of the doors are made from a single material in order to be recyclable.

Headquartered in Gothenburg, Polestar has emphasised design and sustainability since it was spun out of Volvo as a premium EV brand in 2017.

Amid heavy financial losses, it has increased its production of SUVs, which tend to be popular with consumers and deliver higher profit margins. SUVs or SUV-adjacent cars now account for three of the five models in its lineup.

SUVs are often associated with a greater environmental impact than other types of cars, but Polestar denies watering down its ambitions on sustainability.

According to its most recent sustainability report, published in April, the company is ahead of schedule on a target to halve greenhouse-gas emissions per vehicle sold between 2020 and 2030.

It is the only car brand that publishes life-cycle carbon assessments for all its models. Assessments for the upcoming Polestar 2 and Polestar 7 have not yet been calculated.

“Learnings from the cars we have already produced will be channelled into the new cars to bring the CO2e figures in as low as possible,” a spokesperson told Dezeen.

In 2021, Polestar announced a project to produce a “truly climate-neutral car” by 2030. Earlier this year, it pushed this target back to 2035 owing to the “scale and complexity of the challenge”.

Other concept cars recently covered on Dezeen include the flying Tesla Roadster and a Fiat that transforms from an SUV into a pickup truck.

Klas Benjaminsson, creator of the Masters of Pixel Art books, on making a new poster with a real Amiga 1200, why creative limitations matter and the retro software worth trying today.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

“The Amiga was my first school.” For pixel artist Klas Benjaminsson, that’s less nostalgia than a CV. The Swedish creator of the Masters of Pixel Art book series learned his craft on Commodore’s 16-bit wonder, and three decades later, he’s gone back to class, creating a brand-new artwork entirely on an original Amiga 1200 (the Amiga ranks in our best retro consoles guide).

The result is Beyond the Screen: wildlife, lush vegetation and ocean life bursting out of a glowing monitor. It’s built from just 640 x 512 pixels and 32 colours, a canvas that would make a modern phone wallpaper blush. Benjaminsson first sketched in pencil, then brought it to life in Deluxe Paint 4. He calls the Amiga’s limits a “sweet spot”: tight enough to push against, generous enough to make something great.

It’s also a nod to Jim Sachs’ Amiga Lagoon, the picture that showed a generation what these machines could do, and a love letter to an era when your imagination really was the only limit.

The timing is no accident. Retro Games’ full-size Amiga 1200 replica, THEA1200, lands on 4 December. Unlike the A500 Mini we reviewed in 2022, it comes with a working keyboard and Workbench desktop, so it’s built for creating as well as playing.

Artists can join in too, with PosterSpy inviting its community to reimagine Benjaminsson’s piece in their own style. Need a pixel fix first? Dive into our 31 amazing pixel art examples or learn how to break into pixel art. Then read on as Benjaminsson explains why limits still make for better art, and which retro tools you should try first.

The new THEA1200 arrives on 4 December. See more of Klas Benjaminsson's poster art at PosterSpy x THEA1200.

Klas Benjaminsson: One key point in the initiative of THEA1200 is to recreate the Amiga 1200 in modern shape, so it made sense to honor the original platform.

KB: To be honest, the work "Amiga Lagoon" by Jim Sachs was a very important piece from the beginning. It visualised the power and creativity of the Amiga, and we agreed that an indirect homage to this masterpiece would be suitable for this occasion.There was an idea to create a “flow” coming out from the screen, showing waves of animals, nature and wildlife - flowing and growing out from this creative computer. I wanted a feeling that communicated “only your imagination sets the limits”.From sketch to finish, animals changed and shifted positions. But I felt the core idea was good and continued the work until the end.

KB: For me personally, growing up with the Amiga 500 and 1200 graphic standards, these limitations became something of a sweet spot for me. Limited enough to make it interesting to push the borders on what could be done, but also good enough to make it possible to create some great designs.

KB: Deluxe Paint 4 on the Amiga was where bulk of work was done. Photoshop and GrafX2 on the PC: importing the sketches and converting formats for export.

KB: To be honest I think many of modern pixel artists are doing a great job. There are hundreds of active pixel artists right now, posting pixel art on a daily basis with no direct platform or set rules for limits in their work space, but they still set a limited palette and a certain pixel area for their work. I think it's an awesome homage to the old platforms, which lives on so vividly in these modern pixel art works even today.

KB: Digital graphics had a big impact in my youth. As a kid I enjoyed playing video games, but as a young aspiring “artist” I also studied the graphics of the many games I tried (both Arcade and on my own C64). It took several years until a friend of mine showed me his brand new Amiga 500 with Deluxe Paint – that was the moment I realised I might be able to create something like that myself.I took the first steps on a very long and interesting journey on finally becoming an art director. The Amiga was my first school that defined much of my professional life.

KB: There are many techniques that more or less could be described as artistic knowledge, which I learned on the Amiga but aren't unique for this medium/platform. But there are some routines that could be blamed on my background with old-school pixel art:- The importance of setting a palette early on in the design process.- To keep full control of the pixels and resolution.

KB: The Amiga provides an interesting set of limitations to work with if you are into pixel art. Enforcing a specific resolution and a limited colour palette when creating pixel art is a very challenging and demanding practice, which forces the artist to be precise. With these clear restrictions in place, much more focus can be aimed at the actual creative work instead.

KB: I personally find it fascinating to take photos with a classic analogue camera, and see how the film can change with exposure settings. It's a special and rewarding experience to go through the processes by hand. You try and learn by mistakes, testing ideas, creating and discarding concepts, and finally finding a way to express your ideas. Digital tools can be a great help, working alongside you when sketching and trying out ideas. But there is a certain magic about when doing it by yourself, learning the craft.

KB: If you are into pixel art, don't hesitate to try out Deluxe Paint or Brilliance! These are the original software from which most modern pixel art tools has taken their UI concepts, as well as the early versions of Photoshop.If you are into creating music, try out some of the tracker software such as ProTracker, or AHX for unique chip sounds.For young people learning to code, AMOS is a fun and powerful language to start with. Something that could transition into C++ later on.Another nice tool was Dir Opus, file-handling made easy and logical. I wish Microsoft or Apple would have picked it up back in the days....

#8946. Perforated brick walls envelop giant market in Kinshasa by Think Tank Architecture

Photography by Martin Argyroglo excluding top photo by Ville Kinshasa & SZTC

French studio Think Tank Architecture has created a market in the capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo, with space for 20,000 vendors across its geometric brick-and-concrete structure.

Named Zando Central Market, the building replaces a historic market on the same site in Kinshasa that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.

Think Tank Architecture was brought in to design the replacement market after the original building had already been torn down. The studio used this as an opportunity to completely reimagine the role and function of the market, while taking visual cues from the original building and others like it in the city.

Alongside an increased number of vendor stalls, the 82,000-square-metre replacement incorporates storage space, a fire station, a police station, a medical centre, a vet’s, offices and a food court.

“The new market is on the same site as the ancient one, on the 3.7-hectare plot,” Think Tank Architecture told Dezeen.

“However, the building’s footprint has been totally redefined, taking into consideration the scale of the program and the urban context,” it continued.

“We wanted it to be an African market, and not an interpretation of it. Our comprehension comes from academic, historic and architectural research, dialogue with the client and then visits to other markets in Kinshasa.”

Zando Central Market has a rectangular plan measuring 245 metres in length and 150 metres in width. It contains 650 shops with space for 20,000 vendors, which is “more than 5 times its original capacity”, according to the studio.

At its heart is the central covered market, spanning two double-height levels, with three large entrances and outward views used to orient visitors.

It is surrounded by a three-storey building containing the other facilities. Landscaped patios punctuate the plan, carving out space for public squares and informal markets to take place.

“It’s an important part of our approach to keep the building open to the public, including the more modest,” said Think Tank Architecture.

The material palette for the project comprises brick and concrete, chosen to be in keeping with the local context and skills of the region’s construction workers. Demolition waste from the original market was used in the substructure.

“We are quite happy to say that this project reactivated three terracotta factories within a 60-kilometre distance from the market,” reflected the studio.

It uses a mushroom-slab structural system, in which the columns flare at their top, referencing the original market’s design.

Meanwhile, the perforated brick facades were designed to facilitate natural ventilation and provide shade from the sun.

In tandem with the thermal mass from the concrete, this helps cool the building, minimising the need for technical cooling equipment and keeping project costs low.

Interior finishes were also kept deliberately simple for cost reasons. However, the perforations of the facades help add flourish, evoking moucharabiehs – a type of projecting oriel window enclosed with wooden latticework, typically seen in traditional Islamic architecture.

Zando Central Market is on the eight-strong shortlist for the civic project category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, alongside projects including Sydney Fish Market by 3XN and TCC DAKA Renewable Resource Recycling Center by KPF.

It is yet to officially open, as the second phase of the project – involving the renovation of the surrounding streets – needs to be completed to allow access.

“This phase of works is under the city’s supervision and is going slower,” said Think Tank Architecture. “We hope, and it’s in our client’s interest, that the market will be able to open by the end of this year.”

Other market architecture recently featured on Dezeen includes the multi-level Tepoztlán Market in central Mexico by local studios Ramírez Suarez Arquitectos and Laboratorio Regional de Arquitectura, and an open-air market in Colombia designed by Tarq Studio to accommodate community gatherings.

#8945. Bye-Bye Bites: 14 Ways to Get Rid of Mosquito Bites Overnight

Wondering how to get rid of mosquito bites overnight? Discover simple home remedies for quick relief. From crushed ice to aloe vera, explore easy solutions to soothe itching and inflammation for a peaceful night’s sleep.

If you’re caught without bug bite cream or ointment, don’t worry — plenty of simple home remedies can provide quick relief. From soothing aloe vera to the calming effects of oatmeal, discover easy solutions to alleviate itching and inflammation so you can sleep peacefully.

Just as you’d ice an injury, icing a bug bite can help decrease inflammation and temporarily numb the pain.

If icy cold treatments aren’t your vibe, you can apply heat instead to soothe your bump.

Aloe vera gel does more than soothe sunburns! It can also help ease bug bites and help them heal.

Baking soda can remove the itch. To make a paste, mix 1 tablespoon of it with a splash of water (not too much). Apply it to your bite as you would zit cream. Keep it on for 10 minutes before rinsing it off.

Did you know basil (yes, like the kind in your pasta) has a rich history as a skin infection remedy? It contains antioxidants that may bring down bug bite inflammation.

To whip up your own basil rub, boil a couple cups of water with 1/2 ounce of dried basil leaves. Cool the mixture before applying it to a washcloth and gently massaging it onto the bite for sweet relief.

You already know apple cider vinegar (fermented liquid from apples) is a huge player in the natural remedy world.

Some people use it to clean due to its antimicrobial effects, and others mix it into food or drinks for its possible health benefits (like helping with blood sugar issues).

Its beauty with bites is that it can help ease burning or stinging while disinfecting your scratchy little bump.

Onion juice (while not delicious) has antifungal and antibacterial properties, which could possibly help ward off infection. Plus, it could make your bite sting less. Just dab a bit of raw onion juice onto your bites. The downside? We’re not sure how well it works … and it’s kinda stinky.

Thyme has been used to help with skin concerns for a long time. You can use it to help decrease irritation by chopping it up and applying the teeny leaves directly to your bite for 10 minutes. You can also boil thyme, soak a cloth in the cooled liquid, and wrap it around your bite.

Peppermint oil may work as an anti-itch agent. Mix it with carrier oil (like olive oil) before applying it to your skin, though!

Another natural anti-itcher and astringent, lemon balm, may be helpful. You can either apply a lemon balm cream or chop up the leaves and apply them right to the bite.

Witch hazel is a natural wonder with many uses for skin concerns such as acne and psoriasis. It can tackle inflammation and burning while helping your bug bite heal.

This herb may work, but the science is a little dicey. On its own, arnica is toxic, so any over-the-counter products you find have been carefully diluted for your safety.

The yummy tea that calms and soothes at bedtime has many other uses, including potentially calming an irritated bug bite. Steep the tea bag for 20 minutes before squeezing it out and applying it to your bite once it’s cooled.

Blend minced garlic with petroleum jelly or fragrance-free lotion. Place the mixture on your bite for 10 minutes before removing it and applying a cool cloth.

Icing the bite for 10 minutes and then placing a mixture of baking soda and water on it for 10 minutes is a strong choice.

Though not tested for this purpose, some people turn to Vicks to soothe mosquito bites. It’s possible that its antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties could help heal and soothe mosquito bites. But FYI, this product isn’t considered the best defense against mosquito bites.

Some toothpastes are cooling, so that sensation may offer temporary relief. Some people use toothpaste on insect bites since many toothpastes contain astringents, which can help shrink tissues.

Using repellent to prevent bug bites is a good idea. PSA: DEET and lemon eucalyptus oil are safe ways to repel insects.

Mosquitoes are low-key little monsters that cause the most insect bites worldwide. Most bites aren’t serious, but mosquitoes can potentially carry diseases.

Ointments, creams, or simple home remedies can help stop the pesky itch after bites. But remember that some natural substances can cause allergic reactions. That said, it’s always a good idea to do a patch test first.

#8944. SP architects gives antalya’s former expo grounds a second life for COP31

an 88-hectare campus reuses existing pavilions and introduces shaded walkways, modular structures and public spaces intended to outlast the climate summit.

Antalya’s former EXPO 2016 site has taken on a second assignment. As COP31 runs in the Turkish city from November 9 to 20, SP Architects has transformed the 875,117-square-meter horticultural exhibition grounds in Aksu into a conference campus for diplomats, scientists, civil society and visitors. Rather than begin with a blank site, the firm has worked with the existing landscape of gardens, a lake, an observation tower and exhibition halls, folding the infrastructure of one international gathering into another.

Around 65,000 square meters of existing buildings have been brought back into use, while additional spaces combine permanent construction with modular systems intended for later reuse. SP Architects led the project from concept through construction, operating from an office established on site and coordinating with Turkey’s Ministry of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change and the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). It is a rather practical answer to a familiar question: how much new building should a climate conference really require?

The 393,461-square-meter Blue Zone houses the official UNFCCC negotiations and facilities for accredited participants. Its 170,394 square meters of usable space include two general assembly halls seating 1,600 and 815 delegates, 28 meeting rooms, 15 bilateral meeting rooms, and extensive media facilities. At the entrance, a 5,400-square-meter registration building is sheltered by a perforated canopy, whose patterned screens filter the strong Mediterranean sunlight. A covered promenade, lined with slender arches, a lightweight textile canopy, timber decks and a reflecting water channel, connects the different spaces.

Across the site, the 481,656-square-meter Green Zone is dedicated to exhibitions and public engagement. Nearly half of its 94,435 square meters of usable area occupies existing Expo structures, including the convention center, indoor gardens, the Children’s Science and Technology Museum, and open-air amphitheaters. New thematic blocks explore subjects ranging from energy transition and cultural heritage to technology, innovation and climate finance. Exhibition pavilions are complemented by meeting rooms, lounges, podcast studios and informal gathering areas, allowing conversations to unfold beyond the official negotiating tables.

Throughout the complex, SP Architects has sought to balance the demanding requirements of an international diplomatic event with a more adaptable architectural framework. New permanent and temporary structures are integrated into the existing grounds, with modular and reusable components intended to limit unnecessary construction. The approach places particular emphasis on environmental control, operational efficiency and flexible circulation, while making the most of the site’s landscaped setting. Beyond the architectural gestures, the reuse of existing buildings forms a central part of the project’s environmental strategy.

Once COP31 concludes on November 20, the plan is for the grounds to remain active as a venue for fairs, concerts and other events, in coordination with Antalya’s metropolitan and district municipalities. For SP Architects, the redevelopment represents an investment in the city’s future rather than a temporary backdrop for international diplomacy. Whether that promised second life materializes will be an important measure of the project’s sustainability, long after the delegates, cameras and climate declarations have moved on.

Firefly is the safer AI image generator, but with OpenAI, ByteDance and Kling now in the mix, I'm questioning what that promise actually covers.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Adobe spent years selling Firefly on one big reassurance: it was trained on licensed and public-domain content, so you didn't have to worry about where the pixels came from. While other AI companies faced accusations of scraping first and asking questions later, Adobe didn't, and made sure we knew about it. I like that about Firefly and Adobe's push for labelling and clarity, but things are changing.At MAX this week, Firefly got some noisy neighbours. Models from ByteDance, Google, Kling, OpenAI and ElevenLabs now sit alongside Firefly, with Adobe's Creative Agent in the same place. The keynote line was that creators get to choose, which sounds like a way of passing the buck onto us, the users.

Fine. But I'd like to know what "commercially safe" covers once you've picked someone else's model. The clean-data claim was about Firefly, and I guess it still is, but Firefly now sits alongside less open AI models. Adobe's position with Firefly was never a claim about OpenAI's training set or ByteDance's. A designer or artist clicking through the options could be forgiven for assuming the Adobe badge applies to everything inside the Adobe app. Adobe spells out the distinction in its partner-model documentation, but I'd argue this needs to be much clearer at the point of generation, not buried in the small print.

There's an important distinction here, too: Adobe's commercial-use assurances for its own Firefly models shouldn't be taken as a blanket guarantee for everything generated inside Firefly. Partner models have their own terms, training histories and conditions of use, and users need to assess those separately. For agencies and studios, that difference matters. A Firefly badge isn't necessarily the same as a Firefly guarantee.

Even before opening its gated community to other AI models, Adobe came under pressure from people uploading AI versions of other artists' work and claiming them as Adobe Stock, so some bad actors found ways around Adobe's walled garden. Adobe took action and says it respects creators' rights, and that resemblance isn't proof of copying.Still, the complaints point at something licensing can't settle. Licensed training data answers whether Adobe was allowed to use the images. Artists were asking whether the output leans on their look. Those are separate questions, and the marketing has tended to let the first stand in for the second.Add other companies' models and the problem grows. 'Safe' stops describing the product and starts describing one entry on a list. Agencies and art directors who signed off on Firefly because of that word now have to check each model separately, and I suspect most won't. It's this idea that we, the users, the artists and designers, are now responsible for ensuring Firefly outputs are as ethical as they can be.

What I'd want from Adobe is, frankly, very dull and specific. Say in plain language, next to each model, what it was trained on. Say what the safe label does and doesn't cover, style included. Make it easy for studios to lock their workspaces to Firefly models alone, and make those controls available to everyone who needs them.Adobe has earned a fairly good reputation for adopting AI carefully and responsibly in AI's gold-rush free-for-all. It can keep that and run a marketplace, but only by showing which parts of the marketplace are ethical, carefully made and sourced.

To see what's likely coming down the line, read our report on the Adobe Sneaks from Max 2026, including one in particular that caught the eye: Project Link Up, which is set to make vector design more accessible.

#8942. First Ferrari Style flagship store in New York features metallic facade

Photography courtesy Ferrari Style

Architecture studios Formafantasma and Gonzalez Haase AAS have worked with Ferrari Style creative director Rocco Iannone on the brand’s first permanent store in New York, clad in a metallic facade.

Located in Manhattan’s SoHo neighbourhood, the flagship store for Ferrari’s fashion label is in a long, narrow building at the corner of Prince Street and Mercer Street and spreads across two levels.

Berlin-based Gonzalez Haase AAS clad the building in brushed metal, with curved window mullions covering floor-to-ceiling glass along its length.

Under Iannone, the team referenced the Ferrari Officina concept, a central theme of the brand that seeks to connect fashion and automotive. It considers “the workshop as a junction at which artistic instinct, scientific rigour, craftsmanship and mechanical precision converge,” according to the team.

“The Officina is the place where intuition is given form through discipline, and where the human touch works in harmony with mechanical precision,” said Iannone.

The opening follows another Ferrari Style store opened earlier this year in London, designed by the same team, and both stores share pops of red, warm beige finishes, and steel accents.

However, the New York space was designed to fit in with the city. The team said the New York location reflects the “form, scale and material character of SoHo”.

“For New York, we wanted to translate this spirit into a space in which architecture, fashion and object design each retain their own identity while contributing to a single Ferrari language,” said the team.

“Every material and detail has been chosen to express this balance between art and science, creating an environment that is open, evolving and in direct dialogue with the energy of SoHo.”

Men’s ready-to-wear is located on the first floor, with objects displayed on units designed by Formafantasma.

The space is bordered by a deep red curtain and large rectangular ceiling lights.

A staircase to the left side of the store leads to the “more intimate” second level, containing women’s ready-to-wear, footwear and accessories collections.

It also contains the store’s atelier, the second worldwide apart from the London location.

Wrapped in leather curtains, the space provides a private setting for personalisations and alterations. A table containing samples of textiles and hardware sits at the centre.

Ferrari Style, the brand’s luxury fashion line founded in 2021, has other US locations in New Jersey, Miami, and Las Vegas.

Ferrari recently unveiled a laptop collaboration with HP, as well as its first electric vehicle earlier this year.

Supplementing with L-tyrosine is believed by some to boost levels of dopamine, adrenalin, and norepinephrine in particular.

Foods naturally high in tyrosine include:

L-tyrosine may improve your memory and mental alertness. Since L-tyrosine increases dopamine availability in your body, experts think it may boost your cognitive performance. In addition to reward centers, dopamine is linked to working memory processes and plays a key role in the brain’s aging process.

In a 2019 review of several studies, researchers found that a higher intake of L-tyrosine was linked to improved cognition. It also improved executive functions like brain flexibility, convergent thinking, and reasoning.

However, researchers noted that L-tyrosine is most effective when dopamine and norepinephrine levels are reduced (which basically means when you feel stressed AF).

Some L-tyrosine supplement companies claim that their products are both mood boosters and antidepressants, but the results are mixed.

L-tyrosine increases dopamine, the feel-good hormone that’s linked to reward processing and also addiction. In general, it’s been shown to be a vital regulator of mood, behavior, and brainpower – so it makes sense that getting enough of it could benefit your mood, too.

However, the research on supplementation of tyrosine for depression is super dated, so it’s challenging to draw any definitive conclusions RN. (Plus, depression is also a super complex condition that involves more than just dopamine depletion.)

And though there are some people dubbing L-tyrosine “natural Adderall” for its purported beneficial effect on ADHD, so far, there’s no research to support these claims yet, either. (Though it *is* true that there seems to be a link between ADHD and altered dopamine levels.)

Phenylketonuria is a rare genetic disorder in which the body can’t properly process another essential amino acid, phenylalanine.

Since those with the disorder may also be deficient in L-tyrosine, some experts think that supplementing with it could help relieve some symptoms like seizures or skin rashes.

However, according to a 2021 review of several studies, there is not enough evidence to say for sure.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) considers taking L-tyrosine supplements generally safe.

That being said, it’s not recommended to mix with the following medications:

It’s not advisable to take it if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding.

Research suggests that L-tyrosine supplementation likely benefits your brainpower under stress. It also may benefit conditions like depression, but more research is needed to know for sure.

Like any supplement, it is a good idea to contact your healthcare provider before adding it to your medicine cabinet, especially if you have preexisting health conditions or take medications.

The MacBook Air finally offers decent value again.

MacBook Black Friday deals couldn't come soon enough this year following the price hikes amid the ongoing component shortage. Happily, the deals are starting to arrive across major retailers, and some of them may already be as good as they're going to get.

The highlights are $200 off the 2026 M5 MacBook Airs at Amazon, while B&H Photo has up to $300 off M5 MacBook Pros.

Could we still see a discount on the brand-new touchscreen PROLED XDR MacBook Pro released this month? It's unlikely, but perhaps a very small one. If it does come up, you'll find it here because we'll be updating the MacBook deals below throughout Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

If you want to shop around rival brands, see our guide to the best laptops for graphic design. And see our iPad Black Friday hub if you're also after an Apple tablet.

The latest MacBook Airs were released in March 2026, with the M5 chip providing a boost in performance for both Apple Intelligence functions and creative apps. It's more expensive than its predecessor was during last year's Black Friday due to the RAM-inflicted price hikes, and this might be the best deal we see in what remains of 2026.

Also released in March, the M5 Pro MacBook Pros are the laptops to go for if you need a device that won't feel challenged by heavy video editing workflows or 3D rendering. There's also $300 off the larger 16in version, but still no discounts on the new touchscreen PROLED XDR laptop.

This is a decent discount on the latest generation of Apple's most popular laptop, the 13-inch MacBook Air. It's slim and light enough for travel and powerful enough for running 2D design software, photoediting and light video work.

The M5 Pro MacBook Pro provides more processing and graphics power for those who need it for video editing, CFX work and 3D rendering. It also has a brighter screen and more connectivity options.

We've yet to see a bigger saving than this on the newest addition to the MacBook family, but Apple's first 'budget' laptop was already great value. This isn't a MacBook for running demanding motion design or video workflows, but it's a great laptop for general office work, productivity and light photo editing.

MacBook Black Friday deals in previous years have typically ranged from around $200 MacBook Airs to around $300 off MacBook Pros. Higher-configuration MacBook Pros with 2TB SSDs and 36GB+ memory sometimes come in for bigger discounts of up to around $500, particularly on previous-gen models.

Black Friday 2026 takes place amid a slightly different context compared to previous years because of the shortage of components provoked by the boom in AI data centre construction. Apple hiked the starting price of all MacBooks in mid-2026 because of the component crunch, and prices are unlikely to come back down soon. That may also mean that there's less appetite for discounting during the sale season.

Refurbished MacBooks from reputable sellers like Back Market or Apple's own refurbishment programme can offer exceptional value, especially when you're seeing savings of over $800 / £800. These devices are thoroughly tested, come with warranties, and often include replaced batteries and outer shells, so they look and perform like new.

The main consideration is which generation you're buying – an M1 MacBook from 2020 is still perfectly capable for many people's needs, but it won't support all the latest Apple Intelligence features or handle some heavier creative workflows in video or 3D art. We'd recommend refurbished options if you're primarily using your MacBook for web browsing, productivity apps, and light creative work. However, if you need cutting-edge performance or plan to keep the laptop for five or more years, buying new might be the better long-term investment.

The main differences come down to performance, display technology, and connectivity. MacBook Airs are thinner, lighter and fanless, making them silent and incredibly portable, whilst still offering excellent performance for most users. That makes them ideal for students, writers, and casual users who prioritise battery life and portability.

MacBook Pro models feature more powerful chip configurations (like the M5 Pro and M5 Max), active cooling that allows sustained high performance, brighter displays with ProMotion technology, and additional ports including HDMI and SD card slots. They're designed for professionals doing demanding work like 4K video editing, 3D rendering, or software development.

For most people, a MacBook Air provides more than enough power, but if you're regularly pushing your laptop to its limits with intensive creative or technical work, the MacBook Pro's extra capabilities justify the higher price.

What would traditionally be called Black Friday is the Friday after Thanksgiving in the US, so 27 November in 2026. However, most retailers now start their Black Friday sales much earlier than that – as early as the start of November in some cases. As for when it ends, Black Friday now rolls into Cyber Monday, which falls on 30 November this year. That's likely to be the last day for deals before the Christmas holiday period.

#8939. Ocean liner sunk in Florida to become "world's largest artificial reef"

Photography courtesy of Destin-Fort Walton Beach

On Wednesday, the ocean liner SS United States was sunk 180 feet underwater to become an artificial reef off the coast of Florida.

The sinking took approximately eight hours, and dozens of onlookers and officials looked on as the ship underwent a controlled deployment, or scuttling, to the bottom of the ocean.

The ship will join a long stretch of artificial reefs, including 580 other decommissioned vessels and structures, that line the ocean floor off the coast Destin-Fort Walton Beach, Florida.

“A new chapter has begun in Destin-Fort Walton Beach, Florida, where the legendary SS United States, once the fastest ocean liner in the world, has completed her final voyage to become the World’s Largest Artificial Reef,” said a release from the government of Destin-Fort Walton Beach.

The site serves as a tourist and dive destination for SCUBA divers both new and seasoned, as the underwater structures are meant to provide infrastructure for marine life.

“Beyond its appeal as a dive destination, the SS United States will serve an important environmental purpose,” said the team.

“Her massive structure will provide new habitat for marine life, supporting the growth of an underwater ecosystem that includes inhabitants such as sea turtles, grouper, snapper and marlin.”

In preparation for its scuttling, the ship underwent a years-long remediation process, where it was stripped of toxic materials, such as green neotex exterior floor covering and paint.

Elements such as the ventilation system, wiring and the propeller were also removed, with the latter stored for a land-based museum that will accompany the dive site.

“To see a project of this magnitude become a reality is an incredible moment for our team and for the future of marine conservation,” said Destin-Fort Walton Beach natural resources chief Alex Fogg.

“This is so much more than creating a new dive destination. It’s an opportunity to advance marine science on a scale we’ve never experienced before. The sheer scale of the SS United States presents a rare opportunity to study how an artificial reef of this size transforms over time.”

The project has been years in the making. The ship, designed by naval architect William Francis Gibb and known for its speed, served as a passenger vessel between 1952 and 1969.

It was decommissioned in 1969, and eventually bought to a Philadelphia harbour in the 1990s, where it sat inactive for decades as various owners bought and then sold the vessel in failed attempts to restore it and make it profitable.

In 2009, the non-profit SS United States Conservancy purchased and began stewarding the ship.

In 2024, due to rent issues, the ship could no longer stay berthed at its Philadelphia pier, and the SS United States Conservancy sold it to Okaloosa County, Florida, for $1 million.

As of today, it stands upright in its intended position, and its uppermost deck is accessible to divers, who can “now enjoy the site”.

Other artificial reefs around the world include the Reefline project in Miami, which is set to feature underwater sculpture designed by OMA and a LEGO-inspired modular system designed by Alex Goad, intended to restore damaged coral reefs.

Photography courtesy of Destin-Fort Walton Beach

#8938. Nip Slip? The Ultimate Guide to Inverted Nipples

Inverted nipples face inward rather than outward. Though usually harmless, it’s best to check with a healthcare professional to get shy nips the all-clear.

Nipples come in all shapes, including inverted ones. If yours are more like innies than outies, you’re not alone! Inverted nipples, also known as retracted or invaginated, are common and usually harmless.

Nipples can range from popping out when stimulated to constantly staying retracted. While usually harmless, knowing the causes and potential treatments is wise, especially if there’s discomfort. Keep reading to learn more!

Inverted nipples mean your chest cherries retract inward instead of protruding outward. They can be a genetic gift or something that happens over time.

Often, they’re just doing their own thing, but understanding the different grades can help you know if action is warranted.

Nipple inversion comes in three grades, according to the level of drama. Let’s break it down so you know what’s going on with those inward-facing nips.

Grade 1 inverted nipples are like the shy party guests who need a little encouragement to join the fun. They can pop out with stimulation, like a chilly breeze or a gentle touch.

These are the least inverted and usually don’t cause any trouble.

Grade 2 inverted nipples are a bit more stubborn. They can be coaxed out with some effort, but they’re quick to retreat. They might need a bit more attention, mainly if they cause discomfort or issues with breastfeeding.

Grade 3 inverted nipples are the ultimate homebodies. They’re fully retracted and rarely, if ever, make an appearance. These are the most inverted and might need surgical intervention if they’re causing any issues.

So, why do some nipples decide to turn inward instead of standing out proudly? There are a few reasons this might happen:

Sometimes, you’re born with inverted nipples. Doctors call this congenital inversion.

If your parents or siblings have inverted nipples, there’s a higher chance you might too. It’s like inheriting your mom’s eye color or your dad’s knack for bad jokes — genetics is a big player.

For some new parents, the process of chestfeeding can lead to changes in breast tissue that cause nipple inversion. Your boobs are trying to adjust to their new role, and sometimes, things get a little flipped around!

While this can be temporary, it may also stick around long term.

There are a few other culprits that can cause nipples to go inward. These include:

Remember, if your nipples decide to play hide-and-seek and it’s out of the blue, a quick chat with a healthcare professional is always wise to make sure everything’s A-OK. And if there’s pain, nipple discharge, itchy nipples, or bleeding nipples, do so sooner rather than later.

Several options are available for treating nipple inversion:

Gentle manipulation and massage with your fingers can temporarily draw out the nipple.

While this method can help with mild cases (Grade 1), it often provides short-lasting results and needs to be repeated regularly.

Useful for chestfeeding peeps! Nipple shields are soft, silicone covers that fit over the nipple and help coax the nipples outward, making nursing easier.

They provide gentle and continuous pressure that encourages the nipple to protrude.

These devices create a vacuum around the nipple, gently drawing it out gradually. They can be worn for several hours a day over weeks or months to achieve the desired result.

For more severe cases (Grade 2 and 3), a minor surgical procedure can permanently correct nipple inversion.

It involves making small incisions at the nipple’s base to release the tight tissue pulling inward. It’s usually done under local anesthesia and has a quick recovery time.

If they aren’t causing problems, there’s no medical reason to fix them. It’s a personal choice based on comfort and aesthetics.

Grade 1 and sometimes Grade 2 nipples can pop out with stimulation. Grade 3 nipples typically don’t. They’re super shy!

Yes, inverted nipples can be inherited. If family members have them, you might have them, too.

Inverted nipples are a common and typically harmless condition. They could run in the family, show up after breastfeeding, or result from an injury or infection.

Often, they need no treatment. But if they cause issues or occur suddenly, it’s wise to check with a healthcare professional.

#8937. red corrugated metal and pine plywood wrap czech village house’s extension

in nečín village, facha architekti renovates a converted pigsty and weekend cabin with a self-built timber extension that expands living spaces toward a stepped larch terrace.

LINKA News edited by christina vergopoulou November 16, 2026 4 min

Located on the edge of the village of Nečín in the Příbram region of the Czech Republic, House With a Red Addition is the renovation and extension of a compact family residence by Facha architekti. Originally built as a single-story pigsty and subsequently topped with a weekend cabin before becoming a permanent home, the structure retains visible markers of its incremental growth. Rather than unifying the building under a single envelope, the studio designed the new addition as a distinct architectural layer, defined by its sharp geometric form and a ventilated facade clad in red corrugated metal sheets.

The timber-framed extension expands the primary living zone toward the garden while relocating the main entrance and integrating built-in storage. On the west elevation, a large sliding window connects the living room to a larch terrace featuring wide seating steps and a retractable textile awning. Shifting the entrance into the new volume enabled a comprehensive reconfiguration of the raised ground floor, allowing for an enlarged bathroom finished in cement-based plaster and a redesigned kitchen. While the basement and attic were left largely intact, the original volume was thermally insulated, fitted with new timber windows, reroofed in corrugated metal, and upgraded with an air-to-water heat pump. Inside, pine plywood lines both the interior walls of the extension and custom-built furniture, paired with natural linoleum flooring and a rotating wood-burning stove. Consistent with Facha architekti’s hands-on methodology, the architects constructed the timber structure, metal cladding, and interior joinery directly alongside the clients.

#8935. Skin in the Game: Is Adapalene or Salicylic Acid Better for Acne?

If you have acne, you probably know more about skincare than most people. You might even impress friends with terms like “adapalene” and “salicylic acid.”

But do you know what each treatment does for your skin and if one is better for acne? Let’s find out!

Salicylic acid is a keratolytic agent commonly found in over-the-counter creams, face washes, masks, and gels. While it’s often used for acne, it can also help with dandruff, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, calluses, and warts.

Adapalene, often known by its brand name Differin, is a topical retinoid. It comes in various forms, such as gels, cleansers, and creams. And just like salicylic acid, it’s available over-the-counter without a prescription.

On a chemical level, adapalene and salicylic acid work in different ways to clear acne.

Salicylic acid breaks down a protein called keratin in the outer layer of the skin. Studies show this helps remove the buildup of dead skin cells. It also reduces inflammation in the skin, calming the redness that often comes with breakouts.

Adapalene, on the other hand, is a retinoid. And what, you may ask, is a retinoid? It’s a derivative of vitamin A that attaches to receptors in the skin. Doing so prompts cell turnover to speed up, helping skin regenerate more quickly and lowering the likelihood of clogged pores.

So… what do these differences mean for acne? Both adapalene and salicylic acid can treat skin prone to breakouts (though it’s not recommended to use them together since this can over-irritate your skin).

Which one is more potent may depend on your acne type. Research shows that adapalene was among the best treatments for comedonal acne (aka whiteheads and blackheads), whereas salicylic acid was less effective and more affordable.

Long story short: Your dermatologist can help determine which is the smarter choice for your type of acne.

Studies haven’t directly compared adapalene and salicylic acid for blackheads, but both can help. Blackheads form from plugged hair follicles, and salicylic acid’s exfoliating action can clear clogged pores. Adapalene increases cell turnover, which can also help remove blackheads.

Adapalene is a retinoid. Retinoids are well-established anti-aging agents because they stimulate new cell growth and promote collagen production. Some studies have also shown anti-aging benefits from salicylic acid.

While salicylic acid, due to its exfoliating properties, can help reduce wrinkles, adapalene is generally more effective for addressing aging-related concerns like wrinkles.

Adapalene is an over-the-counter acne treatment — so prescription-strength options may work better. According to the American Academy of Dermatology, some of the most potent acne treatments include antibiotics and isotretinoin.

Adapalene isn’t a magic wand for acne. It may be an ideal choice for some people, but depending on your skin type and sensitivity level, salicylic acid, other OTC products, or even a prescription treatment might be your best bet.

Research shows that adapalene can be just as strong for zapping zits as benzoyl peroxide (another potentially powerful weapon in the battle against acne). A 2024 study, for example, found that 0.1% topical adapalene was as safe and effective as a 4% benzoyl peroxide solution in people of color.

Though adapalene may be an effective acne treatment, it’s not the pinnacle of retinoid strength. Of the four “generations” of retinoids, adapalene is considered third-generation. Fourth-generation retinoids are typically stronger and have higher specificity to retinoic acid receptors in the skin. For this reason, they’re available only by prescription.

Feel free to experiment with adapalene and salicylic acid to see which works best for you — after all, it’s your face! You might find one more effective for your skin. For expert advice, be sure to consult your dermatologist.

Last medically reviewed on July 31, 2024

Celebrating a year of success, AdHoc Studios' Nick Herman and Dennis Lenart explain why more choices don't always make a better game.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every interactive story faces the same temptation: give the player more. More branches, more endings, more ways to bend the script until it snaps. Dispatch, AdHoc Studio's episodic superhero workplace comedy, went the other way. It stars Breaking Bad's Aaron Paul as former hero Robert Robertson, who now sends a team of reformed villains out on call-outs.

As the breakout indie game celebrates its one-year anniversary with the Dispatch Deluxe Edition, which lets you play the storyboard art, I caught up with the team. We've heard how Four video tracks and a doughnut shop got it started and how AdHoc made Dispatch feel like an animated TV series, so now I want to know how a choice-driven game gets that far by holding choices back. We put the question to AdHoc co-founders Nick Herman and Dennis Lenart, the studio's COO and CTO and both co-creative directors.

AdHoc starts with the belief that most developers get the equation backwards. "When folks set out to make an interactive narrative game, they incorrectly assume that it's all about the branching narrative that makes it exciting," Herman says. "We believe it's about the quality of that narrative at the core, and then you have to branch that quality narrative."

That's easy to say and hard to do, he admits, and harder still when you have to write multiple good stories at once, which is what the team signed up for. So the development team works from the story's spine and its characters, then figure out what choice space could believably exist alongside them.

Robert Robertson arrives with a backstory and a personality, so options that betray him are off the table. Herman sees that as a gift: it "eliminates blue sky" and lets the team concentrate on a believable character. It's also why he's wary when people ask for thousands of endings. Would 10,000 of them really be as compelling as a six or seven that the team has made as satisfying as possible?

Lenart describes the whole process as "almost an exercise in restraint at times". Picture 10 developers in a room discussing a scene where a character is aggressive towards you. A couple of them will say they wish you could just punch him. "The thing we have to filter that through is, 'Would Robert conceivably punch him in this situation?'" says Lenart. "A lot of times the answer is no."

It isn't a flat ban. If everyone agrees that punching him would be thrilling but there's no motivation for it, Herman says the conversation becomes how to make it a viable choice. Lenart says you go back into the scene and the story and set it up "so that that choice feels like it's a payoff to something that exists".

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Skip that groundwork and the cost is steep. "The more you do that, the more you start diluting your character and then they kind of become a little bit faceless," Lenart warns. Herman puts it more bluntly: the story starts to feel like "a narrative toy" and less like one with believable characters.

So how do you make a choice feel weighty without animating an entirely new story? Lenart says, "A lot of the magic in these types of games is the story that people are telling in their heads". The most effective choices, he says, are the ones where "you're affecting how another character in the story thinks about you".

Treat someone a certain way in front of the group, and players will assume that character's later behaviour is motivated by it. Every glance in a later scene gets read as payback for what you said earlier, which Lenart compares to real life. AdHoc builds on that expectation on purpose.

Herman calls it "the grease between the major cogs of choices". Players carry a decision forward for an hour or so, until the grease runs out and they need an injection of new stuff. If a scene doesn't land that way, he says, "it's probably because something's broken". Contrivance, or a sense of being guided, are the signs to go back and fix.

There's a hard budget reason for the discipline too. "It's also just so expensive to do it the way we're doing it," says Herman, with a vision for cinematic quality and animation that makes 30 different endings impossible.

Lenart gives an example of a branch the team could have offered. Imagine letting players choose at the start whether Robert works as a dispatcher or makes a new suit and heads off to be a hero in another city. It sounds great on a flowchart, but "you'd end up animating an entirely different game", with two separate stories, and Robert's arc would stop being about redemption.

Herman is generous about other approaches. He points to Slay the Princess, The Stanley Parable, and Detroit: Become Human as games where their branchiness and reactivity are major selling points. "Interactive narrative games are not one thing," he says. "The beauty of the medium is that everyone finds ways to express it in different ways."

Where does the line fall between what the player controls and what stays with the writers and developers? Lenart says it comes down to how much agency AdHoc is willing to hand over in order to tell a story it believes in. The more it gives up, the greater the risk of versions that aren't great. "Our goal was always to make it so that any path you play through is compelling and satisfying."

There's a cost, and AdHoc accepts it. Herman says some players will end up on a path that isn't their preference, and with stories it gets personal: "this isn't how I wanted it to go."

Lenart has seen the other side of the argument. On earlier games, multiple endings were mandated as a studio priority, and the takeaway was that "some of them worked". Some people had good playthroughs, others got endings they weren't satisfied with, and some were upset they didn't get the endings their friends did.

He doesn't count loose ends as a failure, either. "Not every story or movie you watch ends with you thinking everything is perfect and wrapped up," he says, and the threads people talk about afterwards are part of the experience. But "it can get out of hand if you don't keep it under control".

#8932. Thai Massage Therapy: Benefits and What to Expect

Feeling stressed? Whether you unwind with yoga or a relaxing massage, Thai massage combines the best of both worlds, benefiting your mind and body. Here’s everything you need to know!

Thai massage is a special kind of bodywork that blends relaxation with flexibility. Think of it as a gentle, full-body, more active experience. It’s all about boosting your flexibility and energizing your body. Just a heads-up: napping during a Thai massage might be a challenge!

Drawing from Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine, this ancient technique mixes assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and soothing rocking for 60 to 90 minutes. Unlike Western-style massages at a local spa, Thai massage takes place on a mat on the floor. A certified therapist will work to stretch your muscles and apply pressure along your body’s energy lines, known as sen, to release stress with a graceful, rhythmic touch.

You can schedule a Thai massage at many spas, massage clinics, and even some yoga studios, but make sure you find someone with the proper training and certification to give you an authentic experience.

When you arrive for a Thai massage, you might be given some comfy clothes, like a T-shirt and drawstring pants. You’ll remove your shoes, silence your phone, place your jewelry in a small dish, and settle onto a floor mat. Before the session, let the therapist know if you have any injuries.

If this is your first session, it can be intense, so focus on breathing and relaxing. You’ll likely start on your back, with the therapist beginning on your feet and legs. Since the therapist uses their body weight to guide you, it might initially feel a bit weird. Some discomfort is normal as your body stretches, but don’t hesitate to let your therapist know if anything feels uncomfortable.As the session progresses, you’ll likely switch positions, including flipping onto your belly or trying various other postures. Go with the flow as your therapist guides you through stretches and yoga-like moves designed to open up your joints, move your energy, and release tension. Keep breathing and communicate with your therapist throughout the process.

As the session wraps up, you’ll enjoy some gentle rocking motions to ease you out of the massage. You might feel sore afterward, especially if it’s your first Thai massage, so hydrate and rest. You’ll likely feel incredibly relaxed, more flexible, and energized.

Pro tip: Clear your mind and be open to guidance. While the stretches may feel awkward initially, allow yourself to let go. This can help you fully experience the massage’s benefits.

Your Thai massage experience won’t resemble a Western-style deep tissue massage. You won’t be naked under a sheet on a raised massage table, and the massage therapist won’t be using long, deep strokes to work your muscles.The other significant difference is that, like some forms of yoga, Thai massage has a spiritual element based on Buddhism. As they use the weight of their bodies to work on your body, your therapist is also trained to send you kind, loving, healing vibes. The ultimate goal is to help you feel better by allowing your energy to flow throughout your body.

The ancient practice of Thai massage combines assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and rhythmic rocking to unknot your body and get your inner energy flowing. Unlike Western massage techniques, you’ll be fully clothed on a floor mat, with the massage therapist using their entire body to release your tension.

Permit yourself to let go, and expect an active, sometimes intense, full-body experience that leaves you relaxed and energized.

Last medically reviewed on July 31, 2024

#8931. This week Sony revived its classic Walkman headphones

This week on Dezeen, Japanese electronics company Sony launched a remake of its original Walkman headphones, which have colourful foam pads and lean into 1980s nostalgia.

The headphones, called MDR-3R, resemble the model that debuted with the first portable Walkman cassette player in 1979. However, the new edition has a USB-C connector that works with most modern devices.

Other design news included Swedish designer Gustaf Westman’s unveiling of his full collection for media company Disney, including a bookstand shaped like Donald Duck and a mirror that resembles Pluto.

“Mickey’s ears and white gloves, Minnie’s bow, Goofy’s playful silhouette – they’re instantly recognisable shapes, and that made them really fun to work with,” Westman told Dezeen about working with the familiar characters.

American architect Steven Holl has designed a colourful watch for Swiss watch brand Cauny informed by a compliment architect Álvaro Siza once gave him, telling Holl he used colour “like Matisse”.

The colourful watch, which has a three-dimensional dial with red, green, yellow and blue colour blocks, was designed to be a dialogue between the two architects.

A housing development in Andorra designed by French studio Ateliers Jean Nouvel and Spanish studio Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos has been damaged in a fire.

Called La Querola, the project is shortlisted in the housing category of this year’s Dezeen Awards and recently won the awards’ public vote. The cause of the fire is unknown and no official estimate of the extent of the damage has been released so far.

In Shanghai, access to the staircase of the Grand Opera House by international studio Snøhetta has been restricted to ticket holders.

Access to the spiral staircase, which leads up to the roof and has become a popular spot for photos, now costs £5.60 per person. Snøhetta told Dezeen that “visitor management is necessary”.

In car news, Swedish brand Polestar has unveiled its Formula 2030 concept car that the brand says “screams performance”.

The low-slung sports car has signature Dual Blade headlights and was intended to project power, with a long bonnet, wraparound windscreen, short overhangs, muscular haunches and 22-inch wheels.

In a roundup, we explored five examples of Mesoamerican modern architecture that combine principles from ancient architecture with modern techniques.

Curator and writer Su Wu chose five homes, which she says “reflect the complex aesthetic cultures of Mesoamerica”, from her book on the subject.

Popular projects on Dezeen this week include a former agricultural barn in Cornwall, a viewpoint informed by Viking rings and a playful Portuguese retreat.

#8930. sanrivatti ONE takes the forward lean of motorcycle racing into hypercar design

inspired by the physical immediacy of motorcycle riding, the apex position moves the driver forward in the cockpit, challenging conventional assumptions about visibility, control, and the experience of speed.

Sanrivatti ONE, the debut hypercar of the company, is developed around a driving architecture that places the driver in a forward-leaning, head-forward position. The vehicle brings together an experimental approach to cockpit ergonomics and a lightweight, naturally aspirated performance platform.

Τhe company’s proprietary Apex Position moves the driver forward and upright compared with the reclined position found in most hypercars. Inspired by the physical immediacy of riding a high-performance motorcycle, the arrangement aims to create a closer relationship between the driver’s body, the vehicle, and the circuit. According to Sanrivatti, the position provides a more open field of vision, a heightened perception of acceleration and cornering, and a more precise understanding of the car’s placement on track.

The Dutch automotive company introduces the Apex Position and influences the relationship between the driver, cockpit, steering system, pedals, and surrounding bodywork. The intention is to make driving a more physical experience, where the driver feels more directly connected to the movements of the vehicle.

Sanrivatti says that the position provides 3.2 times more of the circuit in view at Corner Three at Silverstone, compared with a selection of ten hypercars and track cars. The company also reports a vertical field of view of 28 degrees, against 15.5 degrees for its benchmark hypercar.

The approach has also informed the exterior proportions of the ONE. Its low, elongated body features a sweeping upper line, a single-piece canopy, and pronounced through-body air tunnels. Sanrivatti cites the peregrine falcon in a high-speed dive and the precision of modern fighter aircraft as references for the design. The silhouette appears shaped around the driver’s forward position, with the cockpit integrated into a body that emphasizes directional movement and aerodynamic expression.

Sanrivatti targets an 800 hp output from a naturally aspirated 5.5-liter Judd V10, paired with a six-speed Hewland sequential gearbox and rear-wheel drive. A carbon-fiber monocoque forms the structural foundation, while the targeted dry weight is 1,100 kg.

The company also lists a target torque of 700 Nm and a projected maximum speed of 330 km/h. All these figures remain provisional and subject to development, testing, and validation.

The choice of a naturally aspirated V10 and sequential transmission points toward a driving experience centered on direct mechanical feedback. The ONE proposes an interpretation of contemporary performance that places physical engagement and driver perception at the forefront.
