#8909. Tant A Temps Design "restores the visual characteristics of Tang architecture" in Chinese cafe

Local practice Tant A Temps Design aimed to revive the aesthetics of the Tang Dynasty when designing the interiors for cafe Laibei 1087, located in a historical building in Xi’an, China.

The cafe sits inside the Beilin Museum, originally constructed in 1087 to preserve stone steles inscribed with Confucian philosophy and famous calligraphic works.

The timber columns and beams of the historic building were preserved, with the same approach extended into the cafe interiors.

Guided by a “minimum intervention” and “zero damage” renovation strategy, Tant A Temps Design made every new addition detachable and reversible, which allowed the building’s original features to remain untouched.

In the cafe, the furniture is suspended from wooden beams or arranged around columns to avoid direct contact with the original structures.

Tant A Temps Design also created tables, chairs and display cabinets with designs that draw from elements of the ancient building framework, such as the beams, columns and dougong brackets.

Lightweight and prefabricated materials and modular systems were used throughout the space.

For the main colour palette, Tant A Temps Design chose light green hues complemented by gold accents.

“The purpose of choosing this colour scheme is to restore the visual characteristics of Tang architecture – robust, imposing and richly coloured,” the studio explained.

“Abandoning the rigid replication of ancient architecture, it extracts and reshapes the spiritual core of Tang and Song aesthetics through a restrained colour palette and minimalist structural language, creating a serene and elegant atmosphere that highly matches the cultural temperament of the Stele Forest.”

An integrated functional island was designed to function as the central bar counter.

All modern utility systems, including air conditioning, water, electricity, lighting and exhausts, were concealed and integrated into the top and bottom of the bar counter.

This is consistent with the studio’s commitment to preserving the heritage building while giving it a contemporary, functional upgrade.

“This forms a functional system that is both independent of the original building structure and seamlessly integrated into the historical environment, setting a new paradigm for the adaptive reuse of similar cultural heritage buildings,” said the studio.

The cafe is part of a 220-square-metre development that also includes a rest area, a retail zone and a stone-rubbing workshop that serves as a history learning centre.

According to Tant A Temps Design, the project has transformed a dormant historical building into an accessible and interactive cultural space.

Led by founder Wei Chen, Tant A Temps Design is an interior design practice based in Xi’an.

Elsewhere in China, Linehouse has completed the interiors of the Jen hotel in Hangzhou and Keiji Ashizawa designed an “open and inviting retail space” in the historic building in Shanghai.

#8908. What Does Dark Green Poop Mean? Causes, Diet, and When to See a Doctor

Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.

Most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down. But if the green becomes a recurring (fecal) matter, it might be something else.

Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.

Spotting green or another unexpected color in the toilet can be startling, but it’s more common than you might think. From dietary influences to your body’s digestion speed, several factors can change poop from earthy tones to other shades. Let’s check some out.

Are you chowing down on lots of green leafy veggies like spinach, kale, or broccoli? These foods are high in chlorophyll, which can dye your doodles green. Chlorophyll doesn’t always break down entirely before reaching your intestines, meaning it passes through your system and colors your stool green.

Have you ever had a St. Paddy’s Day-themed milkshake or a brightly colored cake? Artificial colors in foods and drinks can change poop from brown to green. It’s not magic! It’s just the dye in green food passing through your gut unchanged.

When your digestive system processes food too rapidly, it doesn’t allow for the full breakdown of bile, a yellow-green fluid that aids digestion. This often results in a greenish stool, especially during fast-moving episodes of diarrhea.

Have you recently been taking antibiotics? These meds can reset your gut’s bacterial crew. Since these tiny critters play a big part in the shade of your stool, introducing antibiotics might cause green poop sometimes.

If you’ve had certain medical treatments, it can affect digestion and cause bright green poop. One example is graft-versus-host disease, which may occur with bone marrow transplants. This tricky condition can bring about less-than-welcome guests, like diarrhea and green stool. It’s a clear signal from your body that things are out of sync.

Some uninvited microscopic guests like Salmonella bacteria, the water-loving mini parasite Giardia, and norovirus can also be a reason for your poop turning green. These critters can hustle your digestion at an unnaturally quick pace, turning your stool green as they disrupt your gut’s usual rhythm.

Babies can surprise you with a whole crayon box of poop colors, and green is definitely in the mix.

For infants, green stool might stem from the same factors as adults, like dietary changes. This includes adjustments when they start eating solids or changes in a parent’s diet if chestfeeding.

Another harmless cause could be ingesting a small amount of amniotic fluid in the womb. So, if you notice your little one sporting some spring grass-colored diapers, it’s usually no biggie.

If the green theme park in your toilet isn’t closing down, or if it’s accompanied by other symptoms like severe stomach pain, nausea, or diarrhea, it might be time to call in the pros. Persistent changes in stool color may signal underlying health issues that need medical attention.

Dark green poop can result from eating lots of leafy greens or foods with green coloring. However, it can also indicate that food travels quickly through the digestive system.

While liver issues can change stool color, they usually turn it pale or dark, not green. If you’re worried about liver health, look for pale or clay-colored stools instead.

If you haven’t been on a kale-eating spree, dark green poop might be from iron supplements or constipation remedies, which can also give poop a greenish tint.

Dark poop could be a sign of your diet or medications. However, if it’s black and tar-like, it might mean bleeding in your upper gastrointestinal tract. In that case, chatting with a healthcare professional is a must.

While green poop can def throw you through a loop, it’s usually not a sign of anything serious. It’s often your body’s way of dealing with what you eat or how fast you digest. So, unless it’s paired with other worrying symptoms, there’s probably no need to panic.

Visit the Iberia Plus website and locate their published off-peak date chart for your target route. Off-peak windows typically include January through March and October through November. Confirm your travel dates fall within the off-peak range before committing points.

Log into your Iberia Plus account and search for business class award flights on your target dates. Look for flights priced at 34,000 Avios one-way. If availability is not showing, try shifting dates by 1-2 days within the off-peak window.

Once you confirm availability, transfer points from Chase UR, Amex MR, Capital One, Citi ThankYou, or Marriott Bonvoy. Chase and Amex transfers are typically instant. Allow 1-2 business days for others.

Complete the booking through the Iberia website using your Avios balance. Unlike many partner awards, Iberia off-peak bookings can be made entirely online without calling. Select your seat during the booking process.

Madrid is a natural hub for onward travel. Consider booking a separate low-cost carrier flight or Avios short-haul to Barcelona, Lisbon, or Seville. Iberia's short-haul Avios pricing is also excellent for intra-Europe connections.

Picture this: you're settling into a fully flat bed on an Iberia Airbus A350-900, somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Spanish wine in hand, Madrid a few hours away. The cabin is quiet, the seat is wide, and you're sleeping your way to Europe in genuine business class comfort. The person next to you in economy paid $900 for their ticket. You paid $900 in cash too — except your $900 covered taxes, fees, and a couple of nice dinners in Madrid. The flights themselves cost you 34,000 Iberia Avios. That's the magic of this redemption, and once you see it, you can't unsee it. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community light up: a round-trip business class ticket from JFK to Madrid on Iberia regularly retails for **$2,500 to $5,000** in cash. At the off-peak Avios rate of **34,000 points one-way**, you're extracting **7.4 to 14.7 cents per point** — a figure that puts this redemption in a completely different category from most loyalty redemptions, where 1–2 cents per point is considered standard. To put that in human terms: if you transferred 34,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Iberia Plus and used them for this booking, you'd be getting a value equivalent to someone handing you a $2,500–$5,000 check in exchange for points that cost you roughly $340–$510 in credit card spend to earn (at a 1% earn baseline). That's not a deal. That's a pricing inefficiency, and it's one that's been hiding in plain sight for travelers who only know British Airways Avios and never discovered Iberia's **separate, more generous award chart**. The FI mindset is about finding asymmetries — places where the value you receive is wildly disproportionate to what you give up. This is one of the cleanest examples in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. You're not gaming anything. You're simply using Iberia's published off-peak pricing to access a premium cabin product that most people assume is out of reach. Your future self, lying flat at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, will be glad you learned this system.

Europe in a lie-flat seat for fewer points than most domestic first class awards

Here's the insight that separates travelers who occasionally use points from those who systematically fly business class to Europe for nearly free: Iberia Avios and British Airways Avios are the same currency, but they operate on completely different award charts.

Most people who've been in the travel rewards world for a while know about British Airways Avios. They know that BA prices awards by distance, and they know that BA is notorious for hefty fuel surcharges that can turn a "free" business class flight into a $700+ fees bill. So they write off transatlantic Avios redemptions as not worth it.

That's the mistake. Iberia — a fellow Oneworld carrier and Avios partner — publishes its own off-peak award chart for flights operated on Iberia metal (Iberia aircraft, Iberia flight numbers). Flights from the US to Madrid, when booked through Iberia Plus (not British Airways Executive Club), price out at 34,000 Avios one-way in business class during off-peak periods. That's the same Avios currency, same points you can transfer from Chase, but priced under Iberia's more favorable structure.

The fuel surcharge situation is also materially better on Iberia-operated flights booked through Iberia Plus than BA-operated flights booked through BA. Taxes and fees are generally moderate — you're looking at a few hundred dollars in fees rather than the $600–$700+ that sometimes plagues British Airways award bookings.

Off-peak windows are specific. Iberia defines off-peak as January through March and October through November. Mark those months. Outside of those windows, pricing steps up, and the sweet spot math starts to erode.

The transfer path is straightforward. Iberia Plus is a 1:1 transfer partner with Chase Ultimate Rewards, and transfers are instant — a critical advantage when you're chasing limited award availability. You search, you find the seat, you transfer, you book. No waiting 3–5 days for points to land and watching the seat disappear.

Marriott Bonvoy is also a transfer partner (3:1 ratio, 1–5 days), but the math there is less favorable and the speed is slower. Chase Ultimate Rewards is your primary earning vehicle for this redemption.

One important structural note: Avios are shareable across BA, Iberia, Aer Lingus, and Vueling accounts — meaning if you've been accumulating BA Avios, you can move them to an Iberia Plus account to access Iberia's off-peak pricing. This opens the door even if you've been building your Avios balance through the British Airways credit card or BA partners. The accounts need to be linked through the Avios household account feature, but it's a powerful tool that many travelers overlook.

Finally, keep the expiry rule in mind: Iberia Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. A single small transaction — even buying a few Avios — resets the clock. Don't let your points die quietly in an unused account.

If you don't already have one, go to iberia.com and sign up for a free Iberia Plus account. This takes about five minutes. Write down your membership number — you'll need it for the transfer step. Make sure your name matches your passport exactly to avoid issues at check-in.

Go to iberia.com and select "Book with Avios" in the award booking section. Enter your route (e.g., JFK to MAD) and select your travel dates. Critically, target off-peak months: January through March, and October through November. These are the windows where the 34,000 Avios one-way business class pricing applies.

Search one-way first. Iberia's search tool will show you available Avios seats color-coded by price — you're looking for the off-peak pricing tier. If you see 34,000 Avios for business class, that's your seat. Note the specific flight number and date before doing anything with your points.

Before transferring a single point, click through the booking to see the full taxes and fees. Iberia charges moderate fees on transatlantic awards — generally more reasonable than British Airways — but you want to know the number. Confirm you're comfortable with the cash portion before proceeding.

Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards portal at ultimaterewards.com. Navigate to "Transfer to Travel Partners" and select Iberia Plus. Transfer exactly 34,000 points (or the amount required for your specific itinerary). Transfers from Chase to Iberia Plus are 1:1 and instant — your Avios will appear in your Iberia Plus account within minutes.

Go back to iberia.com with your Iberia Plus account logged in. Confirm the award seat is still showing (it should be — you moved fast). Complete the booking using your Avios balance. Pay the taxes and fees with a card that earns well on travel or general spend.

Award space on popular routes can be tight. Here's how to improve your odds:

Most airline programs charge the same award price year-round or use dynamic pricing that moves with demand. Iberia is unusual because it publishes an explicit off-peak calendar with fixed lower pricing during specific date ranges. Off-peak pricing applies to the flight date, not the booking date, so you can book an off-peak flight months in advance and lock in the lower rate. The off-peak discount is roughly 50% compared to peak pricing on the same route. This creates a planning advantage for flexible travelers who can target specific travel windows. Combined with the fact that Avios transfer from five major credit card programs, it is one of the most accessible premium redemptions in the loyalty landscape.

Let's walk through a real example so the numbers are concrete.

It's mid-October — peak fall travel season for most Europeans, but squarely within Iberia's off-peak award window (October through November). You've found award space on IB6251, JFK to MAD, departing John F. Kennedy at 10:30 PM and arriving at Madrid Barajas the following afternoon. The aircraft is an Airbus A350-900 — one of the best long-haul platforms in the sky.

The cash price for this flight in business class: $3,200 one-way, as priced on iberia.com for that week. Round trip in business runs approximately $4,800–$6,000 depending on timing.

The Avios price: 34,000 Iberia Avios plus approximately $250–$350 in taxes and fees.

Your CPP on this redemption: With a retail value of $3,200 and a cost of 34,000 points, you're extracting 9.4 cents per point — comfortably in the 7.4–14.7 cent range that defines this sweet spot as exceptional.

Now let's talk about what you're actually getting for those points. Iberia Business on the A350-900 features fully flat seats in a 1-2-1 configuration — meaning every passenger has direct aisle access. No climbing over a seatmate at 2 AM. The seat converts to a fully flat bed of approximately 73 inches. You'll have a personal entertainment screen, noise-canceling headphones, and amenity kit.

Before you board, you have access to Iberia's business class lounge at MAD (on the return) and partner lounges at JFK — typically the Iberia-operated space or a Oneworld partner lounge. The meal service on this transatlantic route reflects Spanish hospitality: proper courses, wine service, and a breakfast before landing.

For a couple traveling together, this redemption costs 68,000 Avios plus fees — a round figure that's very achievable through the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve welcome bonus alone. You land in Madrid rested, having slept in a flat bed over the Atlantic, having spent a fraction of what cash passengers paid. That's the FI travel rewards system working exactly as it should.

Do this: Book as close to 355 days out as possible for off-peak dates. Iberia releases award space up to 355 days in advance. The most reliable business class availability appears right when that window opens. If your target is January or February travel, set a calendar reminder for April or May of the prior year and search on Day 355. The seats won't last.

Do this: Transfer Avios from a BA account if you've been building there. If you've been earning BA Avios through the British Airways credit card or BA shopping portal, you don't need to start over. Avios are transferable across BA, Iberia, Aer Lingus, and Vueling accounts via the household account feature. Link the accounts, move the Avios to your Iberia Plus account, and access the off-peak pricing. This is an underused feature.

Do this: Earn points primarily through Chase Ultimate Rewards. The Chase Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, and Ink Business Preferred all feed into the same Chase UR pool with a 1:1 instant transfer to Iberia Plus. For this redemption specifically, Chase is your most efficient earning engine. Use the welcome bonus from one of these cards as your foundation — a 60,000–100,000 point bonus gets you most of the way to two one-way business class seats.

Avoid this: Transferring points before confirming award space. Avios are transferred into Iberia Plus and can't be easily moved back or transferred to another program without complexity. Always confirm the exact flight, date, and availability BEFORE you initiate a transfer from Chase. The instant transfer speed from Chase means you can lock in availability quickly — but only once you've verified the seat exists.

Avoid this: Booking during peak periods expecting off-peak pricing. December, July, and August are not off-peak. The 34,000 Avios rate is specifically tied to Iberia's off-peak calendar (January–March and October–November). Outside those windows, pricing increases significantly and the CPP math deteriorates. Don't assume off-peak pricing applies year-round.

Do this: Keep your Iberia Plus account active. Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. If you're holding points for a future redemption, keep the account alive with a small transaction — even earning a few Avios through a partner purchase resets the clock for another 36 months.

This redemption is ideal for couples and solo travelers who want to experience genuine transatlantic business class — flat beds, real meal service, lounge access — without the $3,000–$5,000 cash outlay that normally makes that choice feel irresponsible on a FI journey.

You're a great fit for this redemption if:

This is also an excellent gateway redemption for families with older children who understand that off-peak travel timing is part of the strategy — though booking four or more business class seats requires significant Avios accumulation and tighter award availability.

For the FI community member who's disciplined about earning and has a Chase UR foundation, this is one of the cleanest business class sweet spots available anywhere in the transatlantic market.

This redemption is rated **moderate difficulty** — not because anything about it is technically complex, but because it requires you to navigate a few specific steps that most people haven't done before. **The main challenges are:** 1. **Awareness of the separate Iberia award chart.** Most travelers default to British Airways Avios and never discover that Iberia prices its own flights differently. Once you know this, it's not a challenge — it's an advantage. 2. **Award availability.** Iberia business class award seats on JFK–MAD are genuinely limited, especially as you get closer to the off-peak windows. You're competing with other knowledgeable award travelers. Availability is rated a 3 out of 5 for a reason — the seats are there, but you have to work for them. 3. **Account setup.** You need an Iberia Plus account separate from any BA account, and you need to navigate iberia.com's award search interface, which is functional but not as polished as some other programs. **Three tips to overcome these challenges:** - Search award space **355 days in advance** for maximum selection - Use **iberia.com directly** to search — it shows Iberia-operated availability most accurately - Keep the **Chase UR instant transfer** in your back pocket so you can act the moment you find space If you've ever transferred points to an airline and booked an award flight before, this will feel familiar. If this is your first time, expect to spend an evening learning the process — but the payoff is a flat-bed seat over the Atlantic for a fraction of its cash price. That's worth an evening.

Iberia Avios and British Airways Avios are the same currency and can be transferred between accounts for free. However, Iberia's award chart prices flights on Iberia metal differently than British Airways does. For flights to Madrid on Iberia-operated routes, booking through Iberia Plus is typically cheaper than through BA Executive Club.

No. Iberia's off-peak pricing applies only to Iberia-operated flights. British Airways has its own separate pricing structure through BA Executive Club. For flights to London, you would need to use BA Avios and their own award chart, which does not offer the same off-peak discount.

Yes. Iberia updates its off-peak calendar periodically, and the specific date ranges can shift by a few weeks. Always check the current published calendar before planning your trip. The general pattern of January-March and October-November as off-peak has been consistent, but exact boundaries vary.

Iberia long-haul business class features fully flat seats in a 1-2-1 configuration with direct aisle access on their A350 and A330 aircraft. The seats convert to a flat bed for sleeping. The food and wine service reflects Spanish culinary traditions, including Iberian ham and regional wines. It is a solid European business class product, comparable to Air France or Lufthansa.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Iberia Avios off-peak business class to Madrid is the most efficient way to fly business class to Europe on points. At 34,000 Avios one-way, it costs less than many domestic first class awards. The off-peak calendar rewards flexible travelers with a 50% discount, and the breadth of transfer partners means almost anyone with transferable points can access this redemption. If you can align your European travel with the off-peak windows, this sweet spot delivers exceptional value with minimal complexity.

As rumours about the casting of the next James Bond began to hot up this week, my phone has been busy. Most of my friends (hello, both!) know me as a huge James Bond fan, and have wanted to know who I thought was going to get the role. Well, one thing's for sure, I told them all. It won't be Pattinson. Mark my words. He's just too famous.

So you can imagine my surprise when Robert Pattinson was indeed announced as the new James Bond this afternoon. Everything about the news feels bizarre to me, including the lack of press release and associated fanfare (whereas Daniel Craig rode down the Thames on a speedboat, Pattinson was announced via a simple social media post). But the biggest shock is that Pattinson is by far the most famous person to be cast in the role. He's the first bonafide A-lister to pick up the Walther PPK. He's Batman, for God's sake. For better or worse, the Bond brand changed forever today. And it's thanks to one name: Amazon.

It perhaps isn't surprising that Blofeld's—sorry, Bezos's—company has opted for such a bankable star. The company paid billions to acquire MGM (which owned the rights to Bond), and will want a return on its investment. But the whole thing seems so at odds with the ethos of the previous Bond custodians. "I felt I had to have an unknown actor, not a star," producer Cubby Broccoli said of the search for the very first Bond. "Above all, a man you’d believe could be James Bond."

For decades, Bond has been one of the most carefully controlled brands in entertainment. The gun barrel sequence, the theme tune, the 007 logo, the Aston Martin; every element is instantly recognisable, and has been meticulously protected by the Broccoli family. Bond films have always felt like events, partly because they don't come along very often. But Amazon doesn't do scarcity, it does content. And with the company now in creative control of the franchise, it's hard not to wonder how long it will be before 007 becomes less of a cinematic institution and more of an endlessly expandable IP. I'm not sure I'm ready for the 'Young Q' spin-off.

There are, of course, opportunities here. Bond has arguably been in need of a shake-up for some time, and Pattinson is a genuinely exciting actor, capable of bringing something strange, unpredictable and perhaps even uncomfortable to a character that has occasionally felt trapped by his own iconography. But the choice also feels like a statement of intent from Amazon. Where previous Bond actors were largely blank canvases onto which the 007 identity could be projected, Pattinson arrives with a huge, established brand of his own. Rather than making a star out of Bond, Amazon has bought a star to sell Bond. It's a subtle distinction, but a significant one. Am I going to be able to look up at the screen and see James Bond, rather than Robert Pattinson in a suit?

But while it'll be Pattinson's name that hogs the headlines, the bigger question isn't simply what kind of Bond Pattinson will be, but what kind of brand Amazon wants Bond to become. Will the company recognise that Bond's enduring appeal lies partly in his exclusivity, his mystique, and his ability to remain just a little out of reach? For all of his reinventions, 007 has always felt bigger than the actor playing him. Until today.

#8905. Foster + Partners creates Area worktable for today's office

Foster + Partners Industrial Design aimed to bring expressive and functional workplace design together in its modular Area table system, created with Spanish furniture brand Kettal.

Designed to be durable and adaptable, Area combines aluminium columns, a panoply of tabletop options and concealed power.

The aluminium columns anchor the design, serving as both structural support and discreet container for power cables and electrical components.

Available in three diameters – 90, 160 or 450 millimetres – and either anodised or powder-coated finishes, they also bring customisable personality to the worktable.

The tabletops, meanwhile, come in shapes ranging from round to triangular and rhomboid and materials including timber, linoleum, melamine and Fenix. For larger conference or feature tables, terrazzo or marble are also options.

“Area is a collection of durable, expressive elements that define workstations and gathering points within a space to support both individual and collaborative work,” said Foster + Partners head of industrial design Mike Holland.

“The development of Area involved finding the right balance between structural performance, flexibility and visual simplicity,” he continued.

“The system needed to accommodate a wide variety of tabletop configurations and working arrangements, while integrating the technical infrastructure required in contemporary workplaces.”

The Area system can be accessorised with lighting or fabric screen dividers, the infrastructure for which is built into the table. Screen dividers attach magnetically at designed points, with lighting used in combination or mounted independently.

Cables are hidden underneath the tabletop within a J-profile aluminium beam that also provides structural support, while concealed grommets provide access to plug sockets and USB-C connections.

Holland told Dezeen that designing these accessories so they could function seamlessly across a range of tabletop configurations was the key challenge of the design process for Area, alongside achieving the desired proportions and textures for the aluminium columns.

To realise their vision for the expansive system, the design team undertook extensive prototyping, including using both one-to-one and full-scale models and augmented reality (AR).

“Working with full-scale models, augmented reality and 3D printing allowed us to understand the relationship between the different components and how they would function together in real working environments,” said Holland.

“This approach was particularly important in refining the columns, assessing their proportions, and adapting the surface texture pattern at full scale. It also allowed us to evolve the design from wider diameters into more elegant and efficient forms.”

He said that working with models and AR also allowed manufacturer Kettal to engage in the design process and contribute ideas.

“Collaboration is at the heart of our approach, and we believe it is fundamental to achieving the highest-quality results,” said Holland.

Area was designed for the contemporary workplace, said Holland, where flexible and hybrid working have made the office primarily a place for collaboration and connection, and where the table’s modularity and adaptability allow it to evolve as needs change.

“As designers, we are interested in the points of interaction between people and buildings,” said Holland. “At the heart of industrial design lies the creation of these touchpoints through which people experience space.”

“In the workplace, furniture plays a vital role in shaping how people engage with their environment, influencing how they occupy, navigate and connect with the spaces around them,” Holland concluded.

Part of the architecture firm Foster + Partners, Foster + Partners Industrial Design started by creating site-specific furniture, fixtures and fittings for the company’s buildings and over the last 50 years have expanded to more stand-alone commercial products.

Some of its recent designs include the Join plywood furniture collection, Ori bird feeders and Datum porcelain tableware.

#8903. vhils and marcelo cidade shroud historic são paulo building in a shimmering silver skin

using silver thermal sheets and cornstarch paste, the artists transform an historic building into a study of architecture and urban memory.

Portuguese artist Vhils (Alexandre Farto) and Brazilian artist Marcelo Cidade have wrapped the facade of an old building in São Paulo with reflective silver thermal sheets. Titled 2878, after its address on Rua Cardeal Arcoverde in the Pinheiros neighborhood, the intervention gives the historic structure a metallic new appearance. Its original architectural features are expressed beneath the covering, while the silver surface catches the changing light of the street.

The artists have applied individual sheets of thermal material directly to the facade using a simple adhesive made from cornstarch. The lightweight covering follows the contours of the existing architecture, picking out its openings and decorative details. Depending on the angle of the sunlight, the building appears to glow against its surroundings or reflect them back in fragmented patches. The public artwork plays with this shifting visibility to draw attention to an address that would have otherwise likely blended into the streetscape.

The building itself has an interesting past. Records dating back to 1945 identify the property as the site of a tuberculosis dispensary operated by São Paulo’s public health authorities. A government decree from 1953 further documents its use for the Pinheiros dispensary, while more recent records identify it as a former home of SUCEN, the state’s agency for controlling endemic diseases.

The structure has remained on the same street for decades, and has passed through different uses as the neighborhood has changed around it. By temporarily concealing its original surfaces, Vhils and Cidade bring its architecture back into public view. Their intervention considers how familiar buildings can gradually fade from a city’s collective awareness, even while continuing to occupy a prominent place in the urban landscape.

The project marks the first collaboration between the two artists, whose practices have long engaged with the built environment. Vhils is widely recognized for his portraits carved directly into urban walls, where removing layers of plaster and concrete reveals images beneath the surface. Cidade often works with architectural elements and materials drawn from the street, and examines how buildings shape people’s relationships with public space.

The silver sheeting recalls a protective thermal blanket which suggests an attempt to both preserve the building and obscure its original character. This tension is central to the work. The reflective facade can make the architecture unusually conspicuous, while its shifting surface also allows the building to visually dissolve into the city around it.

The installation arrives alongside Vhils’ exhibition ATRITO: Arqueologia do Presente (Friction: Archaeology of the Present), which opened at Galleria Continua in São Paulo on November 14th, 2026. Curated by Ana Carolina Ralston, the exhibition explores the physical traces left by urban transformation.

Among its central works are fourteen corroded metal cubes arranged as a labyrinth, their surfaces marked with fragments of portraits and signage drawn from cities around the world. Vhils has also created a separate large-scale intervention across the gallery’s glass facade.

Outside the gallery, 2878 brings these ideas directly into the neighborhood. The choice of an existing building, along with the inexpensive materials used to cover it, gives the installation an immediate relationship with the street. For a time, the familiar address becomes a reflective landmark, its architectural details newly apparent beneath the silver covering.

#8901. Pepper & Well designs bathroom that mimics concrete architecture of Paul Couch house

Melbourne-based studio Pepper & Well took cues from crisscrossing concrete walls and ceiling beams when designing Lumeah, a new en-suite for a house by celebrated architect Paul Couch.

Located in Macedon, central Victoria, the linear single-storey house was completed in 2006 by the late Couch, who passed away earlier this year.

When new owners bought the property in 2018, they felt the layout and finishes of the main bathroom didn’t meet the standards of the rest of the house.

They asked Pepper & Well to upgrade it and make it more accessible.

“There was an opportunity to make the space more comfortable and practical as they aged,” said lead architect Andy Dal Pozzo.

The previous layout included a WC, an enclosed shower and a step-in plunge pool, all within a space just 3.5 metres long.

Pepper & Well’s scheme removed the plunge, allowing space for a larger WC and for an open shower to be built in place of the old frosted-glass enclosure.

The defining move was the addition of a cast-concrete element that partitions the toilet and shower areas.

This incorporates an informal bench, allowing for seated showers if preferred.

The geometry of this element clearly references the house’s exposed concrete structure, a rhythmic arrangement of concrete beams over concrete walls.

“Our approach began with understanding the logic of Paul’s work,” explained Dal Pozzo.

“We wanted the renovation to share the original architecture’s material honesty and clarity, while remaining recognisable as a new contribution,” he said.

A change in floor surface marks the junction between old and new.

While most of the room features the bluestone flooring installed 20 years ago, the toilet and shower have a surface of crazy-paved slate.

The stone is the same Mintaro Brown Back slate that Couch installed in the bathroom of his own house, Toolern Vale.

“Laid in crazy paving beside the retained bluestone, it introduces a distinct texture with a direct connection to Paul’s work,” said Dal Pozzo.

The rest of the room was left largely intact, including the solid timber doors and the vanity unit spanning the opposite wall.

There are subtle correlations between the two sides of the room, so as not to make the new insertion feel disparate. For instance, a glass screen matches the height of the mirror opposite.

The shower also includes a stainless-steel handrail that doubles as a towel rail, matching the rest of the bathroom fixtures.

“The scale of the commission demanded close attention to every decision, from the arrangement of the room to the meeting of two stones,” added Dal Pozzo.

“By revealing the original fabric, retaining what worked and introducing a few carefully resolved elements, we sought to give the clients a bathroom that would serve them into the future and continue the architectural story of their home.”

Lumeah is shortlisted for bathroom of the year in Dezeen Awards 2026.

Other projects in this category include Kan Atelier’s design for the William King Apartment, a residence in a 1950s block in Athens, which won the public vote.

#8900. How to Calculate Your Rising and Moon Sign: A Beginner’s Guide

The sun sign is the *it girlie* of the “big three” elements in astrology.

But do you know about your moon sign and rising sign?

We chatted with an astrologer to understand what they are and how to calculate them.

According to Olga Verkhotina — astrologer and personal coach — the big three in astrology are your three most significant chart elements:

“While a natal chart contains so many more intricate details beyond just three elements, the big three is a way to determine the main highlights that make up your personality and overall temperament,” Verkhotina says.

Verkhotina explains that a rising sign is the zodiac sign that falls at the beginning of your First House — basically, the beginning of your natal chart.

“The First House in astrology is associated with a person’s identity, individual activity, even their appearance, and the sign that houses that theme gives its characteristics,” she says.

“Knowing your rising sign describes the way others may perceive you, the way your behavior comes across, as well as how you approach new situations in life.”

You’ll need: date, time and place of birth.

“Knowing the accurate time is important here because even 10 minutes can make a difference in the sign,” Verkhotina explains.

“Once you have the data, you can trust astrology software to calculate it for you. There are a lot of natal chart calculators online, so you can just search ‘rising sign calculator,'” Verkhotina says.

Pro tip: Verkhotina suggests reading horoscopes from your rising sign instead of your sun sign, saying it will likely give more personalized insights on which areas of your life might be impacted by current cosmic events.

“A moon sign describes the position of the moon on the zodiac wheel at the moment of your birth,” Verkhotina says.

She explains that the moon in astrology symbolizes:

“The moon sign helps you better understand how these themes demonstrate themselves in your life,” Verkhotina says.

Unlike the rising sign, you don’t have to have the precise time of birth to know your moon sign, although Verkhotina says it’s still recommended.

You can also use an online calculator to find your moon sign or refer to the ephemeris — a table showing the daily positions of planets.

Verkhotina describes the sun sign as the most important planet in your chart.

“It’s the center of your vitality, your ego, consciousness, and individuality at its core. That’s why it’s the most commonly known element in astrology,” she says.

It represents the zodiac sign the sun was in at the time of your birth, which Verkhotina says gives your individuality certain qualities associated with its specific sign.

“It’s important to understand that although the sun is a huge element in astrology, it doesn’t cover the nuances of one’s character,” Verkhotina explains.

Instead, she says it just represents overall traits.

Verkhotina adds that the specifics of your character are covered in the rest of your astrological chart. “This is why sometimes no two leos are the same,” she says.

This one is easy peasy — you don’t have to have your time or place of birth.

“The sun cycle is very similar every year, so you can look it up by the date, month and year of your birth. Each sign corresponds to a calendar date that year,” Verkhotina says.

Here’s each astro sign, in a nutshell, according to Verkhotina.

Your sun sign is important, but your moon and rising signs add extra details.

Your rising sign reflects your identity and how others see you, while your moon sign reveals your emotions and behavior.

To find these signs, you can use online birth chart calculators. Just make sure you have your birth date and time handy for accurate results.

#8899. B2 Architecture turns North Korean defector testimonies into Prague exhibition

Photography by Radek Šrettr Úlehla

B2 Architecture has created the Life Behind the Walls exhibition in Prague, using a maze of red timber frames and translucent fabric to explore life in North Korea.

The 1,500-square-metre exhibition takes visitors from a bright, interactive installation designed around a children’s book to a darkened gallery featuring portraits and testimonies from North Korean defectors.

B2 Architecture divided the installation into two contrasting environments. The first features a grid of red-painted timber beams, with large sheets of red and pink fabric suspended between the frames to create semi-transparent walls.

The structure forms a maze that visitors can explore, with glimpses of other rooms and activities visible through the fabric.

Illustrated panels, games and interactive activities are fitted into the structure, while photographs by photographer Michal Huniewicz show North Korea as it is presented to the outside world.

Children are encouraged to navigate the maze independently and stop to draw, write and complete activities as they move through the installation.

The displays are based on Tota lítá, a children’s book by North Korean studies scholar and writer Nina Špitálníková, which explains the principles of totalitarianism in language that is accessible to younger readers.

“Children are often given very little space within exhibition formats,” B2 Architecture told Dezeen. “This project consciously challenges that convention.”

The atmosphere changes as visitors pass between two walls displaying photographs of the border between North Korea and China by photographer Tim Franco.

Beyond this threshold, the playful red maze gives way to a dark gallery. This contains black display structures with portraits and personal accounts of people who escaped North Korea, alongside stories of those who did not survive its regime.

Tall, translucent fabric panels printed with shadowy human figures were arranged throughout the space, creating silhouettes that overlap with the portraits displayed behind them.

In a central room, a monumental statue of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un stands on a raised plinth, surrounded by spotlights and theatrical mist.

The temporary installation was constructed using lightweight, modular timber beams and stretched textiles, allowing it to be assembled and dismantled efficiently.

The timber structure was retained for use in another project, while the textiles and flooring were passed on to several theatres for reuse.

Prague-based B2 Architecture was founded by architect Barbara Bencová in 2012 and works across residential and commercial architecture, interiors and public spaces.

Other projects by the studio featured on Dezeen include the DDB Prague office, which features an anamorphic optical illusion that makes the advertising agency’s logo appear complete from a particular viewpoint.

Photography by Radek Šrettr Úlehla

#8898. ways of growing: 20 artists explore plants as design collaborators in lisbon exhibition

20 practitioners utilize bacterial cellulose, living mycelium, plant-dyed textiles, and botanical chemistry to frame plants as active collaborators in design and art.

Haenke edited by christina vergopoulou November 16, 2026 5 min

On view at the Gallery of the Faculty of Fine Arts at the University of Lisbon (FBAUL) through November 28th, 2026, Ways of Growing / Modos de crescer presents works by 20 artists, designers, and researchers examining the intersection of plant biodiversity and material experimentation. Serving as the culmination of the two-year Free Radicals research initiative, led by Haenke (Czech Republic) alongside partners in Portugal, Spain, Armenia, Hungary, and Germany, the exhibition originates from three 2025 field residencies conducted in Galicia’s Courel mountains, a permaculture farm in central Portugal, and northern Armenia’s Lori Mountains.

Rather than treating flora solely as passive raw matter, the exhibited works engage botanical organisms, agricultural byproducts, and local ecologies as active design agents. Material and technical investigations span cyanotypes printed on kombucha-derived bacterial cellulose and toned with plant extracts, bio-composites pairing traditional Portuguese crochet with living mycelium, and textiles woven from chestnut-dyed linen. Additional installations integrate botanical chemistry and digital hardware, including olfactory sculptures formulated from eucalyptus ash and essential oils, plant-based analog film processing, acoustic transmission through organic substrates, and a multimedia system linking historic Armenian herbaria with Raspberry Pi microcomputers. Inaugurated during FBAUL’s 190th anniversary, the exhibition coincides with the release of Free Radicals: Attuning to Plants in Creative Practices (Onomatopee), a publication edited by Sasha Střelcová and Linsey Rendell compiling methodologies from 70 practitioners across design, ecology, and material research.

Elena Falomo’s research-led installation combines field recordings, geographical artefacts and storytelling to question which landscapes are prioritised in responses to climate changeEleonora Edreva’s textile-based poem is woven from vintage linen, chestnut dyes, local language and soundIvana Papić uses ecological fiction to question invasive-species narratives in her experimental video essay imagining a love story between a native chestnut tree and an introduced mimosaAlejandra Díaz-Guerra Acedo’s bio-based textile experiment combines traditional Portuguese crochet with living mycelium, allowing fungi to decompose cotton fabrics buried in contrasting soilsMaria Ilieva’s olfactory compositions trace the lifecycle of eucalyptus from fresh foliage and wildfire to industrial pulp processing and paper productionfood artist and chef Aly Beveridge explores how our proximity to land and ingredients create a bodily intimacy that allows us to reconsider our relationship to foodAdam Kvaček’s performative walk explored the familiar language of recreational tourism to investigate Portugal’s industrial eucalyptus landscapes

name: Ways of Growing / Modos de crescer (Free Radicals)

program: Free Radicals | @freeradicals.space design team: Blanca Allegue, Kač Bártková, Aly Beveridge, Morgane Billuart, Gabriela Carvalho, Alejandra Díaz-Guerra Acedo, Eleonora Edreva, Elena Falomo, Maria Ilieva, Adam Kvaček, Joana Manaia, Jamie McGhee, Ricardo Nugra Madero, Ivana Papić, Béatrice Pépin, Inês Quente, Emilie Rážová, Miguel Tavares, Daria Titova, Yanna Varbanova

lead organization & partners: Haenke (Czech Republic), Quinta das Relvas (Portugal), Fundación Uxío Novoneyra (Spain), Today Art Initiative (Armenia), Pro Progressione (Hungary), Burning Silence (Germany)

venue: Gallery of the Faculty of Fine Arts, University of Lisbon (FBAUL), Lisbon, Portugal

exhibition dates: October 22nd – November 28th, 2026

publication: Free Radicals: Attuning to Plants in Creative Practices (Onomatopee)

publication editors: Sasha Střelcová, Linsey Rendell

support: Co-funded by Creative Europe and the Ministry of Culture of the Czech Republic

#8897. Yoga and Overweight: Health Benefits and Tips for Getting Started

Part of the beauty of yoga is its accessibility for everyone. Yoga practitioners come in all shapes and sizes and are hella modifiable. If you have overweight, there’s 100% a place for you in the world of downward dogs, crescent lunges, and resting pigeons.

Check out these benefits of yoga for overweight.

For wellness, you’d be hard-pressed to find a more holistic practice than yoga. Your physical and mental health can get a boost from busting out your mat.

The limb-stretching, muscle-engaging, bodyweight-bearing nature of yoga has many physical benefits.

For starters, yoga may enhance your metabolism. An older study found that people who practiced had greater metabolic efficiency and lower weight than non-yogis.

It’s clear, too, that yoga’s combo of cardio and strength torches calories. A 160-pound person can burn around 180 calories per hour, popping in and out of poses. A 2021 study revealed that both Hatha and vinyasa yoga led to weight loss, with an average of 3.4 kilograms (7.5 pounds) lost over a 6-month.

Extra strength and flexibility are two other well-known upsides of the practice. Research shows that even sedentary folks can build these elements of fitness by taking up yoga. One study showed that, after 8 weeks of practicing at least twice a week (180 minutes), people with no prior yoga experience had greater muscle strength, endurance, flexibility, and cardio-respiratory fitness.

On the surface, yoga might look like mere stretching — but the practice goes far beyond the physical. Yoga engages the mind in all sorts of ways that may have benefits for overweight.

By training your brain toward calm and focus, yoga sessions encourage mindfulness. A mindful outlook can have far-reaching effects in multiple areas of life, like promoting mindful eating and greater body awareness.

As a form of self-care, yoga can also promote a healthier body image. In a 2018 study, young adults who made it a habit reported higher satisfaction levels with their bodies. Better self-esteem and motivation have also been linked to the practice.

Then, too, yoga’s stress-relieving effects might follow you off the mat and into the dining room. Some research has found that people who do yoga binge eat less often.

Wanna get started with yoga but aren’t sure how? We got you.

It all starts with setting realistic goals and expectations. If you’ve never practiced before, you won’t be pretzel-ing yourself into challenging poses like scorpion or crow overnight — and that’s OK. Consider setting smaller, step-wise goals, such as attending a 30-minute class twice a week or mastering a few basic poses. Little by little, you’ll work your way up to a more advanced practice.

It’s also wise to select a class (or video) for beginners. Check your gym or yoga studio’s schedule for introductory sessions, and don’t be afraid to let an instructor know before class that you may need some modifications. Most are happy to provide adaptations to make the class a better experience for beginners.

Meanwhile, if you’re pursuing a yoga practice for weight loss, remember to pair it with other healthy lifestyle practices for best results. Though stretching and holding poses burn calories, yoga might not take you to your weight loss goal alone. A balanced diet, cardio exercise, and sufficient sleep are other keys to achieving a healthy weight.

Yoga stereotypes of scantily clad gym babes in impossible contortions might make you feel somewhat intimidated about in-person classes. If you’re concerned that a gym session will make you self-conscious, start with an at-home practice. (YouTube is a treasure trove of classes and instructors explicitly geared for people with overweight.) All by yourself in your living room, there’s no one to impress.

Or, if you’re up for in-person yoga, let your instructor know your needs again. Modifications are always possible.

No matter where you practice, credit yourself for showing up for your health. And, at the beginning of your session, don’t forget to set an intention you find motivating or encouraging, such as “I am caring for my body” or “I am worthy of love and respect.”

Overweight doesn’t have to be a barrier to taking up yoga. Start small, knowing that you’ll get more comfortable with each session. With all the physical and mental health benefits a yoga practice provides — and all the modifications that make it more accessible — it’s worth a try, regardless of weight.

#8896. Eight highlights from this year's Sharjah Architecture Triennial

The third Sharjah Architecture Triennial focuses on the myriad ways architecture can be understood through the lens of anthropology. Here are our highlights from the event, including installations and exhibitions.

Curated by anthropologist Vyjayanthi Rao, this year’s edition was centred on the theme Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures.

Rao said the 2026 Sharjah Architecture Triennial, which takes place over five months, will invite discourse about the different ways cities and urban life can be imagined.

“Though I’m not an architect, I’m literally talking to students day in and day out about how they see the world, and how that translates into the practice,” Rao told Dezeen.

“Being an academic, you’re always asked to define yourself in terms of your discipline,” she continued. “It doesn’t make sense to limit yourself, especially when you are in the practice of life.”

“You’re learning from people about the ways in which they live – that’s what I do as an anthropologist, and I think that’s what a lot of architects do because they’re inspired to build for people and the places that they inhabit and thrive in.”

Read on for eight highlights from this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial.

Artist Curry J Hackett created this draping shelter spanning the width of the Old Al Jubail Vegetable Market in homage to the Black community in Virginia’s Prince Edward County, which created improvised learning spaces when schools closed during the Civil Rights Movement.

Videos play in the former stalls at either end of the fabric enclosure, screening archival images of the period, as well as images of Rosenwald Schools – the community-building initiative that established thousands of schools for Black children in the South.

“Rather than integrate, schools closed for five years, and leading up to that, schools were dealing with a lot of overcrowding,” Hackett told Dezeen. “The county begrudgingly funded ‘tar paper shacks’, which were shoddy, demoralising structures, to ease overcrowding, and that’s what you’re seeing interpreted here,” he continued.

“Interspersed sonically and visually throughout the installation is a mashing up of the local story of my home town in Virginia with the regional story of the Rosenwald Schools in the South – their architectural rethinking of materials and retelling the history.”

Research and construction studio Abari showcased a tent-like structure made from a bamboo frame, which was limited in size due to difficulties with material regulations.

The structure is one module of a larger pavilion that was constructed in Nepal, designed as a travelling venue to host bamboo weaving workshops.

“We were not able to create an installation here in the UAE, partly because Abari’s work is based on building with bamboo, and the difficulty with this project was that the global supply chain and its regulations could not be met within the timeframe,” said Rao.

“What you see here is one repeatable module of a pavilion that is currently moving within different communities in Nepal – we improvised and decided Sharjah would travel to Nepal, and we’d just have a piece of it here in this exhibition.”

Drawing upon her fieldwork in Sharjah, Palestinian architect Samar Halloum designed a brick pavilion that was shaded overhead by a draping fabric canopy.

In reference to the historical public drinking-water structures in the Gulf region, Sabeel Negotiated features a water fountain and wooden stools for people to gather around.

According to Rao, the strikes by Iran on countries in the Middle East in February disrupted brick supply in the United Arab Emirates, so Halloum redesigned the pavilion with cloth-filled bricks.

“One of the shortages was bricks because they come from Saudi Arabia, and the factory stopped producing bricks,” said Rao. “There were some leftover bales of cloth from another installation, so Halloum used those bales and cast them in resin, so you’ll see some of the bricks in the installation are actually made of cloth.”

History as Repair: Documenting Karachi by Kishwar Rizvi

This exhibition by art historian Kishwar Rizvi explores how colonised communities in Karachi, Pakistan, took ownership of their urban environment by adapting architectural styles, from European classicism to Mughal-inspired ornament.

Through maps, photographs, sketches and interviews, it aims to shine a light on an architectural history at risk of being forgotten.

The exhibition argues for the protection of colonial-era buildings in Karachi, which are under threat of demolition due to neglect.

Patch-Time by Hiba Bou Akar, Mohamad Hafeda and Nathalie Harb

The Patch-Time installation is a collaboration between researchers Hiba Bou Akar and Mohamad Hafeda and artist Nathalie Harb that explores the displacement of people in Lebanon, from the 1970s to the present day, through the materials used to protect and repair homes.

In workshops organised by Lebanese non-profit Ahla Fawda, displaced women crocheted tarpaulin, sand-bag cloth and sheeting into panels that form a canopy displayed in a courtyard at the triennial’s Al Qasimiyah School venue.

Underneath the canopy, a table made from breeze blocks, wood and a central mirror displays fabric artwork and the stories of women and children affected by war.

“We worked on two levels: one that is the collective, and one that is more of the individual, looking at how people shelter their home through war adversity and displacement,” said Harb. “We asked [the women] what their relationship to their home was, and in the pieces, you see how it changes from generation to generation with their relationship to material.”

After Night There is Nothing by Mohamad Nahleh and Ozayr Saloojee

Architect Mohamad Nahleh and architecture professor Ozayr Saloojee designed a giant globe of the night sky and split it into three parts, which were scattered across different locations at the triennale.

The outer shells of the curved structures are wrapped in thatch, while the interiors feature vinyl surfaces with designs showing man-made military objects in the sky reimagined as creature-like constellations.

“This is ‘night sky optimism’ – optimism through catastrophe,” said Nahleh. “The night sky we are talking about in this project is not the sky of beautiful stars and constellations, but the contemporary sky filled with drones, satellites, rockets and missiles that are changing the way we understand the sky above us.”

“We have noticed in our research that, especially in geographies witnessing prolonged violence, these objects are producing new mythical creatures,” he continued. “We think of these creatures as ones that attempt to tame the military brightness that is populating the sky around us.”

Kuwaiti designer Badriyah Alsalem plotted 41 medieval Arabic poetic names for the sun as cut-outs on the astronomical graph that forms a circular canopy over her pavilion, As the Sun Rests.

Forming patterns of shadow in the sand below, three of the suns were embroidered in red, depicting the sharaq rising sun, saqa’a noon sun and gharab setting sun, while markers on the ground show where these canopy highlights will fall on different dates during the triennial.

“If you look up, you see the static data visualisation, and if you look down, it is animated by the sun itself, so it becomes an analogue device to read this historical data,” said Alsalem.

Lalla Alwyia Khalwa by Ziad Jamaleddine, Makram el Kadi, Iheb Guermazi and Beya Othmani

Situated on Sharjah’s Al Khan Open Beach, Lalla Alwyia Khalwa is an installation designed as a place for reflection away from the busy city, dedicated to the saint Lalla Alwyia Kasserine.

Dried plants form a grid of columns on a raised platform for visitors to walk through. Stone slabs on the floor mark places of pause, and a metal stool provides a reflective space to listen to the accompanying sound installation.

“We chose the beach because it is already a space for retreat, so this is a retreat inside a retreat,” said the design team, Ziad Jamaleddine, Makram el Kadi, Iheb Guermazi and Beya Othmani.

“We carved a series of spaces – one for prayer, one for sitting, and a courtyard to enjoy the sky.”

Sharjah Architecture Triennial 2026 takes place from 14 November 2026 to 14 April 2027 at various locations across Sharjah, UAE. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

#8895. Starvation Mode: How Caloric Restriction Affects Your Body

Cutting back on calories but not losing weight? You might wonder if you’ve gotten stuck in the twilight zone of so-called “starvation mode.”

Everyone from your personal trainer to your grandma may have warned you about this metabolic frenemy that keeps your body holding onto weight. But is starvation mode really a thing — or just an urban legend?

The concept of starvation mode is that when you restrict calories, your body has a “hold it right there” response. To prevent you from losing weight rapidly, your metabolism slows, conserving energy by reducing the calories it burns.

Research shows starvation mode — formally called adaptive thermogenesis or metabolic adaptation — is a legit phenomenon. It’s well documented that sometimes, the more weight you lose (and the more rapidly you do so), the more your body resists the process.

Evolutionarily speaking, this may be a holdover from when humans faced food scarcity and needed a mechanism for self-preservation. But in today’s world, starvation mode can be a frustrating roadblock to weight loss.

What does this metabolic hiccup look like? These symptoms may indicate that starvation mode is becoming a problem for your health:

Starvation mode isn’t the same thing as actual starving. In today’s modern food environment, true starvation is rare. If you’re eating regularly, you won’t experience life-threatening starvation.

However, your body might exhibit some of the same early signs as real starvation. These include the symptoms listed above.

Most commonly, though, starvation mode involves stalled weight loss. You may have hit the wall of adaptive thermogenesis when restricting calories and increasing physical activity without losing weight.

Getting into starvation mode can take just a few days, especially if those days involve severe calorie restriction.

So what counts as severe calorie restriction? Many experts advise not going below 1,200 calories per day for women and 1,500 calories per day for men unless supervised by a doctor. Anything below these numbers could land you in starvation mode faster.

Fortunately, getting your body out of starvation mode isn’t complicated.

First, there’s the obvious solution: Eat a few more calories. But we don’t mean just any calories. By adding a few more nutrient-dense foods (especially those with fiber and protein), you may find weight loss becomes easier, not harder. Both of these nutrients have links to weight loss — so they might help you get out of starvation mode without gaining weight.

If you’re feeling extremely depleted, you might take a temporary break from a weight loss diet to replenish your nutrient stores.

Choosing the proper exercise could also bump you out of starvation mode. Resistance exercises like weightlifting, yoga, push-ups, squats, and others build muscle, which increases your metabolic rate.

According to a 2014 study, people who participated in a 9-month resistance exercise program increased their resting metabolic rate — aka how many calories they burned at rest — by an average of 5%.

Weight loss is a balancing act. It’s normal to experience physical and emotional ups and downs.

That said, it’s time to see a doctor if you’re noticing symptoms like extreme fatigue or lethargy, constipation that lasts more than a few days, sensitivity to cold, or unusual mood changes. Your healthcare team can help you hit the sweet spot of weight loss without lingering in starvation mode.

Despite its name, being in starvation mode doesn’t mean you’ll starve. Instead, it’s a state in which your body has adapted to your weight loss efforts, giving you pushback on how many calories it burns. With strategies like tweaking your calorie intake and adding strength training, you can get out of this mode and back on the path to sustained weight loss.

Last medically reviewed on August 31, 2024
